title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
應天府鄉試錄序
粤自
天厭胡元之穢以天下全畀我
聖祖拓帝王之舊開太平之原于
茲有國盖亦遠矣自我
聖祖洪武甲子參酌成周選舉之
意爰定鄉試之科
===
詔天下凡三歲一舉行焉豐茂
世之規闢延英之路于茲得
人盖亦盛矣而
南畿視天下尤先焉維是金陵
諸郡渾淪靈淑之氣始秘于
一隅偏安之陋繼熏于百年
腥羶之阨而不得不濬發于

粤自天厭胡元之穢，以天下全畀我聖祖，拓帝王之舊，開太平之原，于茲有國，盖亦遠矣。自我聖祖洪武甲子，參酌成周選舉之意，爰定鄉試之科，詔天下凡三歲一舉行焉，豐茂世之規，闢延英之路，于茲得人，盖亦盛矣。而南畿視天下尤先焉。維是金陵諸郡，渾淪靈淑之氣，始秘于一隅偏安之陋，繼熏于百年腥羶之阨，而不得不濬發于
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Ever since Heaven, loathing the filth of the barbarian Yuan, bestowed all the realm upon our Sagely Founder, he extended the heritage of emperors and kings and opened the wellspring of Great Peace. Our dynasty has now endured for a considerable time. In the jiazi year of the Hongwu reign (1384), our Sagely Founder considered the principles underlying selection and appointment under the Zhou and established the Provincial Examination, decreeing that it be held throughout the realm once every three years. This enriched the institutions of a flourishing age [?] and opened a path for inviting worthy men into service. The men obtained through it have indeed been numerous. And the Southern Metropolitan Region stands foremost in this respect throughout the realm. In the prefectures of Jinling, the undivided vital force of spiritual potency and excellence was first concealed within the narrow confines of regimes content to hold one corner of the realm, then steeped in a century of adversity reeking of raw flesh and mutton. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
我
聖祖龍興之地其勢然也廼正德
丙子秋八月復當天下鄉試
之期應天府臣先事以考試
官
請
上特命侍講學士臣廷相左諭德臣
===
仁和往柄其事臣等祗奉
明命兼程而南至則府臣所聘
同考諸臣咸集曁臣等偕之
入院精白將事罔敢怠遑於
是合諸士之須試者凡二千
六百五十人恪遵故事而三
試之拔其尤者一百三十有

punctuated:
我聖祖龍興之地，其勢然也。廼正德丙子秋八月，復當天下鄉試之期，應天府臣先事以考試官請，上特命侍講學士臣廷相、左諭德臣仁和往柄其事。
臣等祗奉明命，兼程而南。至則府臣所聘同考諸臣咸集，曁臣等偕之入院，精白將事，罔敢怠遑。於是合諸士之須試者，凡二千六百五十人，恪遵故事而三試之，拔其尤者一百三十有
translation_en:
…in the land where our sagely founding emperor rose to power: such was the inevitable course of events. In the eighth month of autumn in the bingzi year of the Zhengde reign [1516], the time once again arrived for the Provincial Examinations throughout the empire. The officials of Yingtian Prefecture submitted an advance request for Examiners. His Majesty specially commanded your servant Tingxiang, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, and your servant Renhe, Left Admonisher, to go and preside over the examination.
We reverently received the august command and traveled south with all haste. When we arrived, the Associate Examiners engaged by the prefectural officials had all assembled. Together we entered the examination compound and conducted our duties with utmost purity of purpose, daring neither to slacken nor to take our ease. We assembled all the candidates awaiting examination, 2,650 men in total, and, scrupulously following established precedent, examined them in three sessions. From among them we selected the most outstanding, numbering one hundred and thirty-…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
五人并刻其文之純者為錄
以
獻增
朝廷之榮華昭
聖德之風化傳示四方嘉勵来學
蓋我
祖宗圖治之典莫大于是而臣等
===
所以區區勉圖報稱于萬一
者亦孰有過于此哉錄成臣
〔廷相〕當序諸首簡竊嘗究觀篇
籍凡唐虞三代以上先正之
所以流榮顯號于世者遐哉
邈乎不可得而班已蓋自吾
夫子刪述六學之後為士者

五人，并刻其文之純者為錄，以獻，增朝廷之榮華，昭聖德之風化，傳示四方，嘉勵来學。蓋我祖宗圖治之典，莫大于是，而臣等所以區區勉圖報稱于萬一者，亦孰有過于此哉？
錄成，臣〔廷相〕當序諸首簡。竊嘗究觀篇籍，凡唐虞三代以上先正之所以流榮顯號于世者，遐哉邈乎，不可得而班已。蓋自吾夫子刪述六學之後，為士者
translation_en:
…five men, and we also had the finest of their compositions engraved and compiled into a record for presentation to the throne, to enhance the court’s glory, make manifest the transforming influence of Your Majesty’s sagely virtue, circulate examples throughout the realm, and commend and encourage future students. Among our imperial ancestors’ institutions for securing good government, none is greater than this. And in our humble efforts to repay even one ten-thousandth of the imperial favor, what could surpass this?
When the record was completed, I, your servant Tingxiang 〔廷相〕, was charged with writing a preface on its opening leaves. I have ventured to examine the ancient writings closely. As for the means by which the worthy men of old, from the eras of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties and earlier, transmitted their glory and made their names illustrious in the world, these are so distant and remote that they can no longer be set out in order [?]. Since our Master Confucius edited and transmitted the six branches of classical learning, those who pursued the scholar’s calling…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
□知脩其經術殊師異習各
蘄表見于世而一切縱橫捭
闔刑名之學大氏皆寢不弗
舉抑而靡揚矣然夷考專門
之學莫盛于漢建元以後蓋
其去古未遠先王遺風餘澤

punctuated: □知脩其經術，殊師異習，各蘄表見于世，而一切縱橫捭闔、刑名之學，大氏皆寢不弗舉，抑而靡揚矣。然夷考專門之學，莫盛于漢建元以後。蓋其去古未遠，先王遺風餘澤猶有存者，而上之人又規恢而作厲之，故在當時，疇人子弟各守一經，終身誦習，靡不安焉。如魏相以《易》《禮》輔孝宣，董仲舒以《春秋》匡孝武，王式以三百篇箴昌邑，夏侯勝以《尚書》授東宮，口誦心惟，率皆一物，故其所成卓然為□□
translation_en: …[illegible] knew to cultivate their learning in the classics. Following different teachers and distinct traditions of study, each sought to distinguish himself in the world. Meanwhile, all the arts of diplomatic maneuvering and persuasion, and the learning of punishments and administrative accountability, generally fell into abeyance [?], suppressed rather than promoted. Yet, upon careful examination, specialized study of the classics was never more flourishing than in the Han dynasty from the Jianyuan reign onward. This was because antiquity was not yet far removed: something of the inherited influence and beneficent legacy of the former kings still survived, while those above further broadened and encouraged such learning. Thus, at that time, the sons and younger kinsmen of hereditary specialists each devoted themselves to a single classic, reciting and studying it throughout their lives, all content in that pursuit. For example, Wei Xiang assisted Emperor Xiaoxuan through the Changes and the Rites; Dong Zhongshu guided Emperor Xiaowu through the Spring and Autumn Annals; Wang Shi admonished the Prince of Changyi through the Three Hundred Poems; and Xiahou Sheng taught the Book of Documents to the crown prince. What they recited aloud and pondered in their hearts was, in general, a single subject. Hence their accomplishments were outstanding, making them [two illegible characters]…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
焉逮及隋唐始依緣古道設
科取士然亦不能純用經術
詞華是競心耳淺薄六學從
此微矣有宋百有餘年群儒
輩出講明羽翼而後吾先王
所以治天下之大經大法煥
然以明矣顧其時甫好而輒
===
疎方崇而遽禁君子不無遺
憾焉施我
明興
聖祖
神宗所以尊重經術嘉禮學士大
夫之意又過前代遠甚
今上皇帝篤于繼述尤惓惓焉茲

punctuated: 焉。逮及隋唐，始依緣古道，設科取士，然亦不能純用經術，詞華是競，心耳淺薄，六學從此微矣。有宋百有餘年，群儒輩出，講明羽翼，而後吾先王所以治天下之大經大法煥然以明矣。顧其時甫好而輒疎，方崇而遽禁，君子不無遺憾焉。施我明興，聖祖神宗所以尊重經術、嘉禮學士大夫之意，又過前代遠甚。今上皇帝篤于繼述，尤惓惓焉。茲
translation_en:
… By the Sui and Tang dynasties, men began to draw upon ancient precedents and establish examination categories for recruiting officials. Yet they could not rely exclusively upon classical learning: literary ornament became the object of competition, minds and ears grew shallow, and the six branches of learning declined from this point onward. After more than a hundred years of the Song dynasty, Confucian scholars emerged in succession, elucidating and advancing the teachings. Only then did the great guiding principles and laws by which our former kings had governed the realm shine forth clearly. Yet in those times, scarcely had such learning gained favor before it was neglected; just as it was being honored, it was abruptly prohibited. Gentlemen could not but regret this.

When our Ming arose [reading 施 as “when,” uncertain], its sagely founding and divine ancestral emperors showed a commitment to honoring classical learning and treating scholars and scholar-officials with gracious ceremony that far surpassed previous dynasties. His Majesty the present Emperor, devoted to carrying forward their work, is especially solicitous in this regard. Now …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
爾諸士裒然為有司舉首值
文教攸先之所有同升諸公之
期其尚豫思行其所學以答
我
列聖慇懃期待之厚望也哉是故
治易及禮必如相若京房以
術數取敗戴聖以不法見尤
===
吾無望焉治春秋必如仲舒
若公孫弘之欺世呂步舒之
慘刻吾無望焉治詩必如式
若申公之無益治亂匡衡之
持禄保位吾無望焉治尚書
必如勝若歐陽歙之受賕而
敗李尋之嗜烖而流吾無望

我

punctuated: 爾諸士裒然為有司舉，首值文教攸先之所，有同升諸公之期，其尚豫思行其所學，以答我列聖慇懃期待之厚望也哉！是故治《易》及《禮》，必如相；若京房以術數取敗，戴聖以不法見尤，吾無望焉。治《春秋》，必如仲舒；若公孫弘之欺世，呂步舒之慘刻，吾無望焉。治《詩》，必如式；若申公之無益治亂，匡衡之持禄保位，吾無望焉。治《尚書》，必如勝；若歐陽歙之受賕而敗，李尋之嗜烖而流，吾無望
translation_en:
…you gentlemen have been selected together by the responsible officials, here in this place where cultural instruction takes precedence, with the prospect of advancing together to the court. You should even now consider how to put your learning into practice, thereby answering the great hopes that our successive sage emperors have so earnestly placed in you!

Thus, those who study the Book of Changes and the Book of Rites must emulate Xiang. If, like Jing Fang, they bring ruin upon themselves through divinatory techniques, or, like Dai Sheng, incur censure for unlawful conduct, I have no hope for them. Those who study the Spring and Autumn Annals must emulate Zhongshu. If they deceive the world like Gongsun Hong, or act with cruel severity like Lü Bushu, I have no hope for them. Those who study the Book of Odes must emulate Shi. If, like Master Shen, they contribute nothing to securing order or remedying disorder, or, like Kuang Heng, merely cling to their salaries and safeguard their positions, I have no hope for them. Those who study the Book of Documents must emulate Sheng. If, like Ouyang Xi, they take bribes and meet with ruin, or, like Li Xun, become obsessed with calamity portents and suffer exile, I have no hope…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
焉若然庶不負我
國家開科之意而臣等奉
命求賢之責亦或可以少塞于
他日矣爾諸士其尚勗之哉
或者謂
今治化隆盛遠配唐虞三代而
皇上特輟經帷法從之臣不遠數
===
千里而來者亦惟豫求所謂
唐虞三代之佐焉耳矣是奚
取于炎漢諸臣若彼云云而
已哉噫不然凡臣之所論盖
就其所業者云耳若繇此而
進之與咎繇稷契伊傅周召
之儔齊隆等盛固諸士子之

焉。若然，庶不負我國家開科之意，而臣等奉命求賢之責，亦或可以少塞于他日矣。爾諸士其尚勗之哉！
或者謂：「今治化隆盛，遠配唐虞三代，而皇上特輟經帷法從之臣，不遠數千里而來者，亦惟豫求所謂唐虞三代之佐焉耳矣。是奚取于炎漢諸臣若彼云云而已哉？」噫！不然。凡臣之所論，盖就其所業者云耳。若繇此而進之，與咎繇、稷、契、伊、傅、周、召之儔齊隆等盛，固諸士子之
translation_en:
…in them. If this is so, we may hope not to disappoint our dynasty’s intention in holding the examinations; and we, your servants, may perhaps in days to come discharge in some small measure our duty to seek worthy men under imperial command. You candidates, strive toward this!
Some might say: “Today, government and moral transformation flourish, matching the distant ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. His Majesty has specially released ministers serving at the Classics Mat and in his immediate entourage to come here, undeterred by a journey of several thousand li, solely to seek in advance men like the assistants of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Why, then, draw only upon those ministers of the Han, the dynasty of Fire, discussing them as you have done?” Ah, this is not so! Everything that I, your servant, have discussed has concerned only the particular studies in which those men engaged. As for advancing from this foundation to equal the eminence and flourishing achievements of such men as Gao Yao, Ji, Xie, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao, that surely rests with the candidates’ …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
趨向若何而非臣等之所敢
知也然自
今日稽古右文而觀之則唐虞
三代之佐臣等詎敢謂必無
其人哉是舉也提調則應天
府尹臣宸府丞臣斌監試則
監察御史臣珮臣崧同考則

趨向若何，而非臣等之所敢知也。然自今日稽古右文而觀之，則唐虞三代之佐，臣等詎敢謂必無其人哉？是舉也，提調則應天府尹臣宸、府丞臣斌；監試則監察御史臣珮、臣崧；同考則教授臣昆，學正臣麟、臣惟遠、臣維新，教諭臣甫山、臣坤、臣鳴鳳、臣應禎、臣朝穀。其諸執事姓名巳具載錄中，故不著。
翰林院侍講學士、奉訓大夫李廷相謹序。
translation_en:
…what direction their aspirations may take is something we, your servants, dare not presume to know. Yet, considering how the present reign studies antiquity and honors literary learning, how could we dare assert that there are necessarily no men comparable to the ministerial helpers of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties?
For this examination, the Proctors were your servants Chen, Prefect of Yingtian, and Bin, Vice Prefect. Oversight of the examination was entrusted to your servants Pei and Song, Investigating Censors. The Associate Examiners were your servant Kun, a prefectural school Instructor; your servants Lin, Weiyuan, and Weixin, School Instructors; and your servants Fushan, Kun, Mingfeng, Yingzhen, and Chaogu, county school Instructors. The names of the other functionaries have already been fully recorded in this examination record and are therefore not repeated here.
Preface respectfully composed by Li Tingxiang, Expositor-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Rendering Instruction.

Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination, Eleventh Year of Zhengde (1516)

Proctors

Wang Chen, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel and Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Juzhan; he held official household registration in the Shenwu Right Guard and was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the gengxu year.

Zhao Bin, Grand Master for Medial Compliance and Prefectural Aide of Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Shixian; he held official household registration in Pingliang Guard, Shaanxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiwei year [?; transcribed as 巳未].

Examiners

Li Tingxiang, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Instructional Service. His courtesy name was Mengbi; he was from Puzhou, Shandong, and was a metropolitan graduate of the renxu year.

Wen Renhe, Grand Master for Instructional Service and Left Mentor of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Minhuai; he was from Huayang County, Sichuan, and was a metropolitan graduate of the renxu year.

Associate Examiners

Liu Kun, Professor of the Confucian School of Nanyang Prefecture, Henan. His courtesy name was Yufu; he was from Guizhou Guard and was a tribute scholar (gongshi) of the jiazi year.

Xiao Lin, Instructor of the Confucian School of Dingzhou, Zhending Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Naizhen; he was from Xinye County, Henan, and was a tribute scholar of the jiazi year.

Luo Weiyuan, Instructor of the Confucian School of Deqing Subprefecture, Zhaoqing Prefecture, Guangdong. His courtesy name was Mingzhi; he was from Min County, Fujian, and was a tribute scholar of the xinyou year.

Zheng Weixin, Instructor of the Confucian School of Dongping Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong. His courtesy name was Jingfu; he was from Guishan County, Guangdong, and was a tribute scholar of the jiazi year.

Yang Fushan, Instructor of the Confucian School of Qi County, Weihui Prefecture, Henan. His courtesy name was Dejing; he was from Qingyuan County, Zhili, and was a tribute scholar of the dingmao year.

Xiao Kun, Instructor of the Confucian School of Wei County, Daming Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Maozhen; he was from Shunde County, Guangdong, and was a tribute scholar of the yimao year.

Zhao Mingfeng, Instructor of the Confucian School of Anyang County, Zhangde Prefecture, Henan. His courtesy name was Yuqi; he was from Xianning County, Shaanxi, and was a tribute scholar of the gengwu year.

Gao Yingzhen, Instructor of the Confucian School of Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Zhenfu; he was from Min County, Fujian, and was a tribute scholar of the dingmao year.

He Chaoyi, Instructor of the Confucian School of Shangrao County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Tingshan; he was from Haiyang County, Guangdong, and was a tribute scholar of the dingmao year.

Patrol Officials

Ni Ying, General of Manifest Might (Mingwei Jiangjun), was Assistant Commander of the Nanjing Left Palace Guard. His courtesy name was Shijie, and he was from Jiangyin County, Zhili.

Yang Xi, General of Manifest Might (Mingwei Jiangjun), was Assistant Commander of the Nanjing Front Palace Guard. His courtesy name was Tingyu, and he was from Changli County, Zhili.

Search Officials

Fang Hao, General of Martial Virtue (Wude Jiangjun), was Battalion Commander of the Nanjing Central Palace Guard. His courtesy name was Jinghong, and he was from Shanyang County, Zhili.

Zhai Jizu, General of Military Strategy (Wulüe Jiangjun), was Vice Battalion Commander of the Nanjing Rear Palace Guard. His courtesy name was Zongben, and he was from Datong County, Shanxi.

Wu Yuan, Commandant of Manifest Fidelity (Zhaoxin Xiaowei), was Company Commander of the Nanjing Front Palace Guard. His courtesy name was Daben, and he was from Anlu Subprefecture, Huguang.

Liu Yu, Commandant of Manifest Fidelity (Zhaoxin Xiaowei), was Company Commander of the Nanjing Rear Palace Guard. His courtesy name was Yongzhao, and he was from Baode Subprefecture, Shanxi.

Provisioning Officials

Shi Bomin, Gentleman for Attending to Service (Congshi Lang), was Registrar in the Registry of Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Xuezhi; he was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, and was a student admitted by virtue of an official relative’s status (guansheng).

Li Hao, Gentleman for Upright Service (Chengzhi Lang), was Magistrate of Shangyuan County, Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Weizhi; he was from Lu Subprefecture, Shanxi, and was a tribute student of the renzi year.

Wu Shijun was Magistrate of Jiangning County, Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Shiying; he was from Nanhai County, Guangdong, and was a tribute student of the yimao year.

Wang Chang, Gentleman for Undertaking Service (Chengshi Lang), was Vice Magistrate of Shangyuan County, Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Shirong; he was from Laiyang County, Shandong, and was an Imperial University student.

Qin Hong, Gentleman for Undertaking Service (Chengshi Lang), was Vice Magistrate of Jiangning County, Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Jiuxiao; he was from Gui Subprefecture, Huguang, and was an Imperial University student.

Yan Lan was Station Master of the Jiangdong Horse Relay Station, Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Ruguan; he was from Jiang Subprefecture, Shanxi, and had served as a Runner (chengchai).

Zhang Huai was Station Master of the Longjiang Water and Horse Relay Station, Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Chaoyong; he was from Wuding Subprefecture, Shandong, and had served as a Runner (chengchai).

Zhang Qi was Station Master of the Dasheng Relay Station in Jiangning County, Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Tingzhen; he was from Mayi County in Shuo Subprefecture, Shanxi, and had served as a Runner (chengchai).

Shi Jing was Station Master of the Longtan Water and Horse Relay Station in Jurong County, Yingtian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Tingbiao; he was from Xianning County, Shaanxi, and had served as a Runner (chengchai).

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

述而不作，信而好古，竊比於我老彭。

故至誠無息。不息則久，久則徵，徵則悠遠，悠遠則博厚，博厚則高明。

布帛長短同，則賈相若；麻縷絲絮輕重同，則賈相若；五穀多寡同，則賈相若；屨大小同，則賈相若。曰：「夫物之不齊，物之情也。」

易

顯比之吉，位正中也。

九三：井渫不食，為我心惻；可用汲，王明，並受其福。

易者，象也；象也者，像也。

變動不居，周流六虛，上下无常，剛柔相易。

書

食哉惟時，柔遠能邇，惇德允元，而難任人，蠻夷率服。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“I transmit but do not create; I trust in and cherish antiquity. I venture privately to compare myself to our Old Peng.”

“Thus perfect sincerity never ceases. Never ceasing, it endures; enduring, it becomes manifest; becoming manifest, it extends far and long; extending far and long, it becomes broad and substantial; broad and substantial, it becomes lofty and luminous.”

“If lengths of linen and silk are the same, their prices should be similar; if hemp thread and silk floss are the same in weight, their prices should be similar; if quantities of the five grains are the same, their prices should be similar; if shoes are the same in size, their prices should be similar.” He replied: “That things differ is inherent in their nature.”

Book of Changes

“The good fortune of manifest union arises from the position being correct and central.”

“Nine in the third place: The well has been cleared, but no one drinks from it; this grieves my heart. Its water can be drawn. If the king is enlightened, all will share in its blessings.”

“The Changes consists of images; images are likenesses.”

“Changing and moving without rest, they circulate through the six vacant positions. Their ascent and descent follow no fixed rule; the firm and the yielding exchange places.”

Book of Documents

“Food! Attend to it at the proper seasons. Deal gently with those afar and conciliate those nearby; esteem the virtuous and trust the good, but keep flatterers at a distance. The Man and Yi peoples all submit.”

punctuated:
惟尹躬曁湯咸有一德，克享天心，受天明命，以有九有之師。
弘于天若，德裕乃身，不廢在王命。
惟敬五刑，以成三德。一人有慶，兆民賴之，其寧惟永。

詩
有杕之杜，生于道左。彼君子兮，噬肯適我？中心好之，曷飲食之？
維南有箕，不可以簸揚；維北有斗，不可以挹酒漿。維南有箕，載翕其舌；維北有斗，西柄之揭。
匪手携之，言示之事；匪面命之，言提其耳。
明明魯侯，克明其德。旣作泮宫，淮夷攸服。矯矯虎臣，在泮獻馘。淑問如皐陶，在泮獻囚。濟濟多士，克廣德心。桓桓于征，狄彼東南。烝烝皇皇，不吳不揚，不告于訩。在泮獻功。角弓其觼，束矢其搜。戎車孔博，徒御無斁。旣克淮夷，孔淑不逆，式固
translation_en:
Yi Yin himself and Tang both possessed a single, undivided virtue. They were able to win Heaven’s favor and receive Heaven’s illustrious mandate, thereby coming to possess the multitudes of the nine regions.
Be great in following Heaven; let virtue enrich your person, and do not neglect the king’s commands.
Reverently administer the five punishments, thereby perfecting the three virtues. When the One Man—the ruler—enjoys blessings, the myriad people benefit from them, and their peace will endure forever.

The Book of Odes
A solitary pear tree grows to the left of the road. That gentleman—would he consent to visit me? I cherish him in my heart; how shall I give him food and drink?
In the south is the Winnowing Basket, yet it cannot winnow grain; in the north is the Dipper, yet it cannot ladle wine or other drinks. In the south is the Winnowing Basket, spreading its tongue; in the north is the Dipper, raising its handle westward.
Not merely taking him by the hand, but showing him how things are done; not merely instructing him face to face, but pulling him by the ear.
Illustrious is the Marquis of Lu, able to manifest his virtue. Once he had built the Pan school, the Huai Yi submitted. His mighty, tiger-like warriors presented severed ears at Pan. Skilled in questioning, like Gao Yao, they presented captives at Pan. The numerous worthy officers were able to enlarge their virtuous hearts. Valiant on campaign, they subdued those southeastern lands. Advancing in multitudes, splendid in bearing, they were neither clamorous nor boastful, nor did they resort to contentious accusations. At Pan they presented the fruits of their victories. Their horn bows had buckles [?], and their bundles of arrows were gathered in order. Their war chariots were very broad; their foot soldiers and charioteers were tireless. Having conquered the Huai Yi, they were thoroughly good and met no resistance, thereby making firm …

爾猶，淮夷卒獲。翩彼飛鴞，集于泮林；食我桑黮，懷我好音。憬彼淮夷，來獻其琛：元龜象齒，大賂南金。

《春秋》
初獻六羽。隱公五年。春王正月，作三軍。襄公十一年。
夏六月，公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、鄭伯，同盟于幽。莊公二十七年。冬十有二月，公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、邢侯、曹伯于淮。僖公十六年。春王正月，宋公、曹伯、衛人、邾人伐齊。五月戊寅，宋師及齊師戰于甗，齊師敗績。俱僖公十八年。五月癸丑，公會晉侯、齊侯、宋公、蔡侯、鄭伯、衛子、莒子，盟于踐土。冬，公會晉侯、齊侯、宋公、蔡侯、鄭伯、陳子、莒子、邾子、秦人于溫。俱僖公二十八年。春王二月，秦人入滑。夏四月辛巳，晉人及姜戎敗秦于殽。俱僖公三十三年。
translation_en:
…your plans, and the Huai tribes will finally be subdued. Those owls flying lightly alight in the woods of the Pan school. They eat our mulberries and cherish our pleasing sounds. Those distant Huai tribes come to offer their treasures: great tortoise shells and elephant tusks, and rich gifts of metal from the south.

Spring and Autumn Annals
For the first time, six ranks of feather dancers were presented. Fifth year of Duke Yin. In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, three armies were established. Eleventh year of Duke Xiang.
In summer, in the sixth month, the duke met the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, and the Earl of Zheng, and they jointly concluded a covenant at You. Twenty-seventh year of Duke Zhuang. In winter, in the twelfth month, the duke met the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, the Marquis of Xing, and the Earl of Cao at Huai. Sixteenth year of Duke Xi.
In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, the Duke of Song, the Earl of Cao, and men of Wei and Zhu attacked Qi. In the fifth month, on the wuyin day, the army of Song fought the army of Qi at Yan; the army of Qi suffered a crushing defeat. Both entries are from the eighteenth year of Duke Xi.
In the fifth month, on the guichou day, the duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Viscount of Wei, and the Viscount of Ju, and they concluded a covenant at Jiantu. In winter, the duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Viscount of Chen, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, and men of Qin at Wen. Both entries are from the twenty-eighth year of Duke Xi.
In spring, in the second month of the royal calendar, men of Qin entered Hua. In summer, in the fourth month, on the xinsi day, men of Jin and the Jiang Rong defeated Qin at Yao. Both entries are from the thirty-third year of Duke Xi.

translation_en:
The Viscount of Chu attacked Zheng. Xi Que of Jin led an army to relieve Zheng. Ninth year of Duke Xuan.
Wu attacked our state. Eighth year of Duke Ai.

Record of Rites (Liji)
Thus, the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyous, and its government is harmonious.
To keep the bow drawn without relaxing it was beyond even Kings Wen and Wu; to relax it without drawing it was something Kings Wen and Wu would not do. Drawing and relaxing in alternation was the way of Kings Wen and Wu.
“Music Master, come forward! Let me tell you: the gentleman understands rites and music clearly, and simply puts them into practice.”
The gentleman, though hidden, is manifest; without self-importance, he is dignified; without severity, he inspires awe; without speaking, he is trusted.

Second Session
Discourse
The sage’s methods for inspiring and invigorating the myriad people.

One topic from among imperial edicts, proclamations, and memorials [科, ‘select,’ doubtful].
Compose an imperial edict as if issued by the Han court, dispatching Receptionist Chen Nong to seek out surviving books throughout the realm. Second year of Heping.
Compose a proclamation as if issued by the Tang court, appointing Yao Yuanzhi, Prefect of Tongzhou, as Minister of War and Concurrently Participant in the Administration of the Secretariat and Chancellery, Third Rank. First year of Kaiyuan.

問：有一代之興，必有一代之典，以維持人心，昭視久遠。如唐虞有典謨，夏禹有典則，商有謨訓，周有禮制，尚矣。降及漢唐宋元，亦有三章、六典、會要、經世等作，君子不能無議焉。恭惟我孝宗敬皇帝嘗命儒臣纂輯累朝典制，勒成一書，名曰《大明會典》。

Compose a memorial in the voice of the assisting ministers thanking the emperor for granting silver seals inscribed “Correct faults and rectify errors.” Yongle 22 [1424].

Five legal judgments:
A colleague adjudicating cases and signing documents on another’s behalf; privately manufacturing grain measures, scales, and measuring rules; possessing prohibited books and privately studying astronomy; palace guards and other guards privately arranging substitutes for their duties; officials soliciting or borrowing other people’s money or property.

Third Session
Question Five

Question: Whenever a dynasty arises, it must have its own statutes to sustain the allegiance of the people and provide clear guidance for the distant future. Thus, Tang and Yu had their canons and counsels; Yu of Xia had his statutes and rules; Shang had its counsels and instructions; and Zhou had its ritual institutions. These date from remote antiquity. Coming down to Han, Tang, Song, and Yuan, there were also such works as the Three Articles, the Six Statutes, the Collected Essentials, and the Compendium for Governing the World. These cannot escape the considered judgment of the gentleman.

We reverently recall that our Emperor Xiaozong Jing once commanded his Confucian ministers to compile the statutes and institutions of successive reigns into a single book, entitled the Collected Statutes of the Great Ming (Da Ming huidian) …

text:

典也不知與典謨典則諸書同歟異歟

太祖高皇帝斟酌周禮而作者規模宏遠品式

translation_en: The present Emperor has again commanded Confucian officials to revise and correct it, and to print and promulgate it within the capital and beyond—a truly splendid undertaking. Is it, we wonder, the same as or different from such writings as the Canons and Counsels and the Statutes and Rules? Moreover, this book was largely compiled on the basis of the Duties of the Various Offices (Zhusi zhizhang), with imperially authored works appended. Can the major additions and omissions, continuities and changes within it also be identified and discussed? The Duties of the Various Offices was compiled by our Emperor Taizu Gao after weighing the provisions of the Rites of Zhou. Comprehensive and far-reaching in scope, precise and detailed in its classifications and prescribed forms, it contained virtually all the great principles and laws for governing the realm. Why, then, was the compilation of the Collected Statutes still needed? Some say that affairs had passed through the hands of several sage rulers and time had advanced through several reigns, making the compilation of the Collected Statutes indispensable. Is this indeed so, or not? Earlier reigns had also seen an intention to undertake this compilation, but the work could not be completed. Might Heaven have intended to await these two sage rulers? Without someone to act beforehand, even what is excellent cannot be made manifest; without someone to act afterward, even what is flourishing cannot be transmitted. Here we see how our sage ancestor and his divine descendants, earlier and later, shared one purpose, following a single Way in founding and preserving the dynasty. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
明之治之所以盛
問官多則民擾省則賦輕其理有不可易
者唐虞稽古建官惟百夏商官倍亦克
用乂不可尚矣說者謂成周官制最爲
詳備今周禮一書其跡固在攷其六官
之屬每事必設畿甸之內衆至五萬餘
人不知當時官何以給民何以堪歟兵
多則財耗少則勢分其勢有必至者咎
繇佐舜五服攸明公旦輔周六軍是作
===
不可復矣說者謂西漢兵灋最爲近古
今班固一書其制固存攷其征伐之將
因事而置京師之兵纔盈萬人不知當
時國胡以強民胡以安歟夫周之制善
矣而未免有民擾之慮漢之灋良矣而
未免有兵弱之虞諒茲俊髦必有讜論
問君子論天下之事與天下之人蓋亦難
矣然亦顧其時勢與其所自處何如爾
姑以史冊所疑數事與爾諸士子商之

punctuated:
明之治之所以盛。

問：官多則民擾，省則賦輕，其理有不可易者。唐虞稽古，建官惟百；夏商官倍，亦克用乂，不可尚矣。說者謂成周官制最爲詳備。今《周禮》一書，其跡固在。攷其六官之屬，每事必設，畿甸之內，衆至五萬餘人。不知當時官何以給，民何以堪歟？兵多則財耗，少則勢分，其勢有必至者。咎繇佐舜，五服攸明；公旦輔周，六軍是作，不可復矣。說者謂西漢兵灋最爲近古。今班固一書，其制固存。攷其征伐之將，因事而置；京師之兵，纔盈萬人。不知當時國胡以強，民胡以安歟？夫周之制善矣，而未免有民擾之慮；漢之灋良矣，而未免有兵弱之虞。諒茲俊髦，必有讜論。

問：君子論天下之事與天下之人，蓋亦難矣。然亦顧其時勢與其所自處何如爾。姑以史冊所疑數事，與爾諸士子商之。
translation_en:
…why the governance of our Ming flourishes.

Question: When officials are numerous, the people are harassed; when their numbers are reduced, taxes are light. This principle cannot be changed. Tang and Yu, the rulers Yao and Shun, examined antiquity and established only a hundred offices; Xia and Shang doubled their number, yet likewise achieved good government. These accomplishments cannot be surpassed. Commentators say that the official system of Zhou was the most detailed and comprehensive. Its traces certainly remain in the book Rites of Zhou. Examining the personnel attached to its six ministries, we find that officials were appointed for every task, their numbers within the royal domain reaching more than fifty thousand. How, one wonders, were the officials supported at that time, and how could the people bear the burden? When troops are numerous, resources are depleted; when they are few, strength is dispersed. These are inevitable consequences. Gaoyao assisted Shun, and the five zones of service were clearly defined; Dan, Duke of Zhou, assisted the Zhou, and the six armies were established. Such achievements cannot be reproduced. Commentators say that the military system of the Western Han came closest to that of antiquity. Its institutions certainly survive in Ban Gu’s book, the History of the Han. Examining its generals charged with military campaigns, we find that they were appointed as circumstances required; the troops in the capital barely numbered ten thousand. How, one wonders, was the state then strong, and how were the people secure? The Zhou system was good, yet it could not escape concern that the people would be harassed; the Han arrangements were sound, yet they could not escape concern that the military would be weak. Surely you outstanding scholars will have forthright arguments to offer.

Question: For a gentleman to judge the affairs of the world and its people is indeed difficult. Yet this depends on the circumstances of the times and how those concerned situated themselves within them. Let me take several doubtful matters in the historical records and discuss them with you candidates.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
夫匈奴未滅何以家爲是也而或乃多
請田宅何歟入府端坐召斬弄臣是也
而或乃望塵下拜何歟詩書禮樂足以
彊晉矣而作文賦者何以有河橋之敗
禮義廉耻足以覇齊矣而作四維論者
何以有侄文之附蕭曹舊隙胡何卒而
參相張陳舊德胡耳王而餘戮記書三
篋與藏書萬卷者其事君孰優教子以
諂與遺子以經者其傳家孰善或以布
===
被而取譏或以布被而見美孰得乎或
用鉤距而得事情或用鉤距而固君寵
孰賢乎或勸舉進士而不應與勸無舉
進士而不從者其故何歟或勸見宰相
而不肯與上書宰相而不嫌者其故何
歟從帝至咸陽而獨收圖籍與從主征
伐而獨收人物者其見孰高大將軍尊
重而獨長揖與相王尊重而輒下拜者
其爲孰是不從三國之言而竟達漢天

translation_en:
Now, “The Xiongnu have not yet been destroyed; what use have I for a home?” was a proper sentiment. Yet another man repeatedly requested fields and residences. Why? To enter the government office, sit upright, and summon a court jester for execution was proper. Yet another man bowed down at the mere sight of the dust raised by someone’s approach. Why? The Odes, Documents, rites, and music were sufficient to strengthen Jin; why, then, did the author of the Rhapsody on Literature suffer defeat at Heqiao? Ritual propriety, righteousness, integrity, and a sense of shame were sufficient to make Qi hegemon; why, then, did the author of the Discourse on the Four Bonds lend his support to a document professing nephewhood [?]? Xiao He and Cao Shen had an old quarrel: why did Shen nevertheless become Chief Minister after He died? Zhang Er and Chen Yu had formerly shown kindness to each other: why did Er become a king while Yu was put to death? Of the man who recorded writings in three chests [?] and the man who collected ten thousand scrolls of books, which served his ruler better? Of the man who taught his son to flatter and the man who bequeathed the Classics to his son, which better transmitted his family’s legacy?

One man incurred criticism for using a cloth quilt, while another was praised for it: which acted rightly? One used probing interrogation to discover the facts of cases; another used it to secure his ruler’s favor: which was worthier? One was urged to enter the jinshi examination but did not respond; another was urged not to enter it but would not heed the advice. What explains this? One was urged to visit the Chief Minister but refused; another had no qualms about submitting a letter to the Chief Minister. What explains this? One accompanied the emperor to Xianyang and alone collected maps and registers; another accompanied his lord on campaigns and alone gathered men of talent. Which showed greater insight? One merely made a deep bow with clasped hands before a highly honored General-in-Chief; another bowed down before a highly honored prince serving as chief minister. Which acted rightly? One refused to heed the words of the three states and ultimately conveyed the command of the Han emperor…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子之命與不從楚子之令而卒致晉君
之語者其忠同歟異歟不受故人之請
而竟卻其金與雖受府丞之餽而輒懸
其魚者其廉同歟異歟免胄見回紇與
去兜鍪見突厥者其事奇矣而或者未
免有輕身損威之懼矯命破莎車與矯
命誅郅支者其功偉矣而議者未免有
邀功生事之嫌或天下無冤民或天下
無冤獄何所爲而若是或民不能欺或
===
民不忍欺奚所事而臻茲耻其君不爲
堯舜老臣自任之重也而後世有美其
君爲堯舜者然乎不然乎諫人主不當
觀史史臣所守之職也而異時有錄上
其書者可乎不可乎凡此之類難以一
二數記願聞所以折衷之道毋徒諉曰
夫我則不暇
問生民之休戚係守令之賢否
國家重守令之選必取於科目之傑其雄郡

子之命，與不從楚子之令而卒致晉君之語者，其忠同歟異歟？不受故人之請而竟卻其金，與雖受府丞之餽而輒懸其魚者，其廉同歟異歟？免胄見回紇，與去兜鍪見突厥者，其事奇矣，而或者未免有輕身損威之懼。矯命破莎車，與矯命誅郅支者，其功偉矣，而議者未免有邀功生事之嫌。或天下無冤民，或天下無冤獄，何所爲而若是？或民不能欺，或民不忍欺，奚所事而臻茲？耻其君不爲堯舜，老臣自任之重也，而後世有美其君爲堯舜者，然乎不然乎？諫人主不當觀史，史臣所守之職也，而異時有錄上其書者，可乎不可乎？凡此之類，難以一二數記，願聞所以折衷之道，毋徒諉曰：「夫我則不暇。」
問：生民之休戚，係守令之賢否。國家重守令之選，必取於科目之傑，其雄郡
translation_en:
…the Son of Heaven’s command, and the man who disobeyed the ruler of Chu’s order but ultimately delivered the words of the ruler of Jin: was their loyalty alike or different? The man who refused an old friend’s request and finally rejected his gold, and the man who accepted a gift from a vice prefect but promptly hung up the fish he had received: was their integrity alike or different? Removing one’s helmet to meet the Huihe, and taking off one’s helmet to meet the Tujue—these were extraordinary deeds, yet some could not help fearing that they put the men themselves at needless risk and diminished their authority. Falsifying an imperial command to defeat Shache, and falsifying an imperial command to execute Zhizhi—these were great achievements, yet critics could not help suspecting that they sought merit by provoking trouble. In one case, there were no people suffering injustice throughout the realm; in another, there were no unjust judicial cases throughout the realm. What actions brought this about? In one case, the people could not deceive their official; in another, they could not bear to deceive him. Through what conduct were these results achieved? To feel ashamed that one’s ruler was not a Yao or Shun showed how weighty a responsibility an old minister took upon himself. Yet in later ages there were those who praised their rulers as Yao and Shun. Were they right or wrong? To admonish the sovereign that he ought not to read the historical records was to uphold the duty of a court historian. Yet at another time there were those who copied out their records and presented them to the throne. Was this permissible or not? Instances of this kind are too numerous to enumerate individually. We wish to hear the principles by which you would reach a balanced judgment. Do not merely evade the matter by saying, “I have no time for this.”
Question: The well-being and suffering of the people depend upon whether prefects and county magistrates are worthy. The state attaches great importance to their selection and invariably chooses outstanding men from the examination ranks. As for its major prefectures…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
巨邑
畿甸内輔之地尤加之意非敏鋭通達豈弟
樂易者不以輕授而荷茲任者亦往往
感激思奮勉稱
上意若皆足以副牧民之責者而今之民日益
窮訟日益繁轉徙流亡者日益衆何歟
豈墨吏未盡去考課之法未盡嚴歟考
課之法古人有行之者其得失異同可
考也然有謂歷六代而考績之法不著
===
關七聖而課試之要未立者何歟有官
必有課有課必有賞罰有官無課是無
官也有課無賞罰是無課也顧其法在
人用之何如耳方今
聖明在上賢宰輔在下銓衡公而考課嚴百司
庶府黽勉奉職惴惴焉唯恐清議之或
及課試之失最者盖不獨守令為然也
而民生未安固自守令之不得人始豈
考課之法果不足賴歟抑别有其故歟

巨邑
畿甸内輔之地尤加之意非敏銳通達豈易
樂易者不以輕授而於兹任者亦往往
感激恩奮勉稱

課之法古人有行之者其得失異同可
考也然有謂歷六代而考績之法不著
===
闕七聖而課試之要未立者何歟有官
必有課有課必有賞罰有官無課是無
官也有課無賞罰是無課也顧其法在
人用之何如耳方今
聖明在上賢宰輔在下銓衡公而考課嚴百司
庶府蠲勉奉職惴惴焉唯恐淸議之或
及課試之失最者蓋不獨會令爲然也
而民生未安固自守令之不得人始豈
考課之法果不足賴歟抑别有其故歟
punctuated: 巨邑、畿甸内輔之地，尤加之意，非敏鋭通達、豈弟樂易者，不以輕授。而荷茲任者，亦往往感激思奮，勉稱上意，若皆足以副牧民之責者。而今之民日益窮，訟日益繁，轉徙流亡者日益衆，何歟？豈墨吏未盡去，考課之法未盡嚴歟？考課之法，古人有行之者，其得失異同可考也。然有謂歷六代而考績之法不著，關七聖而課試之要未立者，何歟？有官必有課，有課必有賞罰。有官無課，是無官也；有課無賞罰，是無課也。顧其法在人用之何如耳。方今聖明在上，賢宰輔在下，銓衡公而考課嚴，百司庶府黽勉奉職，惴惴焉，唯恐清議之或及、課試之失最者，盖不獨守令為然也。而民生未安，固自守令之不得人始。豈考課之法果不足賴歟？抑别有其故歟？
translation_en:
…great counties and the territories surrounding and supporting the capital receive particular attention. Such appointments are not lightly entrusted to anyone who is not perceptive, capable, and discerning, as well as kindly, cheerful, and approachable. Those who shoulder these responsibilities, too, are often moved by gratitude to exert themselves and strive to fulfill the sovereign’s wishes, seemingly all equal to the responsibility of governing the people. Yet today the people grow poorer by the day, litigation becomes ever more frequent, and ever greater numbers migrate or flee their homes. Why is this? Is it because corrupt officials have not all been removed, or because the system of performance evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous?

The ancients practiced methods of evaluating officials, and their successes and failures, similarities and differences, can be examined. Yet it has been said that through six dynasties no clear method of evaluating achievements emerged, and through seven sages [?] the essentials of assessing officials were never established. Why is this? Wherever there are officials, there must be evaluations; wherever there are evaluations, there must be rewards and punishments. To have officials without evaluations is equivalent to having no officials; to have evaluations without rewards and punishments is equivalent to having no evaluations. It depends solely on how people apply the system.

Today an enlightened sovereign reigns above, with worthy chief ministers serving below. Selection and appointment are impartial, and performance evaluations are strict. Officials in all offices and agencies diligently discharge their duties, anxiously fearing that public criticism might reach them or that they might fail to receive the highest rating in their evaluations. Surely this is not true only of prefects and county magistrates. Yet the people’s livelihood remains insecure, and this assuredly begins with the failure to obtain suitable men as prefects and county magistrates. Is the system of performance evaluation truly inadequate to rely upon? Or is there some other cause?

問：財賦者，邦國之大本，生人之喉命，天下治亂輕重繫焉，而不可忽也。理財之道，莫詳於《周官》。說者謂《周官》為致太平之書，信則然矣。後世亦有用之而不效者，何歟？不知由周以前，《周官》未作，其理財之道何如也？由周以後，歷秦漢唐宋之世，其理財之道何如也？嘗考前代創業之君，恭儉愛下，財用不期足而自足。至於中世，則侈費而用乏。物理人事，消息盈虛，亦自有然者。當時喜事之臣，有歲進，有月進，有日進，有刺史之進奉，有判官之進奉。而其時人主亦有內藏，如瓊林、大盈是也，亦每每乏用，何歟？然亦有置封椿庫、景福內庫，更景福殿庫名，自製詩以揭之者，而不聞乏用，何歟？宋蘇軾曰：「為國有三計：有萬世之計，有一時之計，有不終月之計。」蘇轍曰：「事之害財
translation_en:
…Please explain this in detail, to assist those in authority.

Question: Revenue is the great foundation of the state and the lifeline of the people. Order and disorder throughout the realm, and its strength or weakness, depend upon it; it cannot be neglected. Nowhere is the way of managing finances set out more fully than in the Offices of Zhou (Zhou guan). Commentators call it a book for bringing about Great Peace, and indeed it is. Yet some in later ages applied it without success. Why? Before the Zhou, when the Offices of Zhou had not yet been written, how were finances managed? After the Zhou, through the Qin, Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, how were they managed? I have examined the founding rulers of earlier dynasties: they were reverent and frugal and cherished those below them, so their resources proved sufficient even without their striving to make them so. By the middle years of a dynasty, however, extravagant expenditure brought shortages. In the workings of things and in human affairs, decline and growth, fullness and depletion, do have their natural course. In those times, ministers eager to undertake projects presented contributions annually, monthly, or daily; there were offerings from Regional Inspectors and from Administrative Assistants. The rulers of those times also possessed palace treasuries, such as the Qionglin and Daying treasuries, yet they repeatedly lacked funds. Why? There were also rulers who established the Fengchun reserve treasury [?] and the Jingfu Inner Treasury, changed the name of the Jingfu Hall Treasury, and personally composed a poem to display there; yet we do not hear of shortages under them. Why? Su Shi of the Song said: “There are three kinds of planning in governing a state: planning for ten thousand generations, planning for the present, and planning that will not last out a month.” Su Zhe said: “The things that impair finances…”

translation_en: …are three: superfluous officials, superfluous troops, and superfluous expenditure. If, indeed, we follow the words of these two thinkers, eliminate the three forms of superfluity, and carefully weigh the three kinds of planning, might we then have enough to meet expenditure? At present, the myriad families, the hundred officials, and the six armies depend most urgently upon the minister of fiscal affairs. Yet floods and droughts, disturbances caused by bandits, and troubles on the frontiers arise on every side, with no provision made against them. By precisely what means can we achieve what the ancients called having sufficient resources for expenditure without increasing taxation? Please explain in detail; your words will be conveyed to His Majesty.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
述而不作信而好古竊比於我老彭
崔桐
同考試官教諭蕭批此題上二句士子類能
發揮至于不為竊比二字所纏繞僅見此篇
同考試官學正鄭批傳述由於信古操筆輒
能言之脫去陳俗而發揮明盡春容周匝趣味悠然
如此篇者殆未多見是用錄之
===
同考試官教授劉批題本平易作者非浮冗
無實則散漫無歸獨此篇體認親切造詞雅健聖人
謙下氣象宛然在目可取可取
考試官左諭德溫批論語義最難得聖人口氣而
謙抑之詞尤難也如此作亦可錄矣
考試官侍講學士李批模擬聖人之言如出諸口發
明聖人之意如出諸心佳作也
聖人自言所以遵乎古道因言欲以學乎古人
甚矣聖人之聖不自聖也不惟不敢當作者之

punctuated:
第壹塲
四書
「述而不作，信而好古，竊比於我老彭。」
崔桐

同考試官教諭蕭批：此題上二句，士子類能發揮；至于不為「竊比」二字所纏繞，僅見此篇。

同考試官學正鄭批：傳述由於信古，操筆輒能言之；脫去陳俗而發揮明盡，春容周匝，趣味悠然，如此篇者，殆未多見，是用錄之。

同考試官教授劉批：題本平易，作者非浮冗無實，則散漫無歸。獨此篇體認親切，造詞雅健，聖人謙下氣象宛然在目，可取，可取！

考試官左諭德溫批：《論語》義最難得聖人口氣，而謙抑之詞尤難也。如此作，亦可錄矣。

考試官侍講學士李批：模擬聖人之言，如出諸口；發明聖人之意，如出諸心，佳作也。

聖人自言所以遵乎古道，因言欲以學乎古人。
甚矣，聖人之聖，不自聖也！不惟不敢當作者之
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“I transmit but do not originate; I trust in and delight in antiquity, privately comparing myself to our Old Peng.”
Cui Tong

Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: Candidates generally manage to expound the first two clauses of this topic. But this is the only essay I have seen that avoids becoming entangled in the two characters meaning “privately compare.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, School Instructor: Any candidate taking up his brush can say that transmission derives from trust in antiquity. But essays like this one—which escapes stale conventions, expounds its meaning clearly and fully, unfolds with unhurried amplitude and thoroughness, and leaves a lingering savor—are rarely seen. For this reason it has been included.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Professor: The topic itself is straightforward, yet those who write on it produce either empty verbosity without substance or rambling prose without a conclusion. This essay alone shows an intimate grasp of the subject and uses elegant, vigorous language. The Sage’s humility appears vividly before our eyes. Worthy of selection, worthy of selection!

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher: In expounding the meaning of the Analects, capturing the Sage’s tone is most difficult; his expressions of modest self-effacement are harder still. A composition like this merits inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor-in-Waiting: It reproduces the Sage’s words as though they came from his own mouth and elucidates his intentions as though they came from his own heart. An excellent composition.

The Sage himself explains why he follows the Way of antiquity and goes on to express his desire to learn from the men of antiquity.
How profound is the Sage’s sageliness: he does not regard himself as a sage! Not only did he not dare claim an originator’s…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖而亦不敢自附於古之賢人其謙已誨人之
意何其切歟昔吾夫子當吾道既絀之餘退而
立言之後脩近聖之事而無自聖之心其意若
曰制作之道有二有述者焉有作者焉作者聖
人之事則吾豈敢當述者賢人之事在人皆可
企是故吾嘗刪詩書矣吾嘗定禮樂矣詩書則
首乎周南斷于堯典禮樂則問于老聃訪于萇
弘刪之定之猶夫舊也吾嘗脩春秋矣吾嘗賛
周易矣春秋則因魯史之文次桓文之事易則
===
明三聖之心附一已之見脩之賛之無所創也
夫我之所以述而不作者何哉誠以詩書也禮
樂也皆古道之所存焉所以立倫彝者在是所
以通神明者在是吾固信而好之不啻若自其
口出焉其奚敢作乎春秋也周易也皆古道之
所寓焉所以繩後王者在是所以明天道者在
是吾固信而好之不知老之將至焉斯其所以
述乎然此抑豈無所自哉古之人有行之者其
惟我老彭乎老彭者何商之賢大夫也彼嘗述

punctuated: 聖，而亦不敢自附於古之賢人，其謙已誨人之意何其切歟！昔吾夫子當吾道既絀之餘，退而立言之後，脩近聖之事，而無自聖之心。其意若曰：「制作之道有二：有述者焉，有作者焉。作者，聖人之事，則吾豈敢當？述者，賢人之事，在人皆可企。是故吾嘗刪詩書矣，吾嘗定禮樂矣。詩書則首乎周南，斷于堯典；禮樂則問于老聃，訪于萇弘。刪之定之，猶夫舊也。吾嘗脩春秋矣，吾嘗賛周易矣。春秋則因魯史之文，次桓文之事；易則明三聖之心，附一已之見。脩之賛之，無所創也。夫我之所以述而不作者何哉？誠以詩書也，禮樂也，皆古道之所存焉。所以立倫彝者在是，所以通神明者在是。吾固信而好之，不啻若自其口出焉，其奚敢作乎？春秋也，周易也，皆古道之所寓焉。所以繩後王者在是，所以明天道者在是。吾固信而好之，不知老之將至焉，斯其所以述乎！然此抑豈無所自哉？古之人有行之者，其惟我老彭乎！老彭者何？商之賢大夫也。彼嘗述
translation_en:
…the sagehood of an originator, nor did he dare even to rank himself among the worthy men of antiquity. How earnest was his intention to humble himself and instruct others! In former times, after our Way had fallen into neglect and our Master had withdrawn to establish his teachings in words, he undertook work approaching that of a sage, yet had no thought of claiming sagehood for himself. His meaning was as though he said:

“The work of establishing institutions and teachings takes two forms: transmitting and originating. Originating is the work of a sage: how could I dare claim it? Transmitting is the work of a worthy man, something to which anyone may aspire. Thus I have edited the Odes and the Documents, and I have established rites and music. For the Odes, I placed ‘Zhounan’ first; for the Documents, I set the boundary at the ‘Canon of Yao.’ For rites and music, I consulted Lao Dan and sought instruction from Chang Hong. In editing and establishing these, I preserved what was old. I have compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals and elucidated the Changes of Zhou. For the Annals, I followed the text of the historical records of Lu and arranged the affairs of Duke Huan and Duke Wen. For the Changes, I clarified the intentions of the three sages and appended my own views. In compiling and elucidating these, I originated nothing.

“Why is it that I transmit rather than originate? It is truly because the Odes and Documents, rites and music, all preserve the ancient Way. Herein lie the means of establishing the enduring norms of human relationships and communicating with the spirits. I indeed trust and cherish them, just as though their words came from the ancients’ own mouths. How could I dare originate anything? The Spring and Autumn Annals and the Changes of Zhou likewise embody the ancient Way. Herein lie the means of holding later kings to a standard and illuminating the Way of Heaven. I indeed trust and cherish them, unaware that old age is approaching. This is why I transmit!

“Yet could this itself be without a precedent? Among the ancients there was someone who practiced it—surely my Lao Peng! Who was Lao Peng? A worthy grand master of the Shang. He once transmitted…”

text:
而不作而無自專之心吾何為而敢專焉彼嘗
信而好古而無自用之意吾何為而敢用焉蓋
我老彭之所為有以先獲我心于數百載之前
而我之所為欲以竊比我老彭于數百載之後
曰竊比以致其尊之之意曰我以致其親之之
心聖人德愈盛而心愈下不自知其辭之謙也
有如此乎抑嘗攷之大戴禮矣孔子嘗稱老彭
之教大夫教士教庶人抑揚德行之語不一而
足合論語而觀之則老彭者其真賢大夫也乎
===
不然何吾夫子之亟稱之若是雖然彭豈若是
班乎蓋吾夫子謙己誨人之心固有不得不然
者焉後有僭擬聖經侈然自足者非惟孔子之
罪人亦老彭之罪人也歟
故至誠無息不息則久久則徵徵則悠遠
悠遠則博厚博厚則高明
高瀹

而不作，而無自專之心，吾何為而敢專焉？彼嘗信而好古，而無自用之意，吾何為而敢用焉？蓋我老彭之所為，有以先獲我心于數百載之前，而我之所為，欲以竊比我老彭于數百載之後。曰「竊比」，以致其尊之之意；曰「我」，以致其親之之心。聖人德愈盛而心愈下，不自知其辭之謙也，有如此乎！抑嘗攷之《大戴禮》矣，孔子嘗稱老彭之教大夫、教士、教庶人，抑揚德行之語不一而足。合《論語》而觀之，則老彭者，其真賢大夫也乎？不然，何吾夫子之亟稱之若是？雖然，彭豈若是班乎？蓋吾夫子謙己誨人之心，固有不得不然者焉。後有僭擬聖經、侈然自足者，非惟孔子之罪人，亦老彭之罪人也歟！

故至誠無息，不息則久，久則徵，徵則悠遠，悠遠則博厚，博厚則高明。

高瀹

translation_en:
…transmitted without creating, and had no wish to act on his own authority. Why should I dare to claim such authority? He believed in and loved antiquity, and had no intention of relying solely on his own judgment. Why should I dare to rely on mine? What my Lao Peng did anticipated my own convictions several hundred years before me; what I do is to venture privately to compare myself with my Lao Peng several hundred years after him. The words “venture privately to compare” express the depth of his reverence; the word “my” expresses the intimacy of his affection. The more abundant the sage’s virtue, the humbler his heart: could his language have been so modest without his even being conscious of it!

I have also examined the Elder Dai’s Record of Ritual. Confucius spoke of Lao Peng’s instruction of grandees, of men of service, and of the common people; his remarks assessing Peng’s virtue and conduct were too numerous to enumerate. Read together with the Analects, does this not show that Lao Peng truly was a worthy grandee? Otherwise, why would our Master have praised him so frequently? Even so, could Peng have belonged to such a rank [?]? Our Master’s desire to humble himself and instruct others surely compelled him to speak thus. If later people presumptuously emulate the sages’ classics and remain arrogantly self-satisfied, are they not offenders against both Confucius and Lao Peng?

“Thus perfect sincerity never ceases. Never ceasing, it endures; enduring, it becomes manifest; becoming manifest, it extends far and long; extending far and long, it becomes broad and substantial; becoming broad and substantial, it becomes lofty and luminous.”

Gao Yue 高瀹

===
之德以明天道謂夫德之在人者惟誠爲難况
誠而極於至乎夫惟聖人之德原於性命之初
得於秉彝之正渾融於一心而不間以人欲之
虚假純粹至善舉天下莫能加也和順於道德

者優游涵泳而自不能已德性安固而和順之

In discussing the virtue of utmost sincerity, the Doctrine of the Mean necessarily describes the fullness of its accumulation within and manifestation without. For the sage’s virtue is sincere in every respect. How, then, could what accumulates within and manifests without fail to attain its fullest measure in each case? Chapter Twenty-Six of the Doctrine of the Mean discusses the sage’s virtue to illuminate the Way of Heaven. Its meaning is that, in human virtue, sincerity is difficult to attain—how much more so sincerity brought to its utmost degree! The sage’s virtue alone has its source in the original endowment of nature and destiny and derives from the correctness of the constant moral norms with which humans are endowed. Wholly integrated in a single mind, it admits no intrusion of the falsity of human desires. Pure and supremely good, it cannot be surpassed by anything in the world. Harmoniously accordant with the Way and virtue, it admits no admixture of selfishness and deception. Genuine and without falsehood, it cannot be excelled throughout past and present. Such is utmost sincerity. I know that sincerity, rooted in human nature, inherently possesses the means to extend from beginning to end without decline; virtue, rooted in the mind, inherently possesses the means to continue uninterrupted from youth to maturity. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
蘊於中者日新月盛而物莫能遷何其乆耶惟
其乆也將見睟於面盎于背而動容周旋莫非
至德之光發乎邇見乎遠而上下四方莫非至
誠之著非徵乎惟其徵也則氣象之在外者優
優乎寛緩而不急迫施之堂陛而實有保天下
之勢也功業之在天下者恢恢乎乆遠而不局
促行之一時而實有裕萬世之規也非悠遠乎
惟悠遠也吾見盛德豐功所以漸涵乎人心者
無所不至深仁厚澤所以覆冒乎天下者無所
===
不周納八荒於度內也歷萬世如一日也何博
厚如之惟博厚也吾見巍乎成功而治化格于
上下煥乎文章而聲光燭于無疆峻極于天也
光被四表也何高明如之夫以至誠之德積中
發外者其盛如此子思子以之明天道其旨深
矣抑考中庸一書誠為樞紐言聖人則曰至誠
言天地則曰不貳若所謂至誠之道可以前知
至誠盡性可以參天地賛化育固皆聖人之事
也而至誠無息之功用未有若此章言之親切

光被四表也何高明如之夫以至誠之德積中
發外者其盛如此予思子以之明天道其旨深

言天地則曰不貳若所謂至誠之道可以前知

也而至誠無息之功用未有若此章言之親切
punctuated:
蘊於中者日新月盛，而物莫能遷，何其乆耶！惟其乆也，將見睟於面、盎于背，而動容周旋，莫非至德之光；發乎邇、見乎遠，而上下四方，莫非至誠之著，非徵乎？惟其徵也，則氣象之在外者，優優乎寛緩而不急迫，施之堂陛，而實有保天下之勢也；功業之在天下者，恢恢乎乆遠而不局促，行之一時，而實有裕萬世之規也，非悠遠乎？惟悠遠也，吾見盛德豐功，所以漸涵乎人心者，無所不至；深仁厚澤，所以覆冒乎天下者，無所不周。納八荒於度內也，歷萬世如一日也，何博厚如之！惟博厚也，吾見巍乎成功，而治化格于上下；煥乎文章，而聲光燭于無疆。峻極于天也，光被四表也，何高明如之！

夫以至誠之德，積中發外者，其盛如此，子思子以之明天道，其旨深矣。抑考《中庸》一書，誠為樞紐。言聖人則曰「至誠」，言天地則曰「不貳」。若所謂「至誠之道，可以前知」，「至誠盡性，可以參天地、賛化育」，固皆聖人之事也，而至誠無息之功用，未有若此章言之親切
translation_en:
…what is stored within grows fresh each day and flourishes each month, and nothing external can alter it. How enduring it is! Because it endures, we shall see it shine clearly in the face and fill out the back: every movement and gesture displays the radiance of consummate virtue. It issues forth nearby and becomes visible far away: above and below, in all four directions, everything manifests utmost sincerity. Is this not its becoming evident? Because it becomes evident, its outward bearing is ample and unhurried, free from urgency or pressure. Applied at court, it truly possesses the power to preserve all under Heaven. Its achievements throughout the world are expansive and enduring, free from narrow constraint. Put into practice in a single age, they truly furnish a design that provides amply for ten thousand generations. Is this not far-reaching duration? Because it is far-reaching and enduring, I see that its abundant virtue and great achievements gradually permeate human hearts, leaving nowhere untouched; its profound benevolence and generous beneficence shelter all under Heaven, leaving nowhere uncovered. It brings the eight remotest regions within its compass and passes through ten thousand generations as though they were a single day. What breadth and depth could equal this! Because it is broad and deep, I see its towering accomplishments, with its transforming governance reaching those above and below; its brilliant cultural refinement, with its renown and radiance illuminating boundless realms. It rises to the very height of Heaven, and its light extends beyond the four outer bounds. What loftiness and brilliance could equal this!

Such is the flourishing of the virtue of utmost sincerity, accumulated within and expressed without. Master Zisi uses it to illuminate the Way of Heaven: profound indeed is his meaning. Moreover, examining the Doctrine of the Mean as a whole, we find sincerity to be its pivot. When speaking of the sage, it says “utmost sincerity”; when speaking of Heaven and Earth, it says “without doubleness.” Statements such as “Through the Way of utmost sincerity, one can know things beforehand” and “Through utmost sincerity, one fully realizes one’s nature and can thus form a triad with Heaven and Earth and assist their transforming and nourishing activity” certainly all concern the sage’s work. Yet concerning the efficacy of utmost sincerity’s ceaseless activity, no passage speaks as directly as this chapter…

translation_en:
…the reality of the principles governing things, to clarify the differences among them. Things cannot be made identical precisely because they possess real principles inherent in their nature. If one supposes that merely making their prices identical suffices to equalize things, can one possibly understand the principles governing them? Formerly, Chen Xiang was convinced that the Way of his teacher Xu Xing was sufficient to govern a state. He therefore cited uniform prices as evidence that there was no deception within the state. His meaning was as if to say: “Differences in the prices of goods arise from the many deceptions in people’s hearts. Master Xu’s Way is otherwise. Among useful goods are cloth and silk fabrics, hemp thread, silk thread, and silk floss. Cloth and silk fabrics differ in length, and hemp thread, silk thread, and silk floss differ in weight. If the Way did not prevail within the state, people would dispute lengths by measuring and weights by weighing; prices would inevitably be far apart and unequal. Now, however, if the measurements of longer and shorter pieces do not differ greatly, their prices are similar; if the measured weights of lighter and heavier quantities do not differ greatly, their prices are similar. What contention could there be between the two parties? Among useful goods are the five grains and shoes. Grain comes in greater and smaller quantities, and shoes in larger and smaller sizes. If trust did not prevail in the marketplace, people would dispute quantities by measures of capacity and sizes by physical dimensions; prices would inevitably be widely separated and unequal. Now, however, if the greater quantity does not much exceed the smaller, their prices are identical; if the smaller size is not much less than the larger, their prices are identical. How could deception find an opening?”
Such were Chen Xiang’s words. Mencius enlightened him, as if saying: “That things differ is their natural principle. How could uniformity be forced upon them? Of all the things in the world that people use, there are more than just cloth, silk fabrics, and hemp thread. To discuss these alone…

之固自有長短有輕重而長短輕重之中又自

translation_en:
…they naturally differ in length and weight; and within these differences of length and weight, some are fine and others coarse. The differences between fine and coarse are innumerable. Each thing is left to be itself, possessing its own natural principle: things neither borrow from one another nor encroach upon and supplant one another. How could I make them alike? Of all the things in the world that people use, there are more than just the five grains and shoes. Even these naturally differ in quantity and size; and within these differences of quantity and size, some are good and others poor. Their distinctions in quality are innumerable. Things fall into groups, each possessing its inherent standard. Those who favor sameness cannot make them alike; those who favor difference cannot make them different. How could I confound them?

Viewed in this light, the claim that market prices should admit no variation reveals only its absurdity. Master Xu’s way is indeed a means of fostering disorder and opening the way to deception. How could it suffice to govern a state? Yet does this principle merely suffice to refute Chen Xiang and rebut Xu Xing? The true circumstances of all things under Heaven are encompassed within it, and none can depart from it. Thus, not going beyond what is proper to things is the way by which the sage perfects himself; nurturing things according to their capacities is the principle by which Heaven and Earth bring them to completion. Even Heaven and Earth and the sages cannot add to or subtract from this! It means simply that each thing has its allotted place. We therefore know that distinctions between close and distant relations, and between noble and lowly stations, cannot forcibly be made uniform; nor can the successive steps of cultivating oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world be applied indiscriminately. This differs from what Laozi and Zhuangzi call the equalization of things. Alas! Was this Xu Xing of whom Chen Xiang spoke a follower of Shennong? Or…

Book of Changes

“The Changes are images; images are likenesses.”

Huang Luzeng

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor: To understand the Changes as images, and to elucidate images through likenesses: seeking images externally is certainly unacceptable, but explaining likenesses on a separate level likewise departs from the meaning of the classic. This composition sustains a coherent argument without repetitive wording; hence its inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, Instructor: This topic is exceedingly difficult to expound. This is the only composition I have seen that is lucid, polished, and flawless.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher: Neither superficial in its wording nor sparing in its reasoning. Should not an interpretation of the meaning of the Changes be just like this?

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician Expositor: It fully expounds the two words “image” and “likeness,” leaving none of their implications unexplored.

When the Great Commentary discusses the Changes, it treats the hexagrams as forms of yin and yang and necessarily explains what makes these forms what they are. What makes the Changes the Changes is simply yin and yang. Yet what constitutes yin and yang—is it not their resemblance to principle? Now, the Changes contain images and principles; in substance, these are simply the two poles of yin and yang. But why are the Changes images? In a yang figure, the line is single and solid, and its numbers are nine and seven: these are images of yang. Thus three undivided lines constitute Qian, an image of pure yang; one undivided line and two divided lines constitute Zhen or Kan…

…or Gen, these are images of mixed yang; and, together with all the trigrams classed as great, how could any fail to be images of yang? For those trigrams that are yin, the line consists of two strokes with a gap, and its numbers are six and eight: these are images of yin. Thus three divided lines form Kun, an image of pure yin; one divided line and two undivided lines form Xun, Li, and Dui, images of mixed yin. Together with all the trigrams classed as small, how could any fail to be images of yin? Through comparison and deliberation, the deepest intricacies of the world are fully explored, and the forms appropriate to things are made clear; through observation, the patterns of Heaven and Earth are constituted, and old and young, movement and stillness, are embodied therein. Hence it is said: “The Changes consists of images.” Yet how do these images constitute likenesses? What is most manifest is image; what is most subtle is principle. Yang cannot in itself be exhaustively comprehended. It is designated by the names pure yang and mixed yang; thus its line, single and solid, and its numbers, nine and seven, are merely approximations of principle. Could yang be confined to these? Yin cannot in itself be given visible form. It is comprehended under pure yin and mixed yin; thus its line, in two strokes with a gap, and its numbers, six and eight, are merely likenesses of principle. Could yin be exhausted by these? What is most difficult to give form is made manifest in visible patterns; what cannot be exhausted is encompassed within a finite number of strokes. Hence it is said: “Images are likenesses.” Ah! …old and young forms. The young does not change or move, but old yang changes into yin and never remains fixed in one state. Yin, too, is one, yet it also has old and young forms. The young does not change or move, but old yin changes into yang and does not remain in its place. Thus, the lower trigram of a hexagram, called zhen, has the empty positions of the first, second, and third lines. Yin and yang occupy these positions in turn, and their designations are not fixed. The upper trigram, called hui, has the empty positions of the fourth, fifth, and top lines. Yin and yang circulate through these positions, and their substance does not remain fixed.

That yang should be above and yin below is the constant order of Heaven and Earth. Yet with repeated changes, six, the yin line, may occupy the upper positions of the fourth, fifth, and top lines, while nine, the yang line, may occupy the lower positions of the first, second, and third lines. Although noble and lowly positions are arrayed in order, yielding and firm lines function in alternation. This can be seen by observing the changes in which the yielding ascends and the firm descends, or the firm ascends and the yielding descends. What constancy is there?

That yang should occupy yang positions and yin occupy yin positions is an unchanging principle. Yet with repeated changes, six is also frequently used in the yang positions of the first, third, and fifth lines, and nine is also frequently used in the yin positions of the second, fourth, and top lines. Although yin and yang are distinguished, their numbers interweave. This can be seen by observing the changes in which the yielding comes to adorn the firm and the firm ascends to adorn the yielding. How do they exchange places [?]?

…such was his intent. For the difficulty in transforming people lies not in reaching those far away, but in putting internal government in order. Once internal government is well ordered, distant peoples will submit of their own accord, without submission being sought. The court historian recorded Emperor Shun’s instructions to the regional governors in these terms. Their meaning was as follows: “In governing, nothing takes precedence over sustaining the people; in sustaining the people, nothing matters more than ensuring sufficient food. Must ensuring sufficient food mean supplying every household and giving more to every person? It requires only that their time for farming not be taken from them. The season of plowing and weeding is what the production of food depends upon: whenever works are undertaken, one must not encroach upon it. The season of reaping and harvesting is what bringing in the food requires: whenever labor services are imposed, one must not obstruct it. Then the people can devote their full efforts to their fields, and food will be sufficient.

“Ordinary human dispositions tend to neglect those nearby and overlook those far away; yet those far away are harder still to govern. Thus, first attend to those far away: soothe them with benevolence and gradually influence them over the months and years; cherish them with generosity and show compassion for what lies beyond their ability. Then attend to those nearby: correct and straighten them, making them content with my instruction; comfort and encourage them, making them delight in my virtue. There will thus be a proper way of dealing with both distant and nearby peoples.

“In the way of governing, nothing demands greater strictness than advancing the worthy and dismissing the unworthy; yet the unworthy are harder still to remove. Thus, for those who possess virtue, one must exalt their positions and make their stipends substantial, never daring to slight them. For those who are benevolent and generous, one must act upon their remonstrances and listen to their words, never daring to estrange them. As for treacherous men, gradually block their access so that they cannot put their schemes into effect; cut them off in accordance with righteousness so that they cannot give free rein to their wickedness. There will thus be a proper way of treating gentlemen and petty men.

“All such measures serve only to bring peace to my people. How could their purpose be to secure the submission of distant peoples? I see that wherever the influence of my teaching reaches, the Man peoples of the eight regions will of themselves…”

…thereupon their hearts are won over. Wherever the transforming influence of the Way reaches, the Nine Yi naturally turn toward his virtue. Although they need not bow their heads to the ground and declare themselves vassals, their aspirations all turn toward the Central Kingdom. Submitting to our righteousness, the myriad states share the same customs. Although they need not discharge their duties and present tribute, their hearts all rest with the royal house. Submitting to our teaching, all within the Four Seas take it as their standard. When the work of shepherding the people is accomplished, distant peoples submit of themselves. This shows that the Central Kingdom is the central standard for the four quarters. Can the Twelve Regional Governors fail to give this their attention? Moreover, when we examine the sages’ government, nowhere was their care more thorough than in internal affairs; and in moving others, nothing took precedence over the foundations. Thus, bringing the myriad states into harmony must be rooted in the transforming influence of concord among relatives; bringing the peoples of the four quarters to acknowledge the king must begin with admonition and vigilance. The Doctrine of the Mean extends this into its nine guiding principles, and the Great Learning elaborates it into its eight articles: all embody this same principle. Later generations did not understand this principle. Neglecting internal government, they instead sought to mobilize armies to subdue distant peoples. Alas! How different this was from the instructions of Shun’s court!

Only when ruler and minister possess virtue capable of reaching Heaven can they naturally win the allegiance of Heaven and humankind. For virtue alone suffices to reach Heaven. Had there then been any discord in the virtue of ruler and minister, Heaven’s mandate would have departed. Pure and undivided, it was truly the highest virtue under Heaven: it was the same in Tang as in Yin. text:
申之重之而意嚮之不貳帝心簡在自不能舍
君臣之一德矣一德格天如此吾知天命雖靡
常也今則眷命用懋申命用休而赫赫然如有
臨天休滋至帝命不違而昭昭乎其如在有不
受天之命者乎九有雖嘗屬於夏也今則民罔
常懷懷于有仁合億兆而歸心誕受多方式于
九圍撫方夏而咸有有不得民之歸者乎夫天
佑民歸咸於一德如此嗣王可不自純其德以
答天人之望也哉伊尹以是為言其所以陳戒
===
之者至矣嗟乎伊尹之所以事太甲者即其所
以事成湯也日新又新湯之所以聖也時乃日
新尹之所以望太甲為成湯也而一德之訓主
善克一之說又實本於精一之傳尹既以堯舜
之道相湯故又以相湯之道相太甲蓋前聖之
心法有商之家法人臣事主不貳之道咸具於
一德篇而惓惓不忍去之意具見於反覆陳戒
之辭於乎老臣愛君憂國之心豈獨於居位之
時為然哉

punctuated:
申之重之，而意嚮之不貳，帝心簡在，自不能舍君臣之一德矣。一德格天如此，吾知天命雖靡常也，今則眷命用懋，申命用休，而赫赫然如有臨；天休滋至，帝命不違，而昭昭乎其如在，有不受天之命者乎？九有雖嘗屬於夏也，今則民罔常懷，懷于有仁，合億兆而歸心；誕受多方，式于九圍，撫方夏而咸有，有不得民之歸者乎？夫天佑民歸，咸於一德如此，嗣王可不自純其德，以答天人之望也哉？伊尹以是為言，其所以陳戒之者至矣。

嗟乎！伊尹之所以事太甲者，即其所以事成湯也。日新又新，湯之所以聖也；時乃日新，尹之所以望太甲為成湯也。而一德之訓、主善克一之說，又實本於精一之傳。尹既以堯舜之道相湯，故又以相湯之道相太甲。蓋前聖之心法、有商之家法、人臣事主不貳之道，咸具於《一德》篇，而惓惓不忍去之意，具見於反覆陳戒之辭。於乎！老臣愛君憂國之心，豈獨於居位之時為然哉？
translation_en:
…Heaven renews and reaffirms its favor, its purpose unwavering. The sovereign above has chosen them in his heart and cannot forsake the single virtue shared by ruler and minister. Such is the power of single virtue to reach Heaven. I know that although Heaven’s mandate is not constant, now its favor bestows encouragement and its renewed mandate brings blessing: resplendent, Heaven seems to look down upon them. Heaven’s blessings arrive in ever greater abundance, and the sovereign above’s mandate does not turn away: manifestly, he seems present. Could they fail to receive Heaven’s mandate? Although the nine regions once belonged to Xia, now the people cherish no one invariably; they cherish those who possess benevolence. The countless multitudes unite in giving their allegiance. Tang received the many lands on a grand scale, became a model throughout the nine regions, and brought all the central lands under his care and possession. Could he fail to win the people’s allegiance? Since Heaven’s aid and the people’s allegiance both thus arise from single virtue, how could the successor king fail to purify his own virtue and fulfill the hopes of Heaven and humankind? Yi Yin spoke in these terms, carrying his admonitions to the utmost.

Ah! The way Yi Yin served Tai Jia was precisely the way he had served Cheng Tang. Renewing himself daily, and renewing himself yet again: this was how Tang became a sage. “Thus renew yourself daily”: this expressed Yi Yin’s hope that Tai Jia would become another Cheng Tang. The teaching of single virtue and the doctrine of taking goodness as one’s guide and attaining unity were, moreover, truly rooted in the transmitted teaching of refinement and singleness. Having assisted Tang through the Way of Yao and Shun, Yi Yin then assisted Tai Jia through the same Way by which he had assisted Tang. The former sages’ teachings concerning the mind, the ancestral precepts of the Shang house, and the Way by which a minister serves his ruler with undivided loyalty are all contained in the chapter “Single Virtue.” His devoted attachment and inability to bear departing are fully revealed in his repeated words of admonition. Ah! Could an old minister’s love for his ruler and concern for his state exist only while he holds office?

Book of Odes

“Not merely taking him by the hand, but showing him how things are done; not merely instructing him face to face, but taking him by the ear.”

Cui Tong

Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: The topic itself is straightforward and balanced, yet most writers tediously piece together stale expressions. This essay alone is clear, concise, and apt, vividly conveying Duke Wu’s intention to admonish himself. Ah! Surely this is the kind of writing that gives its hearers sufficient warning!

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, School Instructor: A topic from the Greater Odes is not difficult to write on; the difficulty lies in treating it precisely and appropriately. This essay alone develops “showing him how things are done” and “taking him by the ear” with clarity, exploring their implications fully and in detail. Moreover, the sincerity of its admonition overflows the words. It is selected for more than its literary merit.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Professor: Duke Wu’s intention to admonish himself is brought out almost completely.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Mentor: Its language is gentle, but its meaning stern. Reading it three times each day would also help one advance in virtue.

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor-in-Waiting: “The Odes can arouse the feelings.” This composition surely comes close to doing so!

The worthy lord entrusted another with admonishing himself [?]: some means would make the admonition easy to understand, and others would make it easy to heed. Showing him how things are done makes it easy to understand without confusion; taking him by the ear makes it easy to heed without forgetting. The worthy lord’s use of another to admonish himself [?] in this way may indeed be called thorough and earnest. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
謂爾小子以一人之身臨萬民之上苟臧否之
罔知則理忽之攸繫故我之于爾小子也朝夕
教誨之有加惟欲其得夫師資之益前後告詔
之無已惟欲其審夫趨避之宜手以攜之若可
止矣猶慮夫謨雖矢而或不能究其意言雖切
而或不能彊其從喻猶弗喻也故我不但手攜
掣之而已而又言示之事焉俾知某事為臧可
以利國而康民某事為否足以蠹政而僨治爰
稽成敗之由用作監觀之地盖凡吾之所當言
===
者惓惓指陳之間而不嫌於瀆庶其睹之而易
悟乎面以命之若云足矣猶慮夫出于驟而或
不能契其深悅于暫而或不能持于久告猶弗
告也故我匪徒面命語之而已而又言提其耳
焉俾知若何為政之臧而所當從若何為政之
否而所當戒儻或聞之于耳將必警之于心盖
凡爾之所宜知者諄諄提撕之際而不厭於煩
庶其識之而弗忘乎是則示之事則視手攜之
者為益詳提其耳則視面命之者為益切我之

…saying: “You, young man, stand as a single person above the myriad people. Whether you understand what is good and what is bad bears upon order and disorder in government. Thus, in dealing with you, young man, I redouble my instruction morning and evening, wishing only that you gain the benefit of a teacher’s guidance. I admonish you unceasingly, time after time, wishing only that you discern what you should pursue and what you should avoid.

“Having led you by the hand, I might seem able to stop. Yet I still fear that, though counsel has been set forth, you may not fully grasp its meaning; though my words are earnest, you may not exert yourself to follow them. To explain would then be as though I had not explained. Thus I do not merely take you by the hand and draw you along; I also show you actual affairs, so that you know that a certain undertaking is good and can benefit the state and bring peace to the people, while another is bad and can corrupt government and ruin its administration. Accordingly, I examine the causes of success and failure, making them examples for scrutiny and reflection. Indeed, in earnestly pointing out everything I ought to say, I do not shrink from importunity, hoping that, seeing these examples, you may readily understand!

“Having instructed you face to face, I might seem to have done enough. Yet I still fear that, because the instruction comes suddenly, you may not grasp its depth; or that, pleased with it for a moment, you may not hold to it for long. To admonish would then be as though I had not admonished. Thus I do not merely address and instruct you face to face; I also take you by the ear, so that you know what is good in government and ought to be followed, and what is bad in government and ought to be guarded against. If you hear it with your ears, you will surely take heed in your heart. Indeed, in patiently bringing to your attention everything you ought to know, I do not tire of repetition, hoping that you may remember it and never forget!

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
所以告乎爾小子者亦無餘蘊矣若復不知謂
之何哉吁武公自懲自艾之意深矣抑是道也
雖古聖賢之檢身亦不過是而衛武公乃能身
體而力行之至使人直呼為小子而無一毫自
恃自高之意於乎其亦有得於切磋琢磨之力
而然歟後之君天下者疾人之規巳至使之無
所容廼巳况能自警之若是也哉讀詩至此不
能不三嘆焉
明明魯侯克明其德旣作泮宮淮夷攸服
===
矯矯虎臣在泮獻馘淑問如皐陶在泮
獻囚濟濟多士克廣德心桓桓于征狄
彼東南烝烝皇皇不吳不揚不告于訩
在泮獻功角弓其觼束矢其搜戎車孔
博徒御無斁旣克淮夷孔淑不逆式固
爾猶淮夷卒獲翩彼飛鴞集于泮林食
我桑黮懷我好音憬彼淮夷來獻其琛
元龜象齒大賂南金
馬津

我桑黮懷我好音憬彼淮夷來獻其琛
元龜象齒大賂南金
馬津
punctuated:
所以告乎爾小子者，亦無餘蘊矣。若復不知，謂之何哉？吁！武公自懲自艾之意深矣。抑是道也，雖古聖賢之檢身，亦不過是，而衛武公乃能身體而力行之，至使人直呼為小子，而無一毫自恃自高之意。於乎！其亦有得於切磋琢磨之力而然歟？後之君天下者，疾人之規巳，至使之無所容廼巳，况能自警之若是也哉？讀詩至此，不能不三嘆焉。
明明魯侯，克明其德。旣作泮宮，淮夷攸服。矯矯虎臣，在泮獻馘。淑問如皐陶，在泮獻囚。濟濟多士，克廣德心。桓桓于征，狄彼東南。烝烝皇皇，不吳不揚。不告于訩，在泮獻功。角弓其觼，束矢其搜。戎車孔博，徒御無斁。旣克淮夷，孔淑不逆。式固爾猶，淮夷卒獲。翩彼飛鴞，集于泮林。食我桑黮，懷我好音。憬彼淮夷，來獻其琛。元龜象齒，大賂南金。
馬津
translation_en:
…What I have told you, young one, leaves nothing unexpressed. If you still fail to understand, what can be said of you? Ah! How profound was Duke Wu’s resolve to discipline and correct himself! Even the ancient sages and worthies went no further than this in examining their own conduct. Yet Duke Wu of Wei personally embodied this way and diligently practiced it, even allowing others to address him directly as “young one,” without the slightest trace of conceit or self-exaltation. Ah! Was this not the result of his having benefited from the work of cutting and polishing, carving and grinding? Later rulers of the realm resented others’ admonitions and would not stop until those who offered them had no place left to stand. How could they possibly have admonished themselves like this? Reading the Book of Odes to this point, one cannot help sighing repeatedly.
Illustrious is the Marquis of Lu, able to make his virtue shine. Having built the Pan Palace school, he brought the Huai Yi into submission. Mighty are his tiger-like warriors; at the Pan school they present the severed ears of enemies. Skilled in judicial questioning, like Gao Yao, they present prisoners at the Pan school. Numerous and dignified are his officers, able to extend his virtuous intentions. Martial and valiant on campaign, they bring order to the southeast. Advancing in multitudes, imposing in bearing, they neither clamor nor vaunt themselves. They report no contentious disputes; at the Pan school they present their achievements. Their horn bows have buckles [?], their arrows are gathered in bundles. Their war chariots are exceedingly numerous; their foot soldiers and charioteers never tire. Having overcome the Huai Yi, they are most gracious toward those who do not resist. Make firm your plans, and the Huai Yi will be wholly won over. Fluttering, those flying owls alight in the woods of Pan. They eat our mulberries and cherish our lovely songs. Those faraway Huai Yi come to offer their treasures: great tortoises and elephant tusks, and abundant gifts of metal from the south.
Ma Jin.
