於作蓋能收拾如此篇者儘難得矣
同考試官學正鄭批題旨明白正大但作者
自難為工惟此篇文法嚴整語意邃密且歸重於明
德尤為有見蓋善於說詩者宜錄以式
同考試官教授劉批作長題能斂束就簡當
是作手
考試官左諭德温批以明德服遠為頌禱辭能達
意詩卷中僅得此耳
===
考試官侍講學士李批題目長而結構頗密頭緒多
而歸宿極當頌義之最佳者也
魯人因賢侯之在學也屢願其有以服乎遠人
焉甚矣淮夷之為魯患也久矣魯人之所以願
其君與夫君之所以自願者舍是其奚釋也哉
昔魯侯飲于泮而詩人頌禱之至此若謂淮夷
之強弱視我魯之盛衰惟願我明明魯侯克明
峻德而上天之所賦者無一之不全既作泮宮
而淮夷之為患者無一之不服我之反而釋奠

Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor, comments: A topic drawn from a eulogy is easy to write on, yet also difficult. Indeed, an essay that brings everything together as this one does is exceedingly rare.

Associate Examiner Zheng, School Instructor, comments: The purport of the topic is clear, upright, and elevated, but writers find it difficult to handle skillfully. This essay alone has rigorous, orderly composition and profound, closely reasoned expression. Moreover, its emphasis on manifesting virtue shows particular insight. This is skillful interpretation of the Poetry; it should be recorded as a model.

Associate Examiner Liu, Professor, comments: To write on a long topic yet draw it together concisely—this surely marks an accomplished writer.

Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher, comments: Taking the submission of distant peoples through manifest virtue as the substance of praise and prayer, this essay successfully conveys the meaning. Among the Poetry examination scripts, this was the only such piece I found.

Examiner Li, Academician Expositor, comments: Though the topic is long, the structure is quite closely knit; though its threads are numerous, their ultimate convergence is entirely appropriate. This is the finest exposition of the eulogy’s meaning.

Because their worthy lord was at the school, the people of Lu repeatedly expressed the hope that he might find the means to bring distant peoples into submission. How grievously the Huai Yi troubled Lu! How long the people of Lu had cherished this hope for their ruler, and the ruler had cherished it for himself! Without accomplishing this, how could they find relief? In former times, when the lord of Lu drank at the Pan school, the poet carried praise and prayer to this point, as though saying: The strength or weakness of the Huai Yi depends upon the flourishing or decline of our Lu. We wish only that our illustrious lord of Lu may manifest his lofty virtue, so that everything bestowed by Heaven above is fully realized; and that, having built the Pan school, he may bring into submission all the Huai Yi who have caused trouble. Upon our return and performance of the sacrificial offering to the sages …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
□安得武勇之臣有如虓虎者在泮以獻馘乎
彼之服而歸罪也又安得淑問之臣有如臯陶
者在泮以獻囚乎自其兵士言之凡我濟濟多
士莫不克廣德心而無一毫固蔽之私桓桓于
征用以狄彼東南而雪累世寇攘之耻兵進而
合有烝烝皇皇之盛師出以律有不吳不揚之
肅戰勝而和不告于訩焉功成而還爭獻于泮
焉又自其武備言之角弓則觩然體之健也可
知束矢則搜然聲之疾也可知戎車孔博而有
===
如霆如雷之勢徒御無斁而有同心同德之良
是固既克淮夷孔淑而不逆矣盖能審固謀猶
則蠢茲淮夷豈終不獲也哉於是即物以興之
曰翩彼飛鴞顧泮林而萃止食我桑黦猶好音
之是懷況憬彼淮夷有不來獻其琛者乎吾知
曰元龜曰象齒盡異物以來輸曰南金曰揚金
望我邦而大賂則其土地之所出固無有不獻
焉者矣由是觀之凡臣士之所以獻其功與夫
淮夷之所以獻其琛者由我侯之能明其德耳

合有烝烝皇皇之盛師出以律有不吳不揚之
肅戰勝而和不告于訩焉功成而還爭獻于泮
焉又自其武備言之角弓則觩然體之健也可
知東矢則搜然聲之疾也可□□□孔博而有
===
如霆如雷之勢徒御無斁而□□心同德之良
是固既克淮夷孔淑而不逆矣蓋能審固謀猶
則蠢玆淮夷豈終不獲也哉於是即物以興之
曰翩彼飛鴞顧泮林而萃止食我桑黮猶好音
之是懷況憬彼淮夷有不來獻其琛者乎吾知
曰元龜曰象齒盡異物以來輸曰荆金曰揚金
望我邦而大賂則其土地之所出固無有不獻
焉者矣由是觀之凡臣士之所以獻其功與夫
淮夷之所以獻其琛者由我侯之能明其德耳
punctuated: □安得武勇之臣有如虓虎者，在泮以獻馘乎？彼之服而歸罪也，又安得淑問之臣有如臯陶者，在泮以獻囚乎？自其兵士言之，凡我濟濟多士，莫不克廣德心，而無一毫固蔽之私；桓桓于征，用以狄彼東南，而雪累世寇攘之耻。兵進而合，有烝烝皇皇之盛；師出以律，有不吳不揚之肅。戰勝而和，不告于訩焉；功成而還，爭獻于泮焉。又自其武備言之，角弓則觩然，體之健也可知；束矢則搜然，聲之疾也可知；戎車孔博，而有如霆如雷之勢；徒御無斁，而有同心同德之良。是固既克淮夷，孔淑而不逆矣。盖能審固謀猶，則蠢茲淮夷，豈終不獲也哉？於是即物以興之曰：「翩彼飛鴞，顧泮林而萃止；食我桑黦，猶好音之是懷。況憬彼淮夷，有不來獻其琛者乎？吾知曰元龜，曰象齒，盡異物以來輸；曰南金，曰揚金，望我邦而大賂。則其土地之所出，固無有不獻焉者矣。」由是觀之，凡臣士之所以獻其功，與夫淮夷之所以獻其琛者，由我侯之能明其德耳。
translation_en: …[?] How might we obtain martial ministers like roaring tigers, to present the ears cut from slain enemies at the Pan school? When the enemy submits and acknowledges its guilt, how might we also obtain ministers of good reputation like Gao Yao, to present captives at the Pan school? Speaking of the soldiers, all our numerous worthy men can broaden their virtuous hearts, without the slightest selfish obstinacy or blindness. Mighty on campaign, they serve to chastise those in the southeast and wipe away the shame of raids and plunder endured for generations. When the troops advance and assemble, they display abundant splendor; when the army marches under discipline, it maintains the solemn order of men who neither clamor nor swagger. Victorious in battle, they remain harmonious, with no quarrels reported; returning after accomplishing their task, they vie to present their offerings at the Pan school. Speaking also of their military equipment, the horn bows are curved and taut, revealing their sturdy construction; the bundled arrows whistle forth, their sound revealing their speed. The war chariots are very broad and possess the force of thunderbolts and thunder; the foot soldiers and charioteers are tireless and possess the excellence of shared purpose and virtue. Thus, having conquered the Huai Yi, they are thoroughly good and do not act perversely. If they can carefully deliberate and firmly establish their plans, how could these unruly Huai Yi ultimately escape capture? The poet then draws upon things to introduce an evocative comparison, saying: “Those owls flying lightly turn toward the woods of the Pan school and gather there. Eating our mulberries [?], even they cherish pleasing notes. How much more, then, will those far-off Huai Yi come to offer their treasures! I know that they will bring great tortoise shells and elephant tusks, delivering all their rarities; they will bring southern metal and metal from Yang [?], looking toward our state and presenting lavish gifts. Of all that their lands produce, there will surely be nothing they do not offer.” Viewed in this light, the ministers and officers present the fruits of their achievements, and the Huai Yi offer their treasures, simply because our lord can make his virtue manifest.

For if he can make his virtue manifest, herein lies the means of establishing the Pan Palace school and of making his counsels firm; the Huaiyi will then naturally all submit. In expressing this wish for their ruler, may the people of Lu not be called skilled in praise and prayer? Yet an intention to admonish lies implicitly beyond their words, and their loyal affection is not forgotten amid drinking and feasting. Though their language verges somewhat on exaggeration, the principles they express do not go beyond this purpose. Looking at this poem, can we fail to believe still more firmly that Lu was a state capable of preserving ritual propriety and righteousness?

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
軍作而舊法遂廢矣春秋致意於魯事也宜
且古者舞佾之數天子八諸侯六大夫四吾聞
魯以諸侯而僭八佾舊矣是成王過賜伯禽過
受非所以康周公也及隱之身初獻六羽者何
蓋仲子有別宮之祀問之衆仲而降用之耳奏
大樂於新庭損舞列於常數尊卑之制定降殺
之等明非復前日之故轍矣故春秋書曰初初
者事之始若曰八佾之舊以臣僭君想夫用之
太廟以祀周公用之列廟以祀羣公其習為非
===
禮可知也噫禮樂之在天下不容一日紊也諸
侯僭於上大夫僭於下故季氏舞八佾于庭三
家歌雍詩于堂上下之辨何有哉聖人書之所
以正天下之大典也如此若古者制軍之法大
國三次國二小國一吾聞魯封大國其有三軍
舊矣故公車千乘公徒三萬詩所以頌僖公也
迨襄之世復作三軍者何蓋季氏以私門之強
謀之叔孫而更置之耳毁私乘以盡征析公室
而專有地皆三家之土民皆三家之兵非復先

punctuated:
軍作而舊法遂廢矣。春秋致意於魯事也宜。
且古者舞佾之數，天子八，諸侯六，大夫四。吾聞魯以諸侯而僭八佾舊矣，是成王過賜，伯禽過受，非所以康周公也。及隱之身，初獻六羽者何？蓋仲子有別宮之祀，問之衆仲而降用之耳。奏大樂於新庭，損舞列於常數，尊卑之制定，降殺之等明，非復前日之故轍矣。故春秋書曰「初」。初者，事之始。若曰：八佾之舊，以臣僭君，想夫用之太廟以祀周公，用之列廟以祀羣公，其習為非禮可知也。噫！禮樂之在天下，不容一日紊也。諸侯僭於上，大夫僭於下，故季氏舞八佾于庭，三家歌雍詩于堂，上下之辨何有哉？聖人書之，所以正天下之大典也如此。
若古者制軍之法，大國三，次國二，小國一。吾聞魯封大國，其有三軍舊矣。故公車千乘，公徒三萬，詩所以頌僖公也。迨襄之世，復作三軍者何？蓋季氏以私門之強，謀之叔孫而更置之耳。毁私乘以盡征，析公室而專有，地皆三家之土，民皆三家之兵，非復先
translation_en:
…armies were established, and the old regulations were consequently abolished. It was fitting that the Spring and Autumn Annals should attend closely to the affairs of Lu.
Moreover, in antiquity the prescribed number of rows of dancers was eight for the Son of Heaven, six for the feudal lords, and four for grand masters. I have heard that Lu, though a feudal state, had long usurped the use of eight rows. King Cheng bestowed more than was proper, and Boqin accepted more than was proper; this was no way to honor the Duke of Zhou. When it came to Duke Yin’s own time, why were six rows of dancers with feathers presented for the first time? It was simply that, for the sacrifices to Zhongzi in a separate temple, he consulted Zhongzhong and reduced the number used. Grand music was performed in the new court, while the ranks of dancers were reduced to the prescribed number. The distinctions between higher and lower rank were fixed, and the gradations of reduction made clear: this no longer followed the mistaken course of earlier days. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals records the word “first.” “First” means the beginning of an undertaking. It is as if to say: the old practice of using eight rows was a subject’s usurpation of his ruler’s prerogative. Consider their use in the Grand Ancestral Temple to sacrifice to the Duke of Zhou, and in the other ancestral temples to sacrifice to the successive dukes: it is clear that their customary practice violated ritual propriety. Alas! The rites and music of the realm cannot be allowed to fall into disorder for even a single day. Feudal lords usurped prerogatives above, and grand masters usurped them below. Thus the Ji lineage had eight rows of dancers perform in its courtyard, and the three lineages had the ode Yong sung in their halls. What distinction between superior and inferior remained? The Sage recorded these matters in order to rectify the great institutions of the realm: such was his purpose.
As for the ancient regulations governing armies, a large state had three, a state of the next rank two, and a small state one. I have heard that Lu was enfeoffed as a large state and had long possessed three armies. Hence the duke’s thousand chariots and thirty thousand foot soldiers were the grounds on which the Book of Odes praised Duke Xi. By Duke Xiang’s time, why were three armies established anew? It was simply that the Ji lineage, relying on the strength of its own house, conferred with Shusun and reorganized them. They abolished the privately maintained chariot units in order to levy their entire manpower, divided up the ducal establishment, and took exclusive possession of it. The land was all the territory of the three lineages, and the people were all their soldiers. This was no longer the established system of the former…

text:
王之成法矣故春秋謂之作作者不宜作也若
曰三軍之舊名存實亡觀夫命救台而季孫有
入鄆之行享范鞅而公臣無三耦之具其民不
屬公可知也噫兵權之在公室不可一日去也
威福移于上黨與成于下故昭公次陽州以出
定公待壞隤而入廢置之事何如哉聖人書之
所以謹天下之大權也如此吁明君之僭也而
馭臣之道以存惡臣之專也而戒君之意有在
春秋于魯君臣之際其嚴矣乎嗟夫天下之事
===

斯偪偪斯危矣故諸侯僭而後大夫強大夫僭
而後家臣強門觀大闕有重祭也三桓強盛緣
世卿也南蒯侯犯據強邑也以此坊民猶有輕
授節鉞如唐藩鎮之禍者其亦可嘅也夫

王之成法矣。故《春秋》謂之作，作者，不宜作也。若曰：三軍之舊，名存實亡。觀夫命救台，而季孫有入鄆之行；享范鞅，而公臣無三耦之具，其民不屬公可知也。噫！兵權之在公室，不可一日去也。威福移于上，黨與成于下，故昭公次陽州以出，定公待壞隤而入，廢置之事何如哉？聖人書之，所以謹天下之大權也如此。吁！明君之僭也，而馭臣之道以存；惡臣之專也，而戒君之意有在。《春秋》于魯君臣之際，其嚴矣乎！嗟夫！天下之事，未始不積于微而成干著。蓋寵斯僭，僭斯專，專斯偪，偪斯危矣。故諸侯僭而後大夫強，大夫僭而後家臣強。門觀大闕有重祭也，三桓強盛緣世卿也，南蒯、侯犯據強邑也。以此坊民，猶有輕授節鉞，如唐藩鎮之禍者，其亦可嘅也夫！

楚子伐鄭，晉郤缺帥師救鄭。宣公九年。
仲選。

translation_en:
…the established institutions of the former kings. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals calls it “creating”: to call it “creating” means that it ought not to have been created. It is as though the text were saying that the old institution of the three armies survived in name but had vanished in substance. Consider how, when orders were given to relieve Tai, Jisun instead undertook a march into Yun; and how, when Fan Yang was entertained, the duke’s retainers could not supply three pairs of archers. Clearly, the people no longer belonged to the duke. Alas! Military authority must not depart from the ducal house for even a single day. The power to punish and reward slipped away from those above, while partisan followings formed below. Thus Duke Zhao departed into exile and encamped at Yangzhou, while Duke Ding had to await the destruction of Tui before entering. What had become of the power to depose and install rulers? Such is how the Sage’s record safeguards the great authority of the realm. Ah! By exposing the ruler’s usurpation of prerogatives, it preserves the way to control ministers; by condemning ministers’ monopolization of power, it conveys a warning to rulers. How strict the Spring and Autumn Annals is concerning the relationship between ruler and ministers in Lu! Alas! The affairs of the world invariably accumulate from minute beginnings until they become manifest. Favor leads to usurpation; usurpation to monopolization of power; monopolization to coercion; and coercion to peril. Thus only after the feudal lords usurped prerogatives did the great officers grow powerful; only after the great officers usurped prerogatives did their household retainers grow powerful. Gate towers and great gate terraces involved repeated sacrifices [?]; the Three Huan clans grew powerful because their ministerial offices were hereditary; Nan Kuai and Hou Fan held fortified towns. Even with these measures to restrain people, there were still those who carelessly bestowed the tally and battle-axe of military command, producing such disasters as those of the Tang military governorships. Is this not lamentable indeed!

“The Viscount of Chu attacked Zheng. Xi Que of Jin led an army to relieve Zheng.” Ninth year of Duke Xuan.
Second selection.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher: Concise yet rigorous; it grasps the significance of recording the noble rank and of writing “rescue.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician Expositor: The Spring and Autumn Annals carefully maintains the distinction between the Chinese states and the outer peoples. This is surely its purport.

The Spring and Autumn Annals directly records the wrong committed by an outer people in using a great army to mistreat a state of divided allegiance; it therefore expressly records the good done by a hegemonic state in employing troops to succor that state. This is evident from its recording the Chu ruler’s noble rank and describing Jin’s action as “rescue.” In approving good and condemning evil, does not the Spring and Autumn Annals exercise the utmost care in distinguishing the Chinese states from the outer peoples?

Ever since Zheng made peace with Chu and [the Chu ruler] fled back to Li [?], Chu had long been frustrated in its ambitions. Unless it unleashed its strength and vented its anger, how could it desist? Thus it again led forth the troops of Fangcheng to attack a state closely related to our royal house. Guisheng was already dead, so there was no crime whose punishment could serve as a stated justification. Its warhorses stood ready for battle solely to bring Zheng into submission. The ruler commanded in person, and the entire host marched forth: the ancestral temples and altars of Dukes Huan and Wu were almost imperiled. Compared with the campaigns repeatedly mounted in earlier years, was this not especially grave?

Viewed in ordinary terms, this was merely the strong bullying the weak—the familiar vicious course of the Spring and Autumn period. The Sage, however, regarded it as an army of outer peoples disrupting the Chinese states, an act upon which a momentous change in the order of the world hinged. Hence he did not designate the ruler merely as a “man,” but identified him by his title and recorded his noble rank. For when a ruler commands, the Annals does not say “led an army”: it records the weightier fact. Does this not reveal the offense of assaulting the Chinese states and bringing a great army against Zheng?

Now Chu had grown unruly and was overbearing toward the central states. At this time Jin had long presided over the covenant of the Chinese states. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
彼無辜橫罹蛇豕之憂恤我同盟聿申簡書之
義拯焚救溺去危即安抑楚之聲勢遂張矣視
彼楚人之虐豈不大相遠哉自常情言之救患
分災霸者之常職耳聖人以為攘夷安夏之師
天下之大防賴此以不潰故不沒其實而書救
焉蓋凡書救未有不善之也救者善則伐者之
罪不于是而亦著乎是則楚可惡也而其君之
暴必書爵而後見晉可善也而於楚之罪則書
救而亦顯春秋之微詞奧義有如是夫抑考詳
===
內畧外先自治而後治人春秋之法也故楚討
鄭亂則予楚以治亂賊之黨鄭無罪見伐則予
晉救以謹華夷之辨自是徵舒不道辰陵受盟
責楚益輕罪在晉矣吁觀春秋進退抑揚之㫖
則知安中國待四夷之道也歟
禮記
是故治世之音安以樂其政和
劉霽

彼無辜橫罹蛇豕之憂，恤我同盟，聿申簡書之義，拯焚救溺，去危即安，抑楚之聲勢遂張矣。視彼楚人之虐，豈不大相遠哉？自常情言之，救患分災，霸者之常職耳。聖人以為攘夷安夏之師，天下之大防賴此以不潰，故不沒其實而書救焉。蓋凡書救，未有不善之也。救者善，則伐者之罪不于是而亦著乎？是則楚可惡也，而其君之暴必書爵而後見；晉可善也，而於楚之罪則書救而亦顯。《春秋》之微詞奧義有如是夫！抑考詳內畧外，先自治而後治人，《春秋》之法也。故楚討鄭亂，則予楚以治亂賊之黨；鄭無罪見伐，則予晉救以謹華夷之辨。自是徵舒不道，辰陵受盟，責楚益輕，罪在晉矣。吁！觀《春秋》進退抑揚之㫖，則知安中國、待四夷之道也歟！

是故治世之音安以樂，其政和。

translation_en:
…those innocent people, unjustly afflicted by the menace of snakes and swine. Showing concern for our fellow members of the alliance, Jin thus upheld the obligations set forth in the written summons: rescuing those amid fire and drowning, bringing them out of danger into safety. Its prestige and strength in restraining Chu consequently grew. How very different this was from the cruelty of the men of Chu! In ordinary terms, relieving distress and sharing the burden of calamity are merely the regular duties of a hegemon. Yet the Sage regarded this as an army that repelled the foreign peoples and secured the Xia; upon it depended the preservation of the great defensive boundary of the realm. He therefore did not obscure the reality of its action, but recorded it as “rescuing.” Whenever “rescuing” is recorded, it invariably conveys approval. If the rescuer is approved, does this not also make manifest the guilt of the attacker? Thus Chu deserves condemnation, but its ruler’s violence becomes apparent only when his rank is recorded; Jin deserves approval, yet recording its rescue also reveals Chu’s guilt. Such are the subtle wording and profound meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals!

Further, consider that treating the inner realm in detail and the outer realm summarily, putting oneself in order before putting others in order, is the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals. Thus, when Chu punished disorder in Zheng, it approved Chu for bringing to justice the partisans of rebels and traitors; when Zheng was attacked despite being innocent, it approved Jin’s rescue in order to uphold carefully the distinction between the Hua and the foreign peoples. On this basis, in the cases of Zhengshu’s lawlessness and the acceptance of the covenant at Chenling, the blame assigned to Chu becomes lighter still, while the guilt rests with Jin. Ah! By observing the intent behind the advancement and demotion, censure and praise in the Spring and Autumn Annals, may one not understand the way to secure the Central States and deal with the foreign peoples of the four quarters?

Record of Rites

“Thus the music of an orderly age is tranquil and joyful: its government is harmonious.”

Liu Ji

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: “The writer devotes much attention to the phrase ‘an orderly age’…”

氣象其亦得政和之涵養者歟宜取以冠本房

考試官侍講學士李批有藻思有關鎖

生於人心之所感也盛世之政既和則音之發

無所感聲音不可以僞爲彼其形於詩歌而雜

translation_en:
…yet when addressing harmony in government, they fall short in their wording. This essay is unassuming and restrained, vividly portraying an age of peace. Might its author, too, have been nurtured by harmonious government? It should be selected to head this examining section.
Examiner Wen, Left Mentor, comments: “Balanced and harmonious; well worth reading.”
Examiner Li, Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “It has literary imagination and closely connected argument.”
The argument: An age of flourishing has music of consummate harmony because it has government that moves people beneficially. Music arises from what stirs the human heart. If the government of a flourishing age is harmonious, how could the music issuing from human hearts fail to be harmonious? The author of the Record of Music holds that the human heart cannot remain unmoved and that vocal sounds cannot be fabricated. What takes form in poetry and song, emerging variously from the feelings of people in the lanes and alleys, and finds expression in chanting and recitation without departing from the proper measures of clear and deep, high and low tones—this is music. The music of a well-governed age issues from human nature and feeling and stays within the bounds of ritual propriety and righteousness. Its words, with their rising and falling cadences, singing and sighing, all conform to the standards of musical pitch and rhythm, with none of what is called discordance. Broad and harmonious, unhurried and easy, richly ornamented yet simple in its rhythmic divisions: throughout its leisurely unfolding and winding turns, it attains the proper balance of harmony and accord, without anything perverse or jarring. It has a gentle, easy, and balanced quality, without sounds of sorrow or resentment; it expresses joy, delight, affection, and love, without an air of melancholy. Such is the music of a well-governed age. Is this not because harmony in government has the power to stir people in this way? Thus ritual and music guide aspirations and harmonize sounds, differing in their functions; government and punishments unify conduct and prevent wrongdoing, yet their ultimate aim is one. All are means of government by which the former kings moved the hearts of the people.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
惟治世之政出於君臣之所講畫而有以即乎
人心之所安則所謂禮者序也樂者和也薰蒸
浸漬乎人心而不可易矣惟治世之政本於天
下之所願欲而不失乎慎感之意則所謂政以
行之刑以防之流動充滿於天下而無所拂矣
保合天下而天下咸囿於樂利之中安養斯民
而人心悉歸於和平之域治世之政如此則音
之發於人心者豈有不和者哉夫以政和則音
和有不可偽為如此先王慎其所以感之者有
===
由然矣抑因是而知先王作樂之本矣采詩觀
風先王實欲求知夫天下之心也心和則聲和
聲和則樂和所謂本之情性稽之度數制之禮
義其制雖出於先王而實本於天下人心之和
之所被也然非善政養之於平時其能驟得於
一旦哉說者謂禮樂積德百年而後興又曰六
律五聲八音在治忽信矣
張而不弛文武弗能也弛而不張文武弗
為也一張一弛文武之道也

punctuated:
惟治世之政，出於君臣之所講畫，而有以即乎人心之所安，則所謂禮者序也，樂者和也，薰蒸浸漬乎人心而不可易矣。惟治世之政，本於天下之所願欲，而不失乎慎感之意，則所謂政以行之，刑以防之，流動充滿於天下而無所拂矣。保合天下，而天下咸囿於樂利之中；安養斯民，而人心悉歸於和平之域。治世之政如此，則音之發於人心者，豈有不和者哉？夫以政和則音和，有不可偽為如此，先王慎其所以感之者，有由然矣。抑因是而知先王作樂之本矣。采詩觀風，先王實欲求知夫天下之心也。心和則聲和，聲和則樂和。所謂本之情性，稽之度數，制之禮義，其制雖出於先王，而實本於天下人心之和之所被也。然非善政養之於平時，其能驟得於一旦哉？說者謂禮樂積德百年而後興，又曰：「六律五聲八音，在治忽。」信矣！

張而不弛，文武弗能也；弛而不張，文武弗為也。一張一弛，文武之道也。
translation_en:
The government of an age of good order proceeds from the deliberations and plans of ruler and ministers and accords with what puts people’s hearts at ease. Thus, what is meant by “rites are order; music is harmony” permeates and suffuses people’s hearts and cannot be altered. The government of an age of good order is rooted in the wishes and desires of all under Heaven and preserves the intention of exercising care over what moves people. Thus, what is meant by “government puts it into practice; punishments guard against violations of it” flows throughout the realm and fills it, meeting no resistance. It preserves and unites all under Heaven, encompassing everyone in happiness and benefit; it settles and nurtures the people, bringing all their hearts into a realm of peace and harmony. When government in an age of good order is like this, how could the sounds issuing from people’s hearts fail to be harmonious? Harmony in government produces harmony in sound: this cannot be feigned. The former kings therefore had good reason to exercise care over the means by which they moved people.

From this we may also understand the foundation upon which the former kings created music. In collecting poems and observing local customs, the former kings truly sought to understand the hearts of all under Heaven. When hearts are harmonious, voices are harmonious; when voices are harmonious, music is harmonious. This is what is meant by grounding it in feelings and human nature, examining it against measures and numbers, and regulating it through ritual and righteousness. Although its regulation came from the former kings, it was actually rooted in the pervasive harmony of people’s hearts throughout the realm. Yet unless good government had nurtured this in ordinary times, could it suddenly have been attained in a single day? Commentators say that rites and music arise only after virtue has accumulated for a hundred years. It is also said: “The six pitch standards, five notes, and eight classes of instruments depend upon whether government is orderly or negligent.” How true!

“To keep the bow drawn without relaxing it was beyond even Kings Wen and Wu; to relax it without drawing it was something Kings Wen and Wu would not do. Now drawing, now relaxing: this was the Way of Kings Wen and Wu.”

治道耳作者於弗張弗弛處語意繁複而於一張一
弛處却晦而不揚間有專說文武事業而不顧本文
者獨此作明白條暢而於治道處甚詳故録
考試官左諭德温批自是說治道文字
考試官侍講學士李批講張弛處非他卷所及
論民之勞息當以其時唯聖人為能得其道也
蓋民力易使而亦易憊也張弛之得其道非文
===
武聖王其孰能哉昔子貢觀蜡祭而不知其樂
夫子曉之若曰蜡祭有恤民之義民樂實君上
之澤賜也知之乎彼弓之為用久張而不弛則
其力必絕民之勞其弓之張乎勞而不暫息焉
則筋力憊於勤苦精神殫於役作雖有文武之
君以倡率於上民將改易而弗從矣文武愛民
之君也豈能強之乎弓之為器久弛而不張則
其體必變民之息其弓之弛乎弛而不知勞焉
則勤苦不習於素養心志或逸於怠惰雖有文

translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: The bow serves as an analogy for the people, borrowed simply to illuminate the way of governing. Writers are repetitious in wording and meaning when discussing neither drawing nor relaxing, yet obscure and insufficiently explicit when discussing alternately drawing and relaxing. Some discuss only the achievements of Kings Wen and Wu, disregarding the passage itself. This composition alone is clear, coherent, and fluent, and discusses the way of governing in considerable detail. It is therefore included.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher: This is indeed an essay explaining the way of governing.

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: Its explanation of drawing and relaxing is beyond the reach of the other examination papers.

In considering the people's labor and rest, each must have its proper season. Only a sage can grasp the right way to regulate them. The people's strength is readily put to use, but it is also readily exhausted. Who but sage kings such as Wen and Wu could achieve the proper balance between drawing taut and relaxing?

Long ago, Zigong witnessed the year-end Zha sacrifice but did not understand its merriment. The Master enlightened him, saying in effect: The Zha sacrifice embodies concern for the people; their enjoyment is truly a blessing bestowed by their ruler. Ci, do you understand this? When a bow is used, if it remains drawn for long without being relaxed, its strength will inevitably fail. Is not the people's labor like the drawing of a bow? If they labor without even a brief respite, their bodily strength is exhausted by toil and their vital energies depleted by service and work. Even with rulers such as Wen and Wu leading them from above, the people will turn away and cease to obey. Wen and Wu were rulers who loved the people: how could they force them?

As an implement, a bow left relaxed for long without being drawn will inevitably lose its proper form. Is not the people's rest like the relaxing of a bow? If they rest without knowing labor, they will not have developed a habitual capacity for toil, and their minds and purposes may drift into idleness and indolence. Even if there were a ruler like Wen…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
武之君以鼓舞於上民將散亂而弗收矣文武
教民之君也忍能為此乎是以於一歲之中而
必勞之於三時凡其率作興事以盡力於田畝
者吾弗得而奪也於三時之勞而必息之於終
歲若其蜡畢醉飽以盡歡於一日者吾弗得而
禁也所以勞之者非厲民也使之足食利用以
厚生耳然有時而息焉則所謂說以使民民忘
其勞者也文武之道不其在兹乎所以息之者
非縱民也使之節力養銳以俟用耳然有時而
===
勞焉則所謂佚道使民雖勞不怨者也文武之
道不其如是乎由是觀之則百日之蜡一日之
澤其義固有攸在賜也顧不達於此乎雖然是
道也亦民之所自有者文武付之無心焉耳觀
天地動靜闔闢之義則天地亦不能違也而况
於人乎况於聖人乎是故張弛之道聖人馭民
之術也闔闢之義天地養物之宜也動靜失宜
天地不能以生萬物張弛失道聖人不能以成
化功後之勞民動衆久而不息者亦可以鑒矣

punctuated:
武之君以鼓舞於上，民將散亂而弗收矣。文武，教民之君也，忍能為此乎？是以於一歲之中，而必勞之於三時，凡其率作興事以盡力於田畝者，吾弗得而奪也；於三時之勞，而必息之於終歲，若其蜡畢醉飽以盡歡於一日者，吾弗得而禁也。所以勞之者，非厲民也，使之足食利用以厚生耳。然有時而息焉，則所謂「說以使民，民忘其勞」者也。文武之道，不其在兹乎？所以息之者，非縱民也，使之節力養銳以俟用耳。然有時而勞焉，則所謂「佚道使民，雖勞不怨」者也。文武之道，不其如是乎？由是觀之，則百日之蜡、一日之澤，其義固有攸在。賜也，顧不達於此乎？

雖然，是道也，亦民之所自有者，文武付之無心焉耳。觀天地動靜闔闢之義，則天地亦不能違也，而况於人乎？况於聖人乎？是故張弛之道，聖人馭民之術也；闔闢之義，天地養物之宜也。動靜失宜，天地不能以生萬物；張弛失道，聖人不能以成化功。後之勞民動衆、久而不息者，亦可以鑒矣。
translation_en:
…even if rulers like Kings Wen and Wu were above them, inspiring them to action, the people would become scattered and disorderly, beyond recovery. Wen and Wu were rulers who instructed the people: could they bear to bring about such a condition? Thus, within each year, the people must be put to work during the three seasons. When they undertake their tasks and set about their work, devoting their strength to the fields, I may not take that time away from them. But after the toil of those three seasons, they must be given rest at the year’s end. When, after the zha sacrifice, they drink and eat their fill, enjoying themselves to the utmost for a single day, I may not forbid it. Putting them to work is not a matter of oppressing them; it is simply to ensure that they have sufficient food and useful resources, thereby enriching their livelihood. Yet they are given rest at the proper times. This is what is meant by: “Set the people to work with gladness, and they forget their toil.” Is this not where the Way of Wen and Wu lies? Giving them rest is not a matter of indulging them; it is simply to conserve their strength and replenish their vigor in readiness for service. Yet they are put to work at the proper times. This is what is meant by: “Employ the people in a way that secures their ease, and though they toil, they do not resent it.” Is this not the Way of Wen and Wu? Viewed in this light, “the zha sacrifice of a hundred days” [?] and the bounty of a single day assuredly have their meaning. Ci, do you really not understand this?

Nevertheless, this Way is also something inherent in the people themselves. Wen and Wu simply entrusted themselves to it without deliberate contrivance. Consider the principles of movement and stillness, closing and opening, in Heaven and Earth: even Heaven and Earth cannot depart from them. How much less can human beings—or even sages! Thus, the Way of tension and relaxation is the sages’ method of governing the people; the principle of closing and opening is the fitting means by which Heaven and Earth nourish all things. If movement and stillness lose their proper balance, Heaven and Earth cannot bring forth the myriad things. If tension and relaxation depart from the Way, the sages cannot accomplish their work of transformation. Those in later ages who put the people to toil and mobilize the multitudes for long periods without respite may also take warning from this.

Second Session

Discourse

The Sages’ Art of Inspiring and Stirring the Myriad People

Cui Tong

Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: The topic itself is upright and substantial, and candidates generally manage to develop it. Few, however, give due emphasis to the sages’ circumspect intentions. This essay draws upon antiquity to substantiate the present; its wording and meaning are concise and apt, and it brings out Yuancheng’s meaning. For this reason it has been selected for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, School Instructor: It proceeds fluently for more than a thousand words, without a single expression that copies old formulations or strays into the bizarre. In its opening and closing, its free-ranging development, everything conforms to proper standards. Its measured, unhurried movement and smooth turns give it a lingering resonance: one singing could well call forth three answering sighs of admiration.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Professor: Among examination discourses, those that are excessively chiseled err toward eccentricity, while those that range unrestrainedly err toward diffuseness. This essay is precise in its use of evidence and sound and correct in its arguments. It has the savor of the plain ceremonial broth and the ‘dark wine’ of ritual water, yet one never tires of it. Moreover, his work in both the preceding and following sessions is equally worthy. For a high recommendation in the autumn Provincial Examination, no one could replace this candidate.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Mentor: Ornament and substance are well matched, and both expression and meaning are fully realized. Examination writing of this kind is indeed accomplished.

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor-in-Waiting: When a discourse concerns the way of government, it readily lapses into borrowing others’ arguments. Only this essay, among those I have seen, casts off habitual conventions and stands distinctly above the rest. Selecting it to rank first in the Southern Metropolitan Region surely accords with general expectations.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
論曰聖人有風天下之道而天下不倦此天下
所以養于善而不自知也天下之心渙而不一
也天下之情靡而未易以起也非得其道以風
之則渙者將至於無所收拾靡者或至於無所
振立驅天下之人心之風俗於無所依藉揚厲
之地而始罪天下曰何其無法守也是誤天下
也故善理天下者必有立頹起懦之道而民不
倦必有勝殘去殺之道而民不知以此而制馭
群動以此而整齊六合以此而始以此而終而
===
後天下之志定而後天下之化成於乎此豈可
以易言哉元城劉安世當宋哲宗時有言曰命
令者聖人所持以鼓舞萬民之術其亦有所警
矣命令何為者也書曰猷告爾四國多方禮曰
王言如絲其出如綸王言如綸其出如綍皆是
也虞夏殷周有典則有訓誥有誓命漢唐宋有
約法有詔令盖一王有一王之法雖損益沿革
繁簡文質之不同而同於軌眾率物以一天下
之心志以新天下之耳目也天下如彼其大也

translation_en: The discourse states: The sage has a way of inspiring all under Heaven without wearying them. Thus they are nurtured in goodness without themselves knowing it. The hearts of the people are scattered and lack unity; their spirits are languid and not easily roused. Unless the proper way to inspire them is found, the scattered will become impossible to gather together, and the languid may become impossible to revive. To drive the hearts and customs of the people into a condition in which they have nothing to rely upon and no means of being invigorated, and only then to blame them, saying, “Why have they no standards to uphold?”—this is to lead the people astray. Thus one who governs the realm well must have a way to raise up the dispirited and rouse the timid without wearying the people, and a way to overcome brutality and dispense with killing without the people being aware of it. By these means he directs and controls all activity; by these means he brings order to the six directions. With these he begins, and with these he ends. Only then are the purposes of all under Heaven settled, and only then is their moral transformation complete. Ah! How could this be spoken of lightly? During the reign of Emperor Zhezong of the Song, Liu Anshi of Yuancheng said: “Commands are the means by which the sage inspires the myriad people.” His words surely convey an admonition. What, then, are commands? The Book of Documents says: “Ho! I announce to you, the many regions of the four quarters.” The Book of Rites says: “The king’s words are like silk thread; when they go forth, they become like cord. The king’s words are like cord; when they go forth, they become like heavy rope.” These both concern this matter. Under Yu, Xia, Yin, and Zhou there were canons and regulations, instructions and proclamations, oaths and mandates; under Han, Tang, and Song there were compacts establishing laws, and edicts and orders. Each sovereign has his own laws. Although these differ in what they remove or add, preserve or change, in complexity or simplicity, and in refinement or plainness, they share the purpose of regulating the multitude and guiding all people, unifying the hearts and purposes of all under Heaven, and giving them something new to hear and see. So vast is all under Heaven…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
智者愚者勇者怯者貴者賤者遠者邇者親者
疎者其趨其習又如彼其不同也故必有大君
焉以主宰之而後天下始定於一大君者豈必
家喻戶曉而後天下乃一哉故必有命令焉布
告於立國之初而持循於經世之遠洋溢乎封
牧之域而咸暨乎蠻貊之地使天下咸知有君
咸知有朝廷而民始不犯其勢盖有不得不然
者易曰天下有風姤后以施命誥四方又曰隨
風巽君子以申命行事風之為物也流行四時
===
周旋八極吹號萬籟無物不遇無物不動者也
聖人觀風之象體巽之義有命令焉呼天下之
昧而以起天下之仆伸天下之氣而以厭天下
之心如風自天而下觸之者折被之者立雨露
滋息之所不能遂日月照臨之所不能及妖氛
欝抑之所不能破水火燥濕之所不能運者而
惟風得以蕩之闢之而有除穢布新之象也是
故風者天之命也命令者聖人之風也而實天
下後世之法也法苟立矣令苟行矣吾見勇者

下後世之法也法苟立矣令苟行矣吾見勇者

智者、愚者、勇者、怯者、貴者、賤者、遠者、邇者、親者、疎者，其趨其習，又如彼其不同也。故必有大君焉以主宰之，而後天下始定於一。大君者，豈必家喻戶曉而後天下乃一哉？故必有命令焉，布告於立國之初，而持循於經世之遠，洋溢乎封牧之域，而咸暨乎蠻貊之地，使天下咸知有君，咸知有朝廷，而民始不犯。其勢盖有不得不然者。《易》曰：「天下有風，姤；后以施命誥四方。」又曰：「隨風，巽；君子以申命行事。」風之為物也，流行四時，周旋八極，吹號萬籟，無物不遇，無物不動者也。

translation_en:
…The wise and the foolish, the brave and the timid, the noble and the lowly, those far away and those nearby, those closely connected and those distantly related—their inclinations and habits likewise differ so greatly. Thus there must be a great ruler to govern them; only then can all under Heaven be brought into unity. But must the great ruler explain matters to every household and every person before all under Heaven can be united? There must therefore be commands, proclaimed at the founding of the state and upheld throughout the long course of governing the world. They spread throughout the territories under administration and reach even the lands of the Man and Mo peoples, so that all under Heaven know that there is a ruler and an imperial court. Only then do the people refrain from transgression. The circumstances make this unavoidable. The Book of Changes says: “Beneath Heaven there is wind: Encounter. The sovereign accordingly issues commands and proclaims them to the four quarters.” It also says: “Winds following one another: The Gentle. The gentleman accordingly reiterates commands and carries out affairs.” Wind circulates through the four seasons, travels throughout the eight extremities, and blows through the myriad openings, making them resound. There is nothing it does not encounter, nothing it does not move.
The sage observes the image of wind and embodies the meaning of the Gentle. He issues commands to awaken the benighted throughout the realm and raise up the fallen, to release the vital energies of all under Heaven and satisfy their hearts. It is like wind descending from Heaven: those it strikes bend, and those it touches stand upright. What the nourishing rain and dew cannot bring to fruition, what the light of sun and moon cannot reach, what cannot be cleared amid oppressive malign vapors, and what the drying and moistening action of fire and water cannot set in motion—wind alone can sweep through and open up. Thus it presents the image of removing corruption and spreading renewal. Wind, therefore, is Heaven’s command; commands are the sage’s wind, and indeed the law for all under Heaven and for generations to come. Once the law is established and commands are carried out, I see that the brave…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
奪其氣智者奪其謀貴者奪其僭親者邇者奪
其貪而怯者愚者賤者疎者莫不有所憑而為
善有所制而不為惡如六軍之行而有耳目旗
鼓以為之令如舟車之用而有師工以為之導
如醫藥之用而有法案以為之方由此者安不
由此者危用此者生不用此者死所以奔走天
下之豪傑所以制伏天下之奸回所以感激天
下之忠義所以噓拂天下之晦潜鼓之舞之其
機在我而彼自不識也有天下者亦豈好為是
改作以求勝於下哉盖無令是無法也無法是
無君也故法為上君位次之君與法固不可一
日而離者是法也其始也為天下立之其既也
君亦不得而踰焉故賞罰以法予奪以法廢置
以法禮自我議也而法之所在則等威由之而
立度自我制也而法之所在則界限由之而明
執法之吏日以法告我而吾自不敢過效法之
子孫日以法視我而吾自不敢違前疑後丞左
史右書日以法事我而吾自不敢亂愆忘之訓

translation_en:
…are stripped of their spirit; the clever are stripped of their schemes; the eminent are stripped of their usurpations; relatives and intimates are stripped of their greed. Meanwhile, the timid, the foolish, the lowly, and those distant from the ruler all have something to rely upon in doing good and something to restrain them from doing evil. It is like the march of the six armies, with eyes and ears, banners and drums to convey commands; like the use of boats and carriages, with masters and craftsmen to guide them; or like the practice of medicine, with established methods and case records to supply prescriptions. Those who follow this are secure; those who do not are endangered. Those who employ it live; those who do not die. By these means the outstanding men of the realm are set to work, its wicked and perverse men are subdued, its loyal and righteous men are stirred to action, and its obscure and hidden men are encouraged and brought forward. The means of rousing and inspiring them lie with me, yet they themselves do not perceive them. Surely the possessor of the realm does not delight in making such changes merely to prevail over those below him! For without commands there is no law, and without law there is no ruler. Thus law comes first, and the ruler’s position comes next. Ruler and law cannot, indeed, be separated for even a single day.

Such law is initially established for the sake of the realm; once established, even the ruler may not transgress it. Thus rewards and punishments accord with law, grants and deprivations accord with law, and dismissals and appointments accord with law. Ritual is deliberated upon by me, but wherever law applies, distinctions of rank and dignity are established through it. Standards are instituted by me, but wherever law applies, boundaries are made clear through it. Officials who enforce the law daily address me in accordance with it, and I myself dare not overstep it. Descendants who take me as their model daily scrutinize me by the law, and I myself dare not violate it. The Counsellor before me and the Aide behind me, the Recorder on the left and the Scribe on the right, daily serve me according to law, and I myself dare not throw it into disorder. The admonition concerning errors and forgetfulness…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
得於詩渙汗之說得於易儆戒無虞得於書如
神物之不敢侮如天墜地設而不敢犯以之而
制馭群動以之而整齊六合以之而安人心以
之而定天下天下之人相安於法守之中而無
倍叛侵陵之禍如陰陽異位而不瀆如萬物長
養而不衂此之謂以天下之道而民不倦天下
養於善而不自知聖人之道大矣哉自古有天
下者不患無法而患法立而不能乆不患法不
行而患法行而或變誠能訏謨遠猶而不為一
===
時之計詢謀用中而不出於一己之私是惟無
發發而必信是惟不行行之必堅不朝令而夕
改不旣舉而復墜則何患其不能乆然而復有
變焉者何哉變者變其所以害吾法者耳若法
善可乆而妄者或欲有所改易是之謂亂法亂
法者不容於堯舜之世此秦皇漢武之所以自
斃而祖宗不足法之說安石以之而誤神宗也
當哲宗時宋家法度不知其幾變而安世為是
言於乎其亦有所警矣

下者不患無法而患法立而不能久不患法不
行而患法行而或變誠能訏謨遠猶而不為一
===

善可久而妄者或欲有所改易是之謂亂法亂
法者不容於堯舜之世此秦皇漢武之所以自
斃而祖宗不足法之說安石以之而誤神宗也
當哲宗時宋家法度不知其幾變而安世為是
言於乎其亦有所警矣
punctuated:
得於《詩》，渙汗之說得於《易》，儆戒無虞得於《書》。如神物之不敢侮，如天墜地設而不敢犯，以之而制馭群動，以之而整齊六合，以之而安人心，以之而定天下。天下之人相安於法守之中，而無倍叛侵陵之禍，如陰陽異位而不瀆，如萬物長養而不衂。此之謂以天下之道而民不倦，天下養於善而不自知。聖人之道大矣哉！

自古有天下者，不患無法，而患法立而不能乆；不患法不行，而患法行而或變。誠能訏謨遠猶，而不為一時之計，詢謀用中，而不出於一己之私，是惟無發，發而必信；是惟不行，行之必堅。不朝令而夕改，不旣舉而復墜，則何患其不能乆？然而復有變焉者，何哉？變者，變其所以害吾法者耳。若法善可乆，而妄者或欲有所改易，是之謂亂法。亂法者不容於堯舜之世。此秦皇、漢武之所以自斃，而祖宗不足法之說，安石以之而誤神宗也。當哲宗時，宋家法度不知其幾變，而安世為是言，於乎！其亦有所警矣！
translation_en:
…is obtained from the Book of Odes; the teaching that proclamations issue like sweat comes from the Book of Changes; and the injunction to remain vigilant when there is no cause for anxiety comes from the Book of Documents. The laws are like sacred objects that one dares not treat with disrespect, like things laid down by Heaven and established by Earth [?] that one dares not violate. Through them, the ruler controls all activity, orders the six directions, sets people’s hearts at ease, and brings stability to all under Heaven. The people of the realm live peacefully together within the bounds of the established laws, free from the calamities of rebellion and aggression. They are like yin and yang, occupying distinct positions without encroaching upon each other, or the myriad things, growing and flourishing without injury. This is what is meant by employing the Way of all under Heaven so that the people do not weary: all under Heaven are nurtured in goodness without themselves knowing it. Great indeed is the Way of the sages!

Since antiquity, those who possess the realm have worried not about lacking laws, but about laws being established yet failing to endure; not about laws going unenforced, but about their being enforced and then altered. If they can truly make grand plans and take counsel for the distant future, rather than devise expedients for the moment, and consult others to adopt the proper mean, rather than act from personal self-interest, then they should either issue no command or, once issued, ensure it is trustworthy; either undertake no measure or, once undertaken, carry it out firmly. If they do not issue an order in the morning and change it by evening, or let a measure collapse after it has been instituted, why worry that their laws cannot endure? Yet changes are still made: why is this? What is changed is simply whatever harms our laws. If a law is good and capable of enduring, but some presumptuous person wishes to alter it, this is called disrupting the laws. Those who disrupt the laws would find no tolerance in the age of Yao and Shun. This is why the Qin emperor and Emperor Wu of Han brought ruin upon themselves; and Anshi 安石 used the claim that the imperial ancestors were not worthy of emulation to mislead Shenzong. By the time of Zhezong, the laws and institutions of the Song ruling house had undergone countless changes, and Anshi 安世 made this statement. Alas! Surely he, too, had something against which to warn!

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor: There are certainly many fine scholars in the discourse session, but the argument of this paper has a distinctive character of its own. Unusual, lucid, and magnificent, it draws upon the author's own insights. Its wording reaches beyond the topic, its meaning overflows its words, and its reasoning is also penetrating. It should be recorded as a model for those who follow convention and cannot free themselves from it.
Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, School Instructor: This discourse brims with extraordinary vitality. Yet in its unfolding and gathering, its restraint and emphasis, it never goes beyond the bounds of proper standards. One might indeed call it the outstanding performance of the session. Ah! I know that your self-cultivation, too, is profound.

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: I happened upon this discourse. Its conception is broad and profound, its phrasing striking and lofty. Like a celestial horse coursing through the sky, its very gait is naturally extraordinary. For this reason I promptly recorded it.
The discourse states: The sage has words through which he reaches all under Heaven. These are his means of moving them with divine efficacy, not of making fools of them. When the sage reaches all under Heaven through words, the extent of his influence may seem superficial. Yet the disparity in power and station is immense, and he cannot meet daily with everyone under Heaven; he therefore uses words to reach them. To reach them is to move them with divine efficacy, not to make fools of them. If, apart from words, he sought to employ techniques to inspire such awe in them, then the people of the world would be clamorous and confused, uncertain about what …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
從其視聖人不啻如神明在上莫敢仰視駭而
弗安渙而弗一而聖人之所以建法設教以為
圖治之道者亦將沮格而莫之信矣於乎曾謂
聖人神天下之術而有出于言之外者乎元城
劉氏論聖人鼓舞萬民之術而歸于命令此愚
所謂神之說而非惑之者也請申其意今夫聖
人之心之於天下之民道始欲其變也德始欲
其漸也禮始欲其飾倫節行也樂始欲其平欲
釋躁也刑始欲其不干也賞始欲其感受也然
===
天下若是其大也生民若是其衆也廣谷大川
通衢巨邑若是其異域也嗜欲言語習俗好尚
若是其不齊也不能一一盡如聖人之願徒使
聖人鬱紆其心而不平也不平非尤之也尤之
則將棄之矣聖人棄其民者乎聖人不棄其民
不得已而假命令以為鼓舞之術焉于以新天
下之耳目定天下之心志同天下之習尚自朝
廷遍於田野自天門敷於日出偃者起之退者
進之弱者強之畏者悅之洽比其懸絕之勢和

translation_en:
…whom to follow. They would regard the sage as nothing less than a divine being on high, whom none dared look up at: frightened and uneasy, dispersed and disunited. The laws and teachings that the sage establishes as the means of securing good government would likewise encounter obstruction, and no one would trust them. Alas! Could one really suppose that the sage’s art of exerting a spirit-like influence upon the world lies outside words? Master Liu of Yuancheng, discussing the sage’s art of inspiring and stirring the myriad people, attributed it to commands and ordinances. This is what I, in my humble view, mean by exerting a spirit-like influence upon them, rather than bewildering them. Let me elaborate upon his meaning. In the sage’s intentions toward the people of the world, the original purpose of the Way is to transform them; of virtue, to imbue them gradually; of ritual, to refine their human relationships and regulate their conduct; of music, to calm their desires and dispel their agitation; of punishments, to keep them from transgression; and of rewards, to move them to grateful acceptance.

Yet the world is so vast, its people so numerous! Broad valleys and great rivers, thoroughfares and immense cities belong to such varied regions; appetites and desires, speech, customs, and preferences differ so greatly. They cannot all, in every particular, accord fully with the sage’s wishes. This only leaves the sage’s heart troubled and unsettled. His unease does not mean that he blames them; to blame them would be to abandon them. Would a sage abandon his people? The sage does not abandon his people, and thus has no alternative but to employ commands and ordinances as the means of inspiring and stirring them. Through these he renews the eyes and ears of all under Heaven, steadies their hearts and purposes, and brings their customs and preferences into accord. From the court they extend throughout the fields; from the gates of Heaven they spread to where the sun rises. Those who lie idle he rouses; those who draw back he advances; the weak he strengthens; the fearful he gladdens. He draws together those whose stations are vastly separated, and harmonizes…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同其疎遠之情道大如天因令之發而變於道
也德輶如毛因令之發而漸於德也禮如履守
禮於發令之餘樂如豫陶樂於發令之後刑如
秋之肅殺惴惴聽罪而惟令之畏也賞如春之
熙和亹亹若德而惟令之悅也改更之均齊薰
染之神速趨向之果决不以高下如天地而息
流通之美也不以貴賤如冠屨而絶融貫之妙
也夫聖人之所以為術者亦神矣非申韓之刻
非黃老之深非儀秦之詐揆之於人情本之於
===
天道參之於群議决之於一心温良而有制簡
肅而有和厚重而有變渾涵而有方用無窮之
意無津涯推無滯礙出無疑謗公卿之所厲翼
郡縣之所欽承綴衣虎賁之所密觀吉士正人
之所樂遇懸之於並觀之地而無所訾議傳之
於無窮之世而無所改遷問之於所甚不屑之
人而無所誹間堅如金石信如寒暑著如日月
驚如雷霆沛如江河詩之所謂遐不作人書之
所謂四方風動孔子之所謂綏來動和者皆是

punctuated: 同其疎遠之情。道大如天，因令之發而變於道也；德輶如毛，因令之發而漸於德也。禮如履，守禮於發令之餘；樂如豫，陶樂於發令之後。刑如秋之肅殺，惴惴聽罪而惟令之畏也；賞如春之熙和，亹亹若德而惟令之悅也。改更之均齊，薰染之神速，趨向之果决，不以高下如天地而息流通之美也，不以貴賤如冠屨而絶融貫之妙也。夫聖人之所以為術者亦神矣！非申韓之刻，非黃老之深，非儀秦之詐。揆之於人情，本之於天道，參之於群議，决之於一心。温良而有制，簡肅而有和，厚重而有變，渾涵而有方。用無窮之意，無津涯，推無滯礙，出無疑謗。公卿之所厲翼，郡縣之所欽承，綴衣虎賁之所密觀，吉士正人之所樂遇。懸之於並觀之地而無所訾議，傳之於無窮之世而無所改遷，問之於所甚不屑之人而無所誹間。堅如金石，信如寒暑，著如日月，驚如雷霆，沛如江河。《詩》之所謂「遐不作人」，《書》之所謂「四方風動」，孔子之所謂「綏來動和」者，皆是
translation_en:
…bring their estranged sentiments into harmony. The Way is as vast as Heaven: through the promulgation of commands, people are transformed in accordance with the Way. Virtue is as light as a feather: through the promulgation of commands, people are gradually steeped in virtue. Ritual is a matter of treading the proper path: people observe ritual after commands have been issued. Music brings delight: people are cultivated through music after commands have been issued. Punishment resembles autumn’s stern destruction: trembling as they await judgment upon their offenses, people fear only the commands. Rewards resemble spring’s genial warmth: diligently responding to beneficence, people delight only in the commands. How uniform the resulting reforms, how wondrously swift their transforming influence, how resolute the direction people take! Differences of rank as great as those between Heaven and Earth do not impede the excellence of this pervasive influence; distinctions between noble and humble as pronounced as those between cap and shoes do not sever its wondrous power to unite and permeate.

Indeed, the methods employed by the sage are wondrous! They involve neither the harshness of Shen Buhai and Han Fei, nor the inscrutability of the teachings of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi, nor the deceit of Zhang Yi and Su Qin. They are measured against human feelings, grounded in the Way of Heaven, considered through collective deliberation, and resolved within a single mind. They are gentle and good, yet disciplined; simple and solemn, yet harmonious; substantial and grave, yet adaptable; all-embracing, yet possessed of definite principles. Their application embodies inexhaustible purpose and knows no bounds [?]; their extension encounters no obstruction, and their promulgation occasions neither suspicion nor slander. Dukes and ministers exert themselves to support them; prefectural and county authorities reverently receive them; wardrobe attendants and Tiger Guards observe them closely; worthy gentlemen and upright men gladly encounter them. Displayed where all may view them together, they occasion no criticism; transmitted through endless generations, they require no alteration; put even to those most disdainful of them, they admit no grounds for slander or disparagement. They are firm as metal and stone, dependable as cold and heat, manifest as the sun and moon, startling as thunder, and abundant as rivers. What the Book of Odes calls “Does he not nurture men?”, what the Book of Documents calls “The four quarters stir as before the wind,” and what Confucius calls “Give them peace, and they come; move them, and they become harmonious”—all these are…

術也。故聖人有是術焉，則耀衮垂旒，非歉也；承大任艱，非孤也；納琛受金，非虚也。蓋聖人之於民，不啻如家人父子，然而不起民幽隱難知之疑；而民之於聖人，亦習其所圖惟，熟其所經畫，而向之駭者以安，渙者以一矣。於乎！聖人之術之神，一至此乎！而豈愚之也哉？可見聖人為天下之主，命令為聖人之主，而聖人之心又命令之主矣。抑嘗因是考諸古之帝王矣。堯舜如天如神，而詢岳訪牧，命元官愷，亦皆有令以及其臣。至於湯武，則令之所及，反覆丁寧，委曲詳盡，至再三而弗置。蓋湯武之於堯舜，征誅揖遜，其事不同；性之反之，其德不同。故其時有順逆，令有繁簡，而要其為術則同也。於乎！此亦勢之使然，而豈聖人之所願哉？謹論。

translation_en:
…such is the method. Thus, when the sage possesses this method, he lacks nothing when wearing the splendid ceremonial robe and pendant-tasseled crown; he is not alone when shouldering great responsibilities and enduring hardship; and he does not receive precious tribute and gold without deserving them. For the sage treats the people as members of his own family, as father and sons, yet harbors no suspicion that their hidden circumstances are difficult to know. The people, in turn, become accustomed to his intentions and familiar with his plans. Those formerly alarmed become settled, and those formerly scattered become united. Ah! Can the wondrous efficacy of the sage’s method reach such a height? How could this be a matter of making the people ignorant? We can see that the sage governs all under Heaven, commands govern the sage, and the sage’s heart in turn governs his commands.
I have also, on this basis, examined the emperors and kings of antiquity. Yao and Shun were like Heaven and like spirits, yet they consulted the chiefs of the Four Mountains and the regional governors, and appointed the chief officers and the Kai [?]; in all these matters they issued commands to their ministers. As for Tang and Wu, their commands contained repeated earnest admonitions, addressing every detail fully and carefully, reiterated again and again without ceasing. Tang and Wu differed from Yao and Shun in their deeds: punitive conquest and execution, as against deferential abdication. They also differed in their virtue: returning to it through cultivation, as against possessing it by nature. Thus their circumstances differed in being favorable or adverse, and their commands in being elaborate or simple; but fundamentally their method was the same. Ah! This too was brought about by the force of circumstances. How could it have been what the sages wished? Respectfully submitted as a discourse.
Memorial
A memorial composed in the role of a grand secretary, thanking the emperor for the gift of a silver seal inscribed “Correct faults and rectify errors.” The twenty-second year of Yongle [1424].
The concluding text 謹然 is unclear [?].

…Shun opened his ears and clarified his sight; Yu hung bells and drums, seeking to be instructed in the Way as ruler. Yue served as a boat and as timely rain, hoping with united purpose to set his sovereign right. From the Three Dynasties onward, rulers prized the achievement of unity in virtue. Wishing to pursue “long gan” [?], they humbled themselves to endure the humiliation of treating a minister as their teacher; seeking the “seven examinations” [?], they willingly accepted the doubts surrounding a young sovereign. Yet they did no more than halt the imperial carriage to receive counsel, obliging ministers to tug at their robes to offer remonstrance. When a minister removed his cap in the ancestral temple, gentle words only occasionally warned against taking advantage of a perilous situation; when a minister laid his audience tablet upon the hall steps, anger appeared over the sovereign’s dying charge. Though rulers placed great expectations upon their ministers, they did not necessarily follow all their advice; though considerate in their treatment of subordinates, they could not be wholly without shame in their hearts.
Now we humbly encounter Your Majesty the Emperor, who has received the destiny that comes once in a thousand years, whose virtue matches Heaven and Earth. Your sincerity and filial devotion spring from the heart: while acting as regent, you declined birthday congratulations. You take magnanimity and benevolence as your standard: when reading a memorial, you pardoned an error of a single character. Early you attended the Gao Emperor, and then succeeded your illustrious deceased father. You opened the granaries as circumstances required, discerning profoundly the factors that determine whether the people’s hearts turn toward or away from their ruler…

translation_en:
…cannot be changed; what must be preserved in the institutions is precisely what must be preserved in the Way. Ah! This is why our dynasty’s Collected Statutes (Huidian) partakes of the subtle workings of creation and accords with what is fitting both now and in antiquity. None but our Sagely Progenitor could have founded it at the outset; none but our Emperor Jing and our present Emperor could have brought it to completion thereafter! How splendid and admirable! Allow me respectfully to set this forth.

Whenever a dynasty arises, it must have its own statutes. In these lie the means to hold the people’s hearts together and to sustain the lifeblood of the state. Thus, in the age of Tang and Yu, the Canons and Counsels were composed; in the age of Yu of Xia, statutes and standards were bequeathed. Shang had its counsels, and Zhou its ritual institutions. All these were rooted in what their rulers had personally practiced and inwardly understood, and took outward form in laws, regulations, and affairs. They were applied within households, states, and courts, and extended beyond the Four Seas and Nine Provinces. Thus, Yao and Shun ruled All-under-Heaven for nearly a hundred years, Xia for more than four hundred years, Shang for more than six hundred years, and Zhou for more than eight hundred years. It was surely through these institutions that they could enjoy Heaven’s favor and secure enduring blessings for their successors.

…seem comprehensive, yet they were not the institutions of the Zhou at its height. The Song’s Collected Essentials followed the Tang precedent, but even at the time there was criticism that it was founded on contemporary preferences and confined to the “three gates” [?]. The Yuan’s Compendium for Ordering the World drew upon both Tang and Song precedents. Yet with their barbarian ways, reeking of flesh and mutton, how could they have any part in the great Way of our former kings?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, endowed with sagely and divine qualities and civil and martial abilities, encountered the moment when Heaven bestowed its favor and the people gave their allegiance. Thus he was able to recover All under Heaven from the hands of those who were not of our people and directly resume the tradition through which the ancient sovereigns established their ruling houses and states. This was an achievement unprecedented since the beginning of the world. He once commanded the compilation of a book, Duties of All Offices, fully recording the official organization and regulations of the time. Examining antiquity, he established offices and apportioned responsibilities among the six ministers. His sagacious plans and divine calculations far surpassed those of all preceding ages: this was truly a magnificent, unalterable canon. Yet the book was compiled in the middle years of the Hongwu reign, and many changes were made in its final years. As our successive sage emperors inherited the throne, they increasingly honored the task of carrying forward their predecessor’s work. After successive reigns of prosperity and good government, however, differences in retention and reform, reduction and augmentation could not be avoided [?]. These arose from the times and also from circumstances. Yet all remained in accord with the intentions of our sagely founder in establishing the institutions.
When Emperor Yingzong Rui was restored to the throne, he once wished to compile the regulations as a continuation of the Duties…

translation_en:
…as a continuation of Official Functions (Zhizhang), but the work was not brought to completion. Heaven presumably awaited the proper moment—how could this have been mere chance? In the tenth year of his reign, Emperor Xiaozong Jing, earnestly intent upon carrying on his predecessors’ work, commanded his scholarly officials to collect the institutions and regulations of successive reigns and compile them into a single work, entitled the Collected Statutes of the Great Ming (Da Ming huidian). Its institutions took the Sagely Founder as their sole model, and its guiding principles took Official Functions as their basis. The various imperially promulgated books were arranged by category, and precedents from successive years were appended, so that officials would take charge of their proper affairs and each affair would fall within its appropriate office. Thus the institutions of our Ming dynasty were comprehensively set forth: nothing great was lacking, and no detail was omitted. Like the sun and stars shining down, like Heaven covering and Earth sustaining all things, this work truly accorded, across different ages, with the ancient canons and counsels, authoritative rules, words of counsel, and ritual institutions. Looking down upon the works produced under the Han, Tang, and Song, would it not put them to shame?
In the fourth year after ascending the throne, His Majesty the present Emperor again commanded scholarly officials to revise and correct the work, and to print and distribute it within and beyond the capital, so that all would know to observe it. Might the heavenly spirits of our one founding emperor and two ancestral emperors, who had cared so earnestly about this book, thereby find some small consolation? You, sir, have further deigned to inquire of [?] about the major instances of institutional continuity and change, reduction and addition…

…learning. Yet how could someone of my humble station, outside official service, be qualified to know the deliberations of the imperial court? Let me venture to mention one or two examples.
At the beginning of the dynasty, imperial princes once headed the Court of the Imperial Clan. Now only one high minister from among the meritorious nobility or imperial relatives is employed, and the full complement of offices is not maintained. At the beginning of the dynasty, offices were established for the Three Dukes. Now these are merely additional or posthumous titles conferred upon high ministers, and their offices are no longer established. The seals of the Secretaries in the Ministry of Personnel were abolished, and responsibility for much of their business devolved upon the Directors. The posts of Expectant Officials at the palace gates were eliminated, and their duties were placed under the concurrent supervision of the Hanlin Academy. The office of Household Administrator of the Heir Apparent had originally not existed; subsequently, such officials as the Household Administrator, Junior Household Administrator, and Assistant Administrator were appointed to divide responsibility for its affairs. This was to give due weight to the officials of the heir apparent’s household. Supervising Secretaries and Investigating Censors were formerly selected together as a category. Now their ability and bearing must be examined before they are appointed to office. This is to give due weight to the censorial and remonstrance offices.
Other examples include the conversion of the Ceremonial Office into the Court of State Ceremonial, the attachment of the Muslim Astronomical Bureau to the Directorate of Astronomy, the abolition of the judicial offices of the Five Chief Military Commissions, and the increase in the authorized number of Secretaries in the Six Ministries. translation_en:
…the Sagely Progenitor; and the provision thereby made to protect and guide our sagely sons and divine grandsons was indeed consummate. It was completed under our Emperor Jing and the present Emperor; was their fulfillment of the legacy of our Sagely Progenitor not profound? For the mind of the Sagely Progenitor is precisely the mind of these two sage sovereigns, and the way these two sage sovereigns govern All under Heaven is precisely the way the Sagely Progenitor governed All under Heaven. Thus it is said: “Earlier sages and later sages follow the same standard.”

Whenever any policy or ordinance is revised, they must say: “The uniform laws of our imperial ancestors remain fully intact; we dare not impair them through our own selfish interests.” Whenever any office or official post is changed, they must say: “Our imperial ancestors’ plans for bequeathing peace to their descendants remain fully in place; we dare not undermine them on account of others’ words.” If this is so, then…

translation_en:
…Heaven will surely accept their selflessness, and the people will all turn in allegiance to those possessed of virtue. Thus the realm of our Ming will be handed down for countless millions of years without deterioration. Respectfully submitted.
Second Question
Huang Luzeng
Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor: “You answer point by point, clearly setting out the merits of the Zhou dynasty’s establishment of offices and the Western Han’s management of military forces, as readily as taking something from a pouch. At the end you have something further to say, yet do not express it fully. Ah! Those who understand the needs of the times are outstanding men. Might you be such a man?”
Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, School Instructor: “Establishing offices and managing military forces are weighty affairs of state. You can enumerate the particulars in your answer: might you, too, have long harbored aspirations like those of Xiwen [Fan Zhongyan] when he was still a commoner? Your answers are all good, but we cannot record them all. For now we record one, to assist those who deliberate on affairs of state.”
Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher: “The system of offices follows the Offices of Zhou; our dynasty has weighed ancient and present practices and already established a settled system. As for military organization, you regard Han methods as inadequate and further maintain that substantial reform is indispensable. I imagine you must have insights uniquely your own, which you could expound at length, like Dong Zhongshu and Jia Yi, in an answer before the imperial court. I certainly have high expectations of you.”
Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor-in-Waiting: “Earlier Confucian scholars already expressed doubts about the Zhou dynasty’s establishment of offices. Your discussion of holding offices concurrently does indeed show insight. Western Han military methods are recorded in scattered passages of Ban Gu’s History of the Han. You bring them together and discuss them as clearly as if pointing to something in your palm. Without having given them sustained attention, one could hardly grasp them fully at short notice. The discussion at the end of your essay is especially outstanding. Ah! …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子之所負則大矣如有用我者請執此以往
對治天下必資于官建官惟其賢而不必
備其人威天下必資于兵治兵惟其要而
不必論其勢此成周建官之制所以名雖
存而實不具事雖瑣而規寔閎西京治兵
之灋所以內若輕而寔則重外若重而寔
則輕者有以也哉今夫無曠庶官天工人
代官之不可不建也其昉于庖羲之代乎
唐虞之疇咨夏商之用乂一皆祖述其道
===
云耳降及于周監觀二代文治蔚興建官
之制始為備矣今周禮一書固可以覽其
切焉天生五材誰能去兵兵之不可不設
也其肇于軒轅之世乎虞廷之命士成周
之詰兵一皆依緣其法云耳下至于漢甫
離戰國去古未遠治兵之灋猶有存者今
班固一史固可以攷其凡焉雖然周禮作
而冬官失其傳班史脩而兵制失其紀是
亦豈非宇宙間之一大缺典也哉且執事

translation_en:
…Great indeed is the responsibility you bear! If someone should employ you, I ask that you take these principles with you.

Answer: Governing All under Heaven necessarily depends on officials. In establishing offices, what matters is the worthiness of those appointed, rather than filling every post. Commanding awe throughout All under Heaven necessarily depends on armed forces. In organizing them, what matters is grasping the essentials, rather than considering their apparent strength. There are reasons why, under the perfected Zhou system of establishing offices, titles could remain without all the posts actually being filled, and why its arrangements, though minute, were broad in conception. There are likewise reasons why, under the Western Han system of military organization, forces at the center appeared weak but were actually strong, while those outside appeared strong but were actually weak.

Now, “Let none of the many offices lie neglected”; “Heaven’s work is performed by men in its stead.” Officials therefore could not but be appointed. Did this practice begin in the age of Paoxi? The consultations under Tang and Yu, and the employment of men to bring order under Xia and Shang, all simply followed and carried forward this way. When the Zhou arose, it took the two preceding dynasties as its models, and civil governance flourished. Only then did the system of establishing offices become complete. In the surviving book, the Rites of Zhou, we can indeed survey its particulars [?].

“Heaven produced the five materials; who can dispense with arms?” Armed forces therefore could not but be established. Did this begin in the age of Xuanyuan? The appointment of a judicial officer at the court of Yu and the ordering of military affairs under the perfected Zhou all simply followed his methods. By the Han, the age of the Warring States had only recently ended, and antiquity was not yet distant; some methods of military organization still survived. In Ban Gu’s history, we can indeed examine their general outlines.

Nevertheless, although the Rites of Zhou was composed, its section on the Ministry of Works was lost to transmission; although Ban Gu’s history was compiled, the military system went unrecorded. Is this not a great lacuna in the records of the world? Moreover, you, sir, …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之所以疑于周之制者謂其官多而民擾
也愚則以為六官之屬雖衆至五萬餘人
大氐多兼官也何以言之周公以三公而
兼冢宰召公以三公而兼宗伯蘇公以三
公而兼司寇畢公毛公以三公而兼司馬
司空夫其大者然且兼之而况于百官羣
有司乎故三公或兼鄉老如二鄉則公一
人是已六卿或兼鄉大夫如一鄉則卿一
人是已六卿或兼六軍之將如軍將皆命
===
卿是已甚者太公以太師而兼司盟之職
所謂載在盟府太師職之是已蘇公以三
公而兼太史之職所謂太史司寇蘇公是
已以至掌荼掌葛之屬無事則不置也行
司馬輿司馬之類臨事而後設也矧又以
成王之賢輔以周公之聖論定而官而官
不及私昵位定而祿而爵罔及惡德而焉
至如執事之所慮也哉愚所謂建官惟其
賢而不必備其人者良以是耳執事之所

punctuated: 之所以疑于周之制者，謂其官多而民擾也。愚則以為，六官之屬雖衆至五萬餘人，大氐多兼官也。何以言之？周公以三公而兼冢宰，召公以三公而兼宗伯，蘇公以三公而兼司寇，畢公、毛公以三公而兼司馬、司空。夫其大者然且兼之，而况于百官羣有司乎？故三公或兼鄉老，如「二鄉則公一人」是已；六卿或兼鄉大夫，如「一鄉則卿一人」是已；六卿或兼六軍之將，如「軍將皆命卿」是已。甚者，太公以太師而兼司盟之職，所謂「載在盟府，太師職之」是已；蘇公以三公而兼太史之職，所謂「太史司寇蘇公」是已。以至掌荼、掌葛之屬，無事則不置也；行司馬、輿司馬之類，臨事而後設也。矧又以成王之賢，輔以周公之聖，論定而官，而官不及私昵；位定而祿，而爵罔及惡德。而焉至如執事之所慮也哉？愚所謂建官惟其賢而不必備其人者，良以是耳。執事之所
translation_en:
…Your reason for doubting the Zhou system is that its numerous officials burdened the people. In my humble view, although the personnel of the six ministries numbered over fifty thousand, many generally held concurrent offices. How can I substantiate this? The Duke of Zhou, while serving as one of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Minister of State; the Duke of Shao, as one of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Minister of Rites; the Duke of Su, as one of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Minister of Justice; and the Dukes of Bi and Mao, as members of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Minister of War and Minister of Works respectively. If even the highest offices were held concurrently, how much more must this have been true of the hundred officials and the various administrative officers?

Thus, members of the Three Dukes sometimes concurrently served as district elders, as indicated by “For every two districts, there is one duke.” The Six Ministers sometimes concurrently served as district grand masters, as indicated by “For each district, there is one minister.” The Six Ministers sometimes concurrently commanded the six armies, as indicated by “The army commanders are all appointed ministers.” Beyond this, the Grand Duke, while serving as Grand Preceptor, concurrently performed the duties of Supervisor of Covenants, as indicated by “It is recorded in the covenant repository, of which the Grand Preceptor has charge.” The Duke of Su, as one of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Grand Scribe, as indicated by “The Grand Scribe and Minister of Justice, the Duke of Su.” As for such officers as those in charge of thatching rushes and kudzu, they were not appointed when there was no work to do. Officers such as the Commandant of Marches and the Commandant of Chariots were appointed only when a task arose.

Moreover, with the worthy King Cheng assisted by the sage Duke of Zhou, appointments followed a settled assessment of merit, and office was not granted to personal favorites; stipends followed the determination of rank, and titles were not bestowed on men of evil character. How, then, could matters have reached the state you fear? This is precisely why I humbly maintain that, in establishing offices, one should appoint only worthy men, without necessarily filling every post. Your reason for…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以疑於漢之灋者謂其將不專而兵不眾
也愚則以為兵制之善自三代以還莫漢
若也何以言之民年二十始傅二十三為
正卒五十六免為庶人是調民有限也每
歲戍邊不過三日至于治城郭築堤防轉
輸力役皆官予庸直是役民有限也其調
發也率皆近地而無遠征之勞其繇役也
率皆自悉而無供億之費有事則檄召而
官無困于賛食事已即罷歸而民亦得以
===
力作將帥奉朝請而無擁兵專制之虞都
試課殿最而無驕蹇難用之患兵農未分
內外相制故當時兵之隸于南北軍者雖
僅盈萬人而不聞有單弱之虞盖兵不常
役則佚而不怨在官之日少則有餘力而
不疲矧又上有仁明之主下有畫一之臣
公卿子弟咸備宿衛材官騎士徧滿郡國
而亦焉至如執事之所云也哉愚所謂治
兵惟其要而不必論其勢者職此之繇耳

也愚則以爲兵制之善自三代以還莫漢
若也何以言之民年二十始傅二十三爲
正卒五十六免爲庶人是調民有限也每

輸力役皆官主庸直是役民有限也其調

率皆自悉而無供億之費有事則檄召而
官無困于贅食事已即罷歸而民亦得以
===

試課殿最而無驕蹇難用之患兵農未分

不疲矧又上有仁明之主下有畫一之臣
公卿子弟咸備宿衛材官騎士徧滿郡國
而亦焉至如執事之所云也哉愚所謂治
兵惟其要而不必論其勢者職此之繇耳
punctuated: 以疑於漢之灋者，謂其將不專而兵不眾也。愚則以為兵制之善，自三代以還，莫漢若也。何以言之？民年二十始傅，二十三為正卒，五十六免為庶人，是調民有限也。每歲戍邊不過三日，至于治城郭、築堤防、轉輸力役，皆官予庸直，是役民有限也。其調發也，率皆近地，而無遠征之勞；其繇役也，率皆自悉，而無供億之費。有事則檄召，而官無困于賛食；事已即罷歸，而民亦得以力作。將帥奉朝請，而無擁兵專制之虞；都試課殿最，而無驕蹇難用之患。兵農未分，內外相制，故當時兵之隸于南北軍者，雖僅盈萬人，而不聞有單弱之虞。盖兵不常役，則佚而不怨；在官之日少，則有餘力而不疲。矧又上有仁明之主，下有畫一之臣，公卿子弟咸備宿衛，材官騎士徧滿郡國，而亦焉至如執事之所云也哉？愚所謂治兵惟其要而不必論其勢者，職此之繇耳。
translation_en:
…the reason you doubt the Han system is that its commanders lacked exclusive authority and its troops were few. I, however, believe that in the excellence of its military institutions, no dynasty since the Three Dynasties equaled the Han. Why do I say this? Men were first entered on the service registers at twenty, became regular soldiers at twenty-three, and were discharged at fifty-six to become commoners: thus there were limits to the conscription of the people. Border garrison duty amounted to no more than three days each year. As for repairing city walls, building embankments, transporting supplies, and performing labor services, the government paid wages for all these tasks: thus there were limits to the labor imposed on the people. When men were mobilized, they generally served nearby, without the toil of distant expeditions; their corvée service was generally undertaken by themselves [?], without the expense of furnishing supplies. When an emergency arose, they were summoned by dispatch, yet the government was not burdened with provisioning them. Once the matter was settled, they were immediately discharged home, and the people could resume their productive labor.

Commanders attended court audiences, so there was no danger of their retaining troops and exercising unchecked power. General military reviews assessed the worst and best performers, so there was no trouble with arrogant, insubordinate soldiers who were difficult to employ. Soldiers and farmers had not yet become separate groups, and forces within and outside the capital checked one another. Thus, although the troops attached to the Southern and Northern Armies at that time numbered barely ten thousand, we hear of no concern about their weakness. Because soldiers were not constantly on duty, they had rest and bore no resentment; because their days in government service were few, they retained surplus strength and were not exhausted. Moreover, above there was a benevolent and discerning ruler, and below there were ministers who maintained uniform administration. The sons and younger relatives of the highest officials all served as palace guards, while trained infantry and cavalry filled the commanderies and kingdoms. How, then, could matters have reached the condition you describe? This alone is why I say that managing an army requires grasping its essentials, without necessarily judging it by its apparent strength.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
於乎由西周之制觀之使其子孫能守而
勿失則天下至今猶存可也惜也穆王耄
荒而周之道缺焉陵遲至于幽厲極矣由
西京之灋觀之使其子孫能守之弗忘則
天下至今猶存可也惜也武帝紛更而漢
之業衰焉因循至於哀平蕩矣然則後之
君天下者必欲盡行周禮固不能也姑取
其遺訓而斟酌之師其意而不師其迹可
也必欲盡行漢灋亦不能也姑取其遺制
===
而參會之損其過而益其所不及可也不
然則亦奚足以為治也哉今
國家建官倣于周禮而適夫繁簡之宜治兵
陋乎西漢而得夫輕重之要固無容議矣
第百餘年来不能不少變于
初者亦其勢之使然也為今之計官有定員
職有常守因仍舊貫亦無不可至于兵制
非大有所更張則愚未見其可也執事儻
與其進尚當以三代治兵之灋為

非大有所更張則愚未見其可也執事儻
與其進尚當以三代治兵之瀍為
punctuated:
於乎！由西周之制觀之，使其子孫能守而勿失，則天下至今猶存可也。惜也，穆王耄荒，而周之道缺焉，陵遲至于幽厲極矣。由西京之灋觀之，使其子孫能守之弗忘，則天下至今猶存可也。惜也，武帝紛更，而漢之業衰焉，因循至於哀平蕩矣。然則後之君天下者，必欲盡行周禮，固不能也；姑取其遺訓而斟酌之，師其意而不師其迹，可也。必欲盡行漢灋，亦不能也；姑取其遺制而參會之，損其過而益其所不及，可也。不然，則亦奚足以為治也哉？
今國家建官倣于周禮，而適夫繁簡之宜；治兵陋乎西漢，而得夫輕重之要，固無容議矣。第百餘年来，不能不少變于初者，亦其勢之使然也。為今之計，官有定員，職有常守，因仍舊貫，亦無不可。至于兵制，非大有所更張，則愚未見其可也。執事儻與其進，尚當以三代治兵之灋為
translation_en:
Alas! Judging from the institutions of the Western Zhou, had its descendants been able to preserve them without loss, its rule over the realm might have endured even to this day. Regrettably, King Mu grew old and heedless, and the Way of Zhou was impaired. Its decline reached its utmost under Kings You and Li. Judging from the laws of the Western Han, had its descendants been able to uphold them without forgetting them, its rule over the realm might likewise have endured to this day. Regrettably, Emperor Wu made changes in profusion, and the enterprise of Han declined. Through continued neglect, it fell into ruin under Emperors Ai and Ping. Thus, for later rulers of the realm, implementing the rites of Zhou in their entirety is certainly impossible. They may, however, take its surviving teachings and weigh them carefully, following their intent rather than their outward forms. Implementing the laws of Han in their entirety is likewise impossible. They may, however, take its surviving institutions and adapt them together, reducing their excesses and supplementing their deficiencies. Otherwise, how could these suffice to bring about good government?
Our present dynasty has modeled its establishment of offices on the Rites of Zhou, achieving a suitable balance between complexity and simplicity. In organizing its military, it puts the Western Han to shame and grasps the essentials of the proper distribution of power. These arrangements certainly leave no room for criticism. Yet over more than a hundred years, some departure from the original arrangements has been unavoidable; circumstances themselves have brought this about. For present purposes, offices have fixed complements and posts have regular duties, so there is nothing wrong with continuing established practices. As for the military system, however, unless substantial reforms are made, I cannot see how it will serve. Should you, sir, approve my advancement, I would further offer the methods of military organization of the Three Dynasties to…

text:
當宁獻
第三問
晉憲
同考試官教諭楊批人物一策非素有學識
