其爲孰是不從三國之言而竟遼漢天
punctuated: 夫匈奴未滅，何以家爲，是也；而或乃多請田宅，何歟？入府端坐，召斬弄臣，是也；而或乃望塵下拜，何歟？詩書禮樂足以彊晉矣，而作文賦者何以有河橋之敗？禮義廉耻足以霸齊矣，而作四維論者何以有伾文之附？蕭曹舊隙，胡何卒而參相？張陳舊德，胡耳王而餘戮？記書三篋與藏書萬卷者，其事君孰優？教子以襴與遺子以經者，其傳家孰善？或以布被而取譏，或以布被而見美，孰得乎？或用鉤距而得事情，或用鉤距而固君寵，孰賢乎？或勸舉進士而不應，與勸無舉進士而不從者，其故何歟？或勸見宰相而不肯，與上書宰相而不嫌者，其故何歟？從帝至咸陽而獨收圖籍，與從主征伐而獨收人物者，其見孰高？大將軍尊重而獨長揖，與相王尊重而輒下拜者，其爲孰是？不從三國之言而竟達漢天
translation_en:
To say, “The Xiongnu have not yet been destroyed; what need have I of a home?” was right. Yet another man repeatedly requested fields and residences: why? To enter the government office, sit upright, and summon an imperial favorite for execution was right. Yet another man prostrated himself at the mere sight of the dust raised by an approaching carriage: why? The Odes, Documents, rites, and music sufficed to strengthen Jin; why, then, did the author of the Rhapsody on Literature suffer defeat at Heqiao? Ritual propriety, righteousness, integrity, and a sense of shame sufficed to make Qi hegemon; why, then, did the author of the Discourse on the Four Bonds attach himself to Wang Pi and Wang Shuwen? Xiao He and Cao Can had an old estrangement: why did Can become chief minister upon He’s death? Zhang Er and Chen Yu had previously shown kindness to one another: why did Er become a king while Yu was executed? Of the man who could recall the writings in three chests and the man who collected ten thousand scrolls of books, which served his ruler better? Of the man who instructed his son by means of a robe [?] and the man who bequeathed a classic to his son, which better transmitted his family’s legacy?

One man incurred criticism for using a cloth quilt, while another was praised for doing so: which acted properly? One used probing and cross-checking to discover the facts of affairs; another used such methods to secure his ruler’s favor: which was worthier? One was urged to present himself for the jinshi examination but did not respond; another was urged not to present himself but would not comply: what were their reasons? One was urged to visit the chief minister but refused; another had no scruples about submitting a letter to the chief minister: what were their reasons? One followed the emperor to Xianyang and alone collected maps and records; another accompanied his ruler on campaigns and alone gathered talented men: whose insight was superior? One alone greeted the highly honored General-in-Chief with a deep bow while remaining standing; another readily prostrated himself before the highly honored Prince of Xiang: whose conduct was right? The man who would not heed the words of the three states and ultimately conveyed the Han Son of Heaven’s …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子之命與不從楚字之令而卒致晉君
之語者其忠同歟異歟不受故人之請
而竟卻其金與雖受府丞之餽而輒懸
其魚者其廉同歟異歟免胄見回紇與
去兜鍪見突厥者其事奇矣而或者未
免有輕身損威之懼矯命破莎車與矯
命誅郅支者其功偉矣而議者未免有
邀功生事之嫌或天下無冤民或天下
無冤獄何所爲而若是或民不能欺或
===
民不忍欺奚所事而臻茲耻其君不爲
堯舜老臣自任之重也而後世有美其
君爲堯舜者然乎不然乎諫人主不當
觀史史臣所守之職也而異時有錄上
其書者可乎不可乎凡此之類難以一
二數記願聞所以折衷之道毋徒諉曰
夫我則不暇
問生民之休戚係守令之賢否
國家重守令之選必取於科目之傑其雄郡

其魚者其廉同歟異歟免胄見回紇與
去幾登見突厥者其事奇矣而或者未

邀功生事之嫌或天下無冤民或天下
無冤獄何所爲而若是或民不能欺或
===
民不忍欺奚所事而臻茲祉其君不爲
堯舜若臣自任之重也而後世有美其
君爲堯舜者然乎不然乎諫人主不當
觀史史臣所守之職也而異時有録上
其書者可乎不可乎凡此之類難以一
二數記頗聞所以折衷之道毋徒諉曰
夫我則不暇
問生民之休戚係守令之賢否
國家重守令之選必取於科目之傑其雄郡
punctuated:
子之命，與不從楚字之令而卒致晉君之語者，其忠同歟異歟？不受故人之請而竟卻其金，與雖受府丞之餽而輒懸其魚者，其廉同歟異歟？免胄見回紇，與去兜鍪見突厥者，其事奇矣，而或者未免有輕身損威之懼；矯命破莎車，與矯命誅郅支者，其功偉矣，而議者未免有邀功生事之嫌。或天下無冤民，或天下無冤獄，何所爲而若是？或民不能欺，或民不忍欺，奚所事而臻茲？耻其君不爲堯舜，老臣自任之重也，而後世有美其君爲堯舜者，然乎不然乎？諫人主不當觀史，史臣所守之職也，而異時有錄上其書者，可乎不可乎？凡此之類，難以一二數記，願聞所以折衷之道，毋徒諉曰：「夫我則不暇。」

問：生民之休戚，係守令之賢否。國家重守令之選，必取於科目之傑，其雄郡
translation_en:
…the command of the Han Son of Heaven, and the one who disobeyed the order of Chu zi [?] but ultimately conveyed the words of the ruler of Jin: was their loyalty alike or different? The one who refused an old friend's request and ultimately rejected his gold, and the one who accepted a gift from an Assistant Prefect but promptly hung up the fish: was their integrity alike or different? Removing one's helmet to meet the Huihe, and taking off one's helmet to meet the Tujue—these were extraordinary deeds, yet some could not help fearing that they put their persons at risk and diminished their authority. Falsely claiming imperial authorization to conquer Shache, and falsely claiming imperial authorization to execute Zhizhi—these were great achievements, yet critics could not help suspecting that they sought personal merit and stirred up trouble. Under one, there were no wronged people in the realm; under another, there were no unjustly adjudicated cases. What did they do to bring this about? One could not be deceived by the people; another the people could not bear to deceive. By what conduct did they attain these results? To feel ashamed that one's ruler was not a Yao or Shun shows how weighty a responsibility a veteran minister took upon himself. Yet in later ages some praised their rulers as Yao and Shun. Was this right or wrong? To remonstrate that the sovereign ought not to read the historical records was to uphold the duty of a court historian. Yet at another time someone copied out his history and presented it to the throne. Was this permissible or not? Instances of this kind are too numerous to enumerate individually. We wish to hear the principles by which you would arrive at a balanced judgment. Do not merely evade the matter by saying, “For my part, I have no time.”

Question: The well-being and suffering of the people depend on whether prefects and magistrates are worthy. The state attaches great importance to selecting prefects and magistrates and invariably chooses outstanding men from the examination graduates. As for its major prefectures…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
巨邑
畿甸內輔之地尤加之意非敏銳通達豈弟
樂易者不以輕授而荷茲任者亦往往
感激思奮勉稱
上意若皆足以副牧民之責者而今之民日益
窮訟日益繁轉徙流亡者日益衆何歟
豈墨吏未盡去考課之法未盡嚴歟考
課之法古人有行之者其得失異同可
考也然有謂歷六代而考績之法不著
===
闋七聖而課試之要未立者何歟有官
必有課有課必有賞罰有官無課是無
官也有課無賞罰是無課也顧其法在
人用之何如耳方今
聖明在上賢宰輔在下銓衡公而考課嚴百司
庶府黽勉奉職惴惴焉唯恐清議之或
及課試之失最者蓋不獨守令為然也
而民生未安固自守令之不得人始豈
考課之法果不足賴歟抑別有其故歟
alt_text:
巨邑
畿甸內輔之地尤加之意非敏銳通達豈𡻕
樂易者不以輕授而荷玆任者亦往往
感激恩奋勉稱
上意若皆足以副牧民之責者而今之民日益
窮訟日益繁轉徙流亡者日益衆何歟
豈墨吏未盡去考課之法未盡嚴歟考
課之法古人有行之者其得失異同可
考也然有謂歷六代而考績之法不著
===
闕七聖而課試之要未立者何歟有官
必有課有課必有賞罰有官無課是無
官也有課無賞罰是無課也顧其法在
人用之何如耳方今
聖明在上賢宰輔在下銓衡公而考課嚴百司
庶府罔不勉奉職惴惴焉唯恐淸議之或
及課試之失最者盖不獨守令爲然也
而民生未安固自守令之不得人始豈
考課之法果不足賴歟抑別有其故歟
punctuated: 巨邑、畿甸內輔之地，尤加之意，非敏銳通達、豈弟樂易者，不以輕授。而荷茲任者，亦往往感激思奮，勉稱上意，若皆足以副牧民之責者。而今之民日益窮，訟日益繁，轉徙流亡者日益衆，何歟？豈墨吏未盡去，考課之法未盡嚴歟？考課之法，古人有行之者，其得失異同可考也。然有謂「歷六代而考績之法不著，闋七聖而課試之要未立」者，何歟？有官必有課，有課必有賞罰；有官無課，是無官也；有課無賞罰，是無課也。顧其法在人用之何如耳。方今聖明在上，賢宰輔在下，銓衡公而考課嚴，百司庶府黽勉奉職，惴惴焉唯恐清議之或及、課試之失最者，蓋不獨守令為然也。而民生未安，固自守令之不得人始，豈考課之法果不足賴歟？抑別有其故歟？
translation_en:
…large counties and places within the capital region that form its inner bulwark receive particular attention. Appointments are not lightly bestowed upon anyone lacking acuity, sound judgment, gentleness, and an agreeable disposition. Those who shoulder these responsibilities, moreover, are often moved by gratitude to exert themselves, striving to meet the sovereign’s expectations. They would all seem capable of fulfilling their responsibility to shepherd the people. Yet today the people grow poorer by the day, litigation becomes ever more abundant, and ever more people migrate or flee their homes. Why is this? Is it because corrupt officials have not all been removed, or because the procedures for evaluating officials’ performance are not sufficiently strict?

The ancients practiced methods of performance evaluation, and their successes and failures, similarities and differences, can be investigated. Yet why has it been said that “through six dynasties, methods of evaluating merit remained unclear, and through seven sage rulers [?], the essentials of assessing performance had still not been established”? Wherever there are officials, there must be evaluations; wherever there are evaluations, there must be rewards and punishments. To have officials without evaluations is as though there were no officials; to have evaluations without rewards and punishments is as though there were no evaluations. It depends only on how people apply these methods.

Now an enlightened sage sovereign reigns above, with worthy chief ministers serving below. Selection and appointment are impartial, and performance evaluations are strict. Officials throughout the various agencies and offices diligently discharge their duties, anxiously fearing that public criticism might touch them or that they might fail to obtain the highest assessment. This is certainly not true only of prefects and magistrates. Yet the people’s livelihood remains insecure, and this surely begins with the failure to obtain suitable men as prefects and magistrates. Can the methods of performance evaluation really be inadequate to rely upon? Or is there some other cause?

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
願詳言之以為當道者助
問財賦者邦國之大本生人之喉命天下
治亂輕重繫焉而不可忽也理財之道
莫詳於周官說者謂周官為致太平之
書信則然矣後世亦有用之而不效者
何歟不知由周以前周官未作其理財
之道何如也由周以後歷秦漢唐宋之
世其理財之道何如也嘗考前代創業
之君恭儉愛下財用不期足而自足至
===
於中世則侈費而用乏物理人事消息
盈虛亦自有然者當時喜事之臣有歲
進有月進有日進有刺史之進奉有判
官之進奉而其時人主亦有內藏如瓊
林大盈是已亦每每乏用何歟然亦有
置封椿庫景福內庫更景福殿庫名自
製詩以揭之者而不聞乏用何歟宋蘇
軾曰為國有三計有萬世之計有一時
之計有不終月之計蘇轍曰事之害財

translation_en:
…Please explain this in detail, to assist those in authority.

Question: Fiscal revenues are the great foundation of the state and the very lifeline of the people. The empire’s order or disorder, and the balance between them, depend upon these; they must not be neglected. No work treats the management of finances more fully than the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan). Commentators call the Offices of Zhou a book for bringing about Great Peace, and indeed this is so. Yet some in later ages applied it without success. Why was this? Before the Zhou, when the Offices of Zhou had not yet been written, how were finances managed? After the Zhou, through the Qin, Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, how were finances managed?

I have examined how the founding rulers of earlier dynasties were reverent and frugal and cherished those below them: without deliberately seeking fiscal sufficiency, they attained it naturally. By the middle years of their dynasties, however, expenditure had become extravagant and resources insufficient. In the workings of things and in human affairs, decline and growth, fullness and depletion, do have their natural course. In those times, ministers eager to undertake new initiatives presented annual, monthly, or daily offerings; there were offerings from Regional Inspectors and from Administrative Assistants. The rulers of those times also possessed inner treasuries, such as Qionglin and Daying. Yet they repeatedly lacked funds. Why was this?

There were also rulers who established the Fengchun Treasury and the Jingfu Inner Treasury, renamed the latter the Jingfu Palace Treasury, and personally composed a poem to be displayed there. Yet we do not hear that they lacked funds. Why was this?

Su Shi of the Song said: “There are three kinds of planning in governing a state: planning for ten thousand generations, planning for the needs of the moment, and planning that will not last out a month.” Su Zhe said: “The things that damage the finances…”

translation_en: …are three: superfluous officials, superfluous troops, and superfluous expenditure. If, indeed, the words of these two masters are sound, could eliminating these three excesses and carefully considering the three kinds of planning likewise suffice to meet expenditure? Today, the people, the officials, and the armies depend most urgently upon the minister of finance. Yet floods and droughts, disturbances caused by bandits, and troubles on the frontiers arise on every side, with no provision made against them. By what means, then, can one truly achieve what the ancients called meeting expenditure without increasing taxation? Please explain in detail; your proposals will be conveyed to His Majesty.

崔桐
同考試官教諭蕭批此題上二句士子類能
發揮至于下句竊比二字所纒繞僅見此篇

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“I transmit but do not originate; I trust in and cherish antiquity. I venture to compare myself to our Old Peng.”

Cui Tong

Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: Candidates generally can expound the first two clauses of this topic. But as for addressing the implications bound up in the two words “venture to compare” in the final clause, I have seen it done only in this essay.

Comment by Associate Examiner Kuang, Instructor: That transmission proceeds from trust in antiquity is something anyone taking up a brush can readily say. But an essay such as this, which casts off stale conventions, expounds the meaning clearly and fully, and is unhurried and comprehensive, with a lingering savor, is seldom seen. For this reason it is included here.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Professor: The topic is inherently straightforward, but writers either become verbose and insubstantial or ramble without reaching a conclusion. This essay alone shows an intimate grasp of the meaning and employs elegant, vigorous language. The Sage’s humility appears vividly before our eyes. Worthy of selection, worthy of selection!

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher: In interpreting the Analects, capturing the Sage’s tone is most difficult; his expressions of humility and self-restraint are especially difficult. A composition like this merits inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: It reproduces the Sage’s words as though they came from his own mouth, and elucidates the Sage’s meaning as though it came from his own heart. An excellent composition.

The Sage himself explains why he follows the Way of antiquity, and thereby expresses his wish to learn from the ancients.

Now, the Sage’s sageliness lies in his not regarding himself as a sage. Not only does he not dare claim the sageliness of an originator…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖而亦不敢自附於古之賢人其謙已誨人之
意何其切歟昔吾夫子當吾道旣絀之餘退而
立言之後脩近聖之事而無自聖之心其意若
曰制作之道有二有述者焉有作者焉作者聖
人之事則吾豈敢當述者賢人之事在人皆可
企是故吾嘗刪詩書矣吾嘗定禮樂矣詩書則
首乎周南斷于堯典禮樂則問于老聃訪于萇
弘刪之定之猶夫舊也吾嘗脩春秋矣吾嘗贊
周易矣春秋則因魯史之文次桓文之事易則
===
明三聖之心附一已之見脩之贊之無所創也
夫我之所以述而不作者何哉誠以詩書也禮
樂也皆古道之所存焉所以立倫彛者在是所
以通神明者在是吾固信而好之不啻若自其
口出焉其奚敢作乎春秋也周易也皆古道之
所寓焉所以繩後王者在是所以明天道者在
是吾固信而好之不知老之將至焉斯其所以
述乎然此抑豈無所自哉古之人有行之者其
惟我老彭乎老彭者何商之賢大夫也彼嘗述

周易矣春秋則因魯史之文次桓文之事易則
===
明三聖之心附一巳之見脩之贊之無所創也
夫我之所以述而不作者何哉誠以詩書也禮
樂也皆古道之所存焉所以立倫彝者在是所
以通神明者在是吾固信而好之不啻若自其
口出焉其奚敢作乎春秋也周易也皆古道之
所寓焉所以繩後王者在是所以明天道者在
是吾固信而好之不知老之將至焉斯其所以
述乎然此抑豈無所自哉古之人有行之者其
惟我老彭乎老彭者何商之賢大夫也彼嘗述
punctuated:
聖，而亦不敢自附於古之賢人，其謙已誨人之意何其切歟！昔吾夫子當吾道旣絀之餘，退而立言之後，脩近聖之事，而無自聖之心。其意若曰：「制作之道有二：有述者焉，有作者焉。作者，聖人之事，則吾豈敢當？述者，賢人之事，在人皆可企。是故吾嘗刪詩書矣，吾嘗定禮樂矣。詩書則首乎周南，斷于堯典；禮樂則問于老聃，訪于萇弘。刪之定之，猶夫舊也。吾嘗脩春秋矣，吾嘗贊周易矣。春秋則因魯史之文，次桓文之事；易則明三聖之心，附一已之見。脩之贊之，無所創也。
夫我之所以述而不作者何哉？誠以詩書也，禮樂也，皆古道之所存焉。所以立倫彛者在是，所以通神明者在是。吾固信而好之，不啻若自其口出焉，其奚敢作乎？春秋也，周易也，皆古道之所寓焉。所以繩後王者在是，所以明天道者在是。吾固信而好之，不知老之將至焉，斯其所以述乎！然此抑豈無所自哉？古之人有行之者，其惟我老彭乎！老彭者何？商之賢大夫也。彼嘗述
translation_en:
…the sagehood of an originator, but he did not even dare rank himself among the worthy men of antiquity. How earnest was his intention to humble himself and instruct others! In former times, after our Way had suffered rejection and our Master had withdrawn to set forth his teachings, he undertook work approaching that of a sage, yet had no thought of claiming sagehood for himself. His meaning was as though he said: “There are two ways of establishing cultural institutions and teachings: transmission and origination. Origination is the work of a sage—how could I dare claim it? Transmission is the work of a worthy man, something to which anyone may aspire. Thus I have edited the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, and I have fixed the rites and music. For the Odes and Documents, I began with ‘The Odes of Zhou and the South’ (Zhou nan) and set the starting point at ‘The Canon of Yao’ (Yao dian), respectively. For rites and music, I questioned Lao Dan and consulted Chang Hong. In editing and fixing them, I preserved what had come down from the past. I have compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals and elucidated the Changes of Zhou. For the Annals, I followed the text of the Lu historical records and arranged the affairs of Duke Huan and Duke Wen; for the Changes, I clarified the intentions of the three sages and appended my own views. In compiling and elucidating these works, I originated nothing.
“Why is it that I transmit rather than originate? Truly, it is because the Odes and Documents, rites and music, all preserve the ancient Way. Here are the means to establish the enduring norms of human relationships; here are the means to communicate with the spirits. I trust and cherish them, just as though these teachings had issued from the ancients’ own mouths. How could I dare originate anything? The Spring and Autumn Annals and the Changes of Zhou likewise embody the ancient Way. Here are the means to set standards for later kings; here are the means to illuminate the Way of Heaven. I trust and cherish them, unaware that old age is approaching. This is why I transmit! Yet could this practice itself be without a source? Among the ancients who practiced it, was there not my Lao Peng? Who was Lao Peng? A worthy Grand Master of the Shang dynasty. He once transmitted…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而不作而無自專之心吾何爲而敢專焉彼嘗
信而好古而無自用之意吾何爲而敢用焉蓋
我老彭之所爲有以先獲我心于數百載之前
而我之所爲欲以竊比我老彭于數百載之後
曰竊比以致其尊之之意曰我以致其親之之
心聖人德愈盛而心愈下不自知其辭之謙也
有如此乎抑嘗攷之大戴禮矣孔子嘗稱老彭
之敎大夫敎士敎庶人抑揚德行之語不一而
足合論語而觀之則老彭者其真賢大夫也乎
===
不然何吾夫子之亟稱之若是雖然彭豈若是
班乎蓋吾夫子謙以誨人之心固有不得不然
者焉後有僭擬聖經侈然自足者非惟孔子之
罪人亦老彭之罪人也歟
故至誠無息不息則久久則徵徵則悠遠
悠遠則博厚博厚則高明
高瀹

punctuated:
而不作，而無自專之心，吾何爲而敢專焉？彼嘗信而好古，而無自用之意，吾何爲而敢用焉？蓋我老彭之所爲，有以先獲我心于數百載之前，而我之所爲，欲以竊比我老彭于數百載之後。曰「竊比」，以致其尊之之意；曰「我」，以致其親之之心。聖人德愈盛而心愈下，不自知其辭之謙也，有如此乎！抑嘗攷之《大戴禮》矣，孔子嘗稱老彭之敎大夫、敎士、敎庶人，抑揚德行之語，不一而足。合《論語》而觀之，則老彭者，其真賢大夫也乎？不然，何吾夫子之亟稱之若是？雖然，彭豈若是班乎？蓋吾夫子謙以誨人之心，固有不得不然者焉。後有僭擬聖經、侈然自足者，非惟孔子之罪人，亦老彭之罪人也歟！

故至誠無息，不息則久，久則徵，徵則悠遠，悠遠則博厚，博厚則高明。

高瀹

同考試官敎諭高批：中庸義，士子多不能體貼題義，草草說過，殊厭人觀。此作敷陳明暢，無一字
translation_en:
…and did not innovate, harboring no wish to act on his own authority. Why should I dare to claim such authority? He trusted in and loved antiquity, harboring no wish to rely solely on his own judgment. Why should I dare to rely on mine? What my Lao Peng did several hundred years before me anticipated what was in my heart; what I do several hundred years after him seeks privately to compare myself with my Lao Peng. Saying “privately compare myself” expresses his reverence for him; saying “my” expresses his affection for him. The more abundant the sage’s virtue, the humbler his heart: could his words have reached such modesty without his even being aware of it!

I have also examined the Elder Dai’s Record of Rites. Confucius repeatedly praised Lao Peng’s teachings for grand masters, servicemen, and common people, with numerous statements commending or censuring moral conduct. Read together with the Analects, these show that Lao Peng truly was a worthy grand master, do they not? Otherwise, why would our Master have praised him so repeatedly? Even so, could Peng really be ranked alongside him in this way [?]? Our Master’s desire to teach others through humility necessarily led him to speak thus. If later people presumptuously compose works to rival the sages’ classics and are arrogantly self-satisfied, are they not offenders against both Confucius and Lao Peng?

“Thus utmost sincerity never ceases. Never ceasing, it endures; enduring, it manifests itself; manifesting itself, it extends far and long; extending far and long, it becomes broad and substantial; broad and substantial, it becomes lofty and luminous.”

Gao Yue 高瀹

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor: In essays interpreting the Doctrine of the Mean, candidates often fail to grasp closely the meaning of the topic, treating it cursorily—a most tiresome thing to read. This composition develops its argument clearly and fluently, without a single character…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
懶怠讀之風味自别也
同考試官學正羅批理學文字作者病於浮
泛不切如此作精當老成場中亦未易得也錄之
考試官左諭德温批平實雅健是亦善說理者
考試官侍講學士李批中庸義語意開闊而段落完
好可錄也
中庸於至誠之德必叙其積中發外之盛焉蓋
聖人之德無乎不誠也則夫所以積諸中而發
於外豈不各極其盛哉中庸二十六章言聖人
===
之德以明天道謂夫德之在人者惟誠爲難况
誠而極於至乎夫惟聖人之德原於性命之初
得於秉彜之正渾融於一心而不間以人欲之
虚假純粹至善舉天下莫能加也和順於道德
而不參以私僞之錯雜真實無妄亘古今莫能
尚也至誠如此吾知誠本諸性自有以貫始終
而不替德根于心自有以歷少壯而無間非不
息乎夫既不息則天理流行而實德之渾於心
者優游涵泳而自不能已德性安固而和順之

Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher, comments: Plain and substantial, elegant and vigorous: this too is the work of someone skilled in expounding principle.

Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: This exposition of the Doctrine of the Mean is expansive in language and meaning, and its sections are complete and well formed. It merits inclusion.

In discussing the virtue of utmost sincerity, the Doctrine of the Mean necessarily describes the fullness of its accumulation within and manifestation without. For there is no aspect of the sage’s virtue that is not sincere. How, then, could what accumulates within and manifests without fail to attain its fullest measure in each case? Chapter Twenty-six of the Doctrine of the Mean speaks of the sage’s virtue to illuminate the Way of Heaven. Its meaning is that, in human virtue, sincerity alone is difficult to achieve—how much more so sincerity brought to its utmost degree! The sage’s virtue originates in the beginnings of his nature and Heaven’s mandate and derives from the rectitude of the constant moral endowment he receives. It blends into a unified whole within his heart, uninterrupted by the falsity of human desires. Pure and supremely good, it cannot be surpassed by anything in the world. Harmoniously accordant with the Way and virtue, it is unmixed with the confusion of selfishness and artifice. Real and without falsity, it cannot be exceeded in any age, past or present. Such is utmost sincerity. I know that sincerity, rooted in one’s nature, inherently has the means to extend from beginning to end without declining; virtue, rooted in the heart, inherently has the means to endure from youth to maturity without interruption. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
蘊於中者日新月盛而物莫能遷何其久耶惟
其久也將見睟於面盎于背而動容周旋莫非
至德之光發乎邇見乎遠而上下四方莫非至
誠之著非徵乎惟其徵也則氣象之在外者優
優乎寬緩而不迫設施之堂陛而實有保天下
之勢也功業之在天下者恢恢乎久遠而不局
促行之一時而實有裕萬世之規也非悠遠乎
惟悠遠也吾見盛德豐功所以漸涵乎人心者
無所不至深仁厚澤所以覆冒乎天下者無所
===
不周納八荒於度內也歷萬世如一日也何博
厚如之惟博厚也吾見巍巍乎成功而治化格于
上下煥乎文章而聲光燭于無疆峻極于天也
光被四表也何高明如之夫以至誠之德積中
發外者其盛如此子思子以之明天道其旨深
矣抑考中庸一書誠為樞紐言聖人則曰至誠
言天地則曰不貳若所謂至誠之道可以前知
至誠盡性可以參天地贊化育固皆聖人之事
也而至誠無息之功用未有若此章言之親切

punctuated: 蘊於中者日新月盛，而物莫能遷，何其久耶！惟其久也，將見睟於面、盎于背，而動容周旋莫非至德之光；發乎邇、見乎遠，而上下四方莫非至誠之著，非徵乎？惟其徵也，則氣象之在外者優優乎寬緩而不迫，設施之堂陛，而實有保天下之勢也；功業之在天下者恢恢乎久遠而不局促，行之一時，而實有裕萬世之規也，非悠遠乎？惟悠遠也，吾見盛德豐功所以漸涵乎人心者，無所不至；深仁厚澤所以覆冒乎天下者，無所不周。納八荒於度內也，歷萬世如一日也，何博厚如之！惟博厚也，吾見巍巍乎成功，而治化格于上下；煥乎文章，而聲光燭于無疆。峻極于天也，光被四表也，何高明如之！夫以至誠之德，積中發外者，其盛如此，子思子以之明天道，其旨深矣！抑考《中庸》一書，誠為樞紐。言聖人則曰至誠，言天地則曰不貳。若所謂至誠之道可以前知，至誠盡性可以參天地、贊化育，固皆聖人之事也。而至誠無息之功用，未有若此章言之親切
translation_en:
…what is stored within grows daily fresher and monthly more abundant, and nothing external can alter it. How enduring it is! Precisely because it endures, we shall see it shine clearly in the face and fill out the back: every movement and gesture displays the radiance of consummate virtue. It issues forth nearby and becomes visible afar: above and below, in all four directions, everything manifests utmost sincerity. Is this not its becoming evident? Precisely because it becomes evident, its outward bearing is ample, unhurried, and free of urgency. Its measures are put into effect within the palace halls and steps [?], yet possess the power to secure all under Heaven. Its achievements throughout the world are expansive and lasting, free of narrow confines. Though enacted in a single age, they contain a plan that will enrich ten thousand generations. Is this not far-reaching duration?

Precisely because it is enduring and far-reaching, I see that abundant virtue and great achievements gradually permeate human hearts, reaching everywhere; profound benevolence and generous beneficence shelter all under Heaven, encompassing everything. It brings the eight distant regions within its compass and passes through ten thousand generations as though they were a single day. What breadth and depth could equal this! Precisely because it is broad and deep, I see towering accomplishments, with transforming governance reaching those above and below; brilliant cultural forms, with renown and radiance illuminating boundless expanses. Its lofty height reaches Heaven; its light extends to the four outermost regions. What loftiness and brilliance could equal this!

Such is the abundance of the virtue of utmost sincerity, accumulated within and expressed without. Master Zisi uses it to elucidate the Way of Heaven: profound indeed is his meaning! Moreover, if we examine the Doctrine of the Mean as a whole, sincerity is its pivot. When it speaks of the sage, it says “utmost sincerity”; when it speaks of Heaven and Earth, it says “not being two.” Statements such as “the Way of utmost sincerity permits foreknowledge,” and that through utmost sincerity and fully realizing one's nature one can form a triad with Heaven and Earth and assist their transforming and nourishing work, certainly all concern the sage. Yet nowhere are the efficacy and operation of utmost sincerity's ceaseless activity expressed as directly and intimately as in this chapter…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而明著者故必以天地不貳並舉而互見焉說
者謂非天地不足以見聖人聖人與天地合德
信矣
布帛長短同則賈相若麻縷絲絮輕重同
則賈相若五穀多寡同則賈相若屨大
小同則賈相若曰夫物之不齊物之情
也
一旨憲
同考試官教諭楊批此題不難於說物情而
===
難於說物賈蓋陳相之言曲說也既代陳相又代孟
子辨析明白語意渾厚其自得之學也錄之
同考試官學正蕭批講同字頓着若字講情
字頓勝他掌獨此篇體認親切辭氣爾雅熟讀之或
亦足以盡子之意也

讀此作亦可以觀物矣

埧人即物賈之同以見其道之行大賢指物理

而明著者，故必以天地不貳並舉而互見焉。說者謂非天地不足以見聖人，聖人與天地合德，信矣。

「布帛長短同，則賈相若；麻縷絲絮輕重同，則賈相若；五穀多寡同，則賈相若；屨大小同，則賈相若。」曰：「夫物之不齊，物之情也。」

一旨憲

同考試官教諭楊批：「此題不難於說物情，而難於說物賈。蓋陳相之言，曲說也。既代陳相，又代孟子，辨析明白，語意渾厚，其自得之學也。錄之。」

同考試官學正蕭批：「講同字，頓着若字；講情字，頓勝他掌。獨此篇體認親切，辭氣爾雅。熟讀之，或亦足以盡子之意也。」

考試官左諭德温批：「聖賢常以人情物理為訓，細讀此作，亦可以觀物矣。」

考試官侍講學士李批：「講同處，絕不類眾作。」

埧人即物賈之同以見其道之行，大賢指物理
translation_en:
…and clearly manifest. Thus he necessarily sets it alongside Heaven and Earth’s unwavering constancy, so that each illuminates the other. Commentators say that nothing short of Heaven and Earth suffices to reveal the sage, and that the sage shares their virtue. Truly so.

“When lengths of linen and silk are the same, their prices should be comparable; when weights of hemp thread and silk floss are the same, their prices should be comparable; when quantities of the five grains are the same, their prices should be comparable; when sizes of shoes are the same, their prices should be comparable.” He replied: “That things are unequal is inherent in their nature.”

Yi Zhixian [?; the name as transcribed is 一旨憲].

Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: “The difficulty of this topic lies not in explaining the nature of things but in explaining their prices. Chen Xiang’s words are, after all, a distorted argument. The writer speaks first for Chen Xiang and then for Mengzi, drawing clear distinctions in language and meaning that are substantial and profound. This is learning he has made his own. Selected for inclusion.”

Associate Examiner Xiao, Director of Studies, comments: “In explaining ‘the same,’ he places the emphasis on ‘comparable’; in explaining ‘nature,’ he immediately surpasses the other essays [?; the transcription reads 他掌]. This essay alone shows an intimate understanding, with refined diction and tone. Read closely and repeatedly, it may suffice to convey the Master’s full meaning.”

Examiner Wen, Left Mentor, comments: “Sages and worthies have always grounded their teachings in human dispositions and the principles of things. A close reading of this composition can also teach one to observe things.”

Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “His treatment of ‘the same’ is entirely unlike that of the other compositions.”

The man [?; the transcription reads 埧人] takes the uniformity of commodity prices as evidence that his Way is put into practice; the great worthy points to the principles of things …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之實以明其物之異蓋物之不可同正以其有
自然之實理也苟徒以物賈之同為足以齊物
是豈知物理者哉昔陳相自信其師許行之道
足以治國家故舉物賈之同以見國中之無偽
其意若曰物賈之不同者人心之多偽也許子
之道則不然彼用物有布帛焉有麻縷絲絮焉
而布帛有長短麻縷絲絮有輕重也使道不行
於國中則長短以度爭輕重以權爭其賈固相
懸而不侔矣今也長者與短者之度不甚遠則
===
其賈相若矣輕者與重者之劑不甚遠則其賈
相若矣何彼此之有爭乎用物有五穀焉有屨
焉而五穀有多寡屨有大小也使信不孚於闤
市則多寡以量爭大小以形爭其賈固隔絕而
不一矣今也多者不甚加於寡者則其賈即同
矣小者不甚損於大者則其賈即同矣何偽妄
之可入乎陳相之言如此孟子曉之若曰物之
不固者廼其自然之理夫豈可以強乎彼天下
之物凡用於人者不特布帛麻縷也就此而論

punctuated:
之實，以明其物之異。蓋物之不可同，正以其有自然之實理也。苟徒以物賈之同為足以齊物，是豈知物理者哉？昔陳相自信其師許行之道足以治國家，故舉物賈之同，以見國中之無偽。其意若曰：「物賈之不同者，人心之多偽也。許子之道則不然。彼用物有布帛焉，有麻縷絲絮焉，而布帛有長短，麻縷絲絮有輕重也。使道不行於國中，則長短以度爭，輕重以權爭，其賈固相懸而不侔矣。今也，長者與短者之度不甚遠，則其賈相若矣；輕者與重者之劑不甚遠，則其賈相若矣。何彼此之有爭乎？用物有五穀焉，有屨焉，而五穀有多寡，屨有大小也。使信不孚於闤市，則多寡以量爭，大小以形爭，其賈固隔絕而不一矣。今也，多者不甚加於寡者，則其賈即同矣；小者不甚損於大者，則其賈即同矣。何偽妄之可入乎？」
陳相之言如此，孟子曉之，若曰：「物之不固者，廼其自然之理，夫豈可以強乎？彼天下之物，凡用於人者，不特布帛麻縷也。就此而論
translation_en:
…the actual principles, to make clear the differences among things. Things cannot be made identical precisely because they possess real principles inherent in their nature. If one merely considers uniform prices sufficient to equalize things, how can one understand the principles of things? Formerly, Chen Xiang believed that the Way of his teacher Xu Xing was sufficient to govern a state. He therefore cited uniform prices as evidence that there would be no deception within the state. His meaning was as follows: “Differences in the prices of goods arise from the abundant deceit in human hearts. Master Xu’s Way is otherwise. Among useful goods are cloth and silk, hemp thread and silk floss. Cloth and silk differ in length, while hemp thread and silk floss differ in weight. If the Way did not prevail within the state, people would contend over the measurements of longer and shorter pieces and the weighing of lighter and heavier quantities; their prices would certainly be far apart and unequal. But now, when the measurements of longer and shorter pieces do not differ greatly, their prices are alike; when the measured amounts of lighter and heavier quantities do not differ greatly, their prices are alike. What contention could there be between them? Among useful goods are the five grains and shoes. Grain comes in greater or smaller quantities, and shoes in larger or smaller sizes. If trust did not prevail in the marketplace, people would contend over the measuring of greater and smaller quantities and the dimensions of larger and smaller sizes; their prices would certainly be widely separated and unequal. But now, when the greater quantity does not much exceed the smaller, their prices are the same; when the smaller size is not much less than the larger, their prices are the same. How could deception and falsehood find an opening?”
Such were Chen Xiang’s words. Mengzi enlightened him, as if saying: “That things are not constant [?] is a principle inherent in their nature. How could this be forced? Of all the things under Heaven that serve human needs, there are more than cloth, silk, and hemp thread alone. To discuss just these…”

text:
之固自有長短有輕重而長短輕重之中又自
有精者有粗者其精粗之相去萬有不齊蓋物
各付物而實有自然之理爾不相假借也不相
陵奪也吾豈可得而同邪天下之物凡用於人
者不特五穀與屨也即是而論之固自有多寡
有大小而多寡大小之中又自有美者有惡者
其美惡之相判萬有不一蓋物以羣分而實有
本然之則爾好同者不能使之同也好異者不
能使之異也吾豈可得而亂邪由是觀之則市

translation_en:
…these naturally differ in length and weight; and among their differences in length and weight, some are fine and others coarse. Their degrees of fineness and coarseness vary in countless ways. Each thing is left to be what it is, possessing its own natural principle: things neither borrow from one another nor encroach upon and supplant one another. How could I make them all the same? Of all the things in the world that people use, there are more than just grain and shoes. Even these naturally differ in quantity and size; and within these differences in quantity and size, some are good and others poor. The distinctions between good and poor vary in countless ways. Things fall into their respective kinds, each possessing its inherent norm. Those who favor sameness cannot make them the same; those who favor difference cannot make them different. How could I confound them?
Viewed in this light, the claim that market prices should admit of no variation reveals only its absurdity. Master Xu’s way is in fact a means of fostering disorder and opening the door to deceit. How could it suffice to govern a state? Yet does this principle merely suffice to refute Chen Xiang and repudiate Xu Xing? The true conditions of all things under Heaven are encompassed within it, and none can depart from it. Thus, not exceeding what is appropriate to things is the way by which the sage perfects himself; nurturing things according to their capacities is the principle by which Heaven and Earth bring things to completion. Could even Heaven and Earth and the sages add to or subtract from this? It is simply that each thing has its allotted place.
From this we know that distinctions between close and distant relations, and between the noble and the humble, cannot forcibly be made uniform; nor can the ordered steps of cultivating oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world be applied indiscriminately. …a follower of Laozi and Zhuangzi?

Book of Changes

“The Changes consists of images; images are likenesses.”

Huang Luzeng

Associate Examiner Gao, Instructor (jiaoyu), comments: “The Changes is explained in terms of images, and images are elucidated through likenesses. Seeking images outside this framework is certainly inadmissible; explaining likenesses on a separate level likewise fails to accord with the classic’s purport. This composition sustains a coherent argument without repetitive wording, and therefore has been selected.”

Associate Examiner Luo, Instructor (xuezheng), comments: “This topic is exceedingly difficult to develop. Only this composition achieves such crystalline clarity without a flaw.”

Examiner Wen, Left Exhorter, comments: “Neither superficial in its language nor sparing in its treatment of principle: should not an interpretation of the meaning of the Changes be like this?”

Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “It elucidates the two words ‘image’ and ‘likeness,’ leaving none of their implications unexplored.”

In discussing how the hexagrams of the Changes are all forms of yin and yang, the Great Commentary necessarily explains what makes those forms what they are. What makes the Changes the Changes is simply yin and yang. Yet what constitutes yin and yang—is it not their likeness to principle? The Changes contains images and principles; in substance, these are simply the two poles of yin and yang. But in what sense does the Changes consist of images? In a yang figure, the line is single and solid, and its numbers are nine and seven: this is an image of yang. For example, three undivided lines constitute Qian, an image of pure yang; figures with one undivided line and two divided lines constitute Zhen and Kan…

text:
為艮則雜陽之象與凡卦之大者何莫非陽象
乎卦之為陰者其畫則二而虛其數則六與八
陰之象也如三偶為坤乃純陰之象一偶二奇
者為巽為離為兌則雜陰之象與凡卦之小者
何莫非陰象乎擬議以極天下之賾而形容物
宜以明觀察以成天地之文而老少動靜以寓
故曰易者象也然是象也何以為像哉盖至著
者為象焉至微者為理焉陽本不可得而盡也

===

不可得而形也為純陰雜陰以該之故畫之二

translation_en: …and Gen: these are images of mixed yang! Among all the trigrams classed as great, which is not an image of yang? In the yin trigrams, the line consists of two parts with a gap between them, and its numbers are six and eight: these are images of yin. Thus three broken lines form Kun, the image of pure yin; one broken line and two unbroken lines form Xun, Li, and Dui, images of mixed yin. Among all the trigrams classed as small, which is not an image of yin? Through comparison and deliberation, the deepest complexities of the world are fathomed, and representations of what is fitting to things become clear; through observation, the patterns of Heaven and Earth are completed, and old and young, movement and stillness are embodied therein. Hence it is said: “The Changes consists of images.” But how are these images likenesses? What is most manifest constitutes the images; what is most subtle constitutes principle. Yang cannot in itself be exhaustively comprehended, so it is designated as pure yang or mixed yang. Thus its line, single and solid, and its numbers, nine and seven, are merely approximations of principle. Could yang be confined to these? Yin cannot in itself be given visible form, so it is comprehended under pure yin and mixed yin. Thus its line, divided in two with a gap, and its numbers, six and eight, are merely likenesses of principle. Could yin be exhausted by these? What is most difficult to give form to is made manifest in visible patterns; what cannot be exhausted is encompassed within a limited number of lines. Hence it is said: “Images are likenesses.” Ah! Fathoming the subtlety of principle and image, and revealing the origin of the making of the Changes—how refined is the purport of the Great Commentary! Alas! The sages made the Changes entirely for the people's sake. Why, then, does deceit among the people of later ages increase daily, while those who study the Changes fall ever further short of the ancients? When gentlemen of antiquity dwelt at ease, they contemplated the images: it was these images they contemplated. When they grasped the meaning and forgot the images, it was these images they forgot. Today, though the lines and patterns are present, still…

…there are old and young forms. The young indeed does not change, but old yang changes into yin, never remaining fixed in one state. Yin, likewise, is one, yet it too has old and young forms. The young indeed does not change, but old yin changes into yang, surely not remaining in its place. Thus the lower trigram of a hexagram, called zhen, has the empty positions of the first, second, and third lines: yin and yang occupy these in turn, and their designations are not fixed. The upper trigram, called hui, has the empty positions of the fourth, fifth, and top lines: yin and yang circulate through these, and their qualities do not remain rigidly fixed.

That yang should be above and yin below is the constant order of Heaven and Earth. Yet, through repeated shifting, a six may occupy the upper positions—the fourth, fifth, or top—and a nine may occupy the lower positions—the first, second, or third. Although noble and lowly positions are arrayed in order, yielding and firm lines function in alternation. This can be seen by observing the changes in which the yielding ascends and the firm descends, or the firm ascends and the yielding descends. What constancy is there? That yang occupies a yang position and yin a yin position is an unchanging principle. Yet, through repeated shifting, the yang positions—the first, third, and fifth—also frequently employ a six, while the yin positions—the second, fourth, and top—also frequently employ a nine. Although yin and yang are distinguished, their numbers interweave. This can be seen by observing the changes in which the yielding comes to adorn the firm and the firm ascends to adorn the yielding. How do they interchange [?]?

Ah! Within the distinction between yin and yang, repeated shifting takes these forms: not remaining in place, circulating, having no constancy, and interchanging. How could anyone keep this at a distance? Generally, the Way cannot be departed from; what can be departed from is not the Way. How much more so the Way of the Changes! Book of Documents
“Food! Attend to its proper seasons. Be gentle toward those far away and cultivate good relations with those nearby. Esteem the virtuous and trust the good, but make it difficult for flatterers to gain office; then the Man and Yi peoples will all submit.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: Policies for nourishing the people are fundamentally intended for the central realm. Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, School Instructor: The argument is upright and broad in scope, and the language concise and antique in tone. The intent behind the appointment of officials at Shun’s court appears vividly before our eyes. Expositions of the Book of Documents like this are seldom found among the examination papers.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Mentor: The language and meaning are balanced and correct, while the treatment of “all submit” particularly distinguishes it from other papers. It is among the finest expositions of the Classics.

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor-in-waiting: These words with which Shun charged the regional governors encompass even the way of governing all under Heaven. translation_en:
…Such is the intent. For the difficulty lies not in extending transforming influence to distant peoples, but in putting internal government in order. Once internal government is in order, distant peoples will submit of themselves, without submission being sought. The court historian records Emperor Shun’s instructions to the regional governors in these terms. Their meaning is as though he said:

“In governing, nothing takes precedence over nourishing the people; in nourishing the people, nothing matters more than ensuring sufficient food. As for ensuring sufficient food, must one personally provide enough for every household and individual? It lies simply in not taking away the time they need. The seasons of plowing and cultivating are those on which the production of food depends: whenever works are undertaken, one must not encroach upon them. The season of reaping is that in which food must be brought in: whenever labor services are imposed, one must not obstruct it. Then the people can devote their full strength to their fields, and food can be sufficient.

“People commonly neglect those nearby and overlook those far away; yet those far away are harder still to govern. Therefore, first tend to those far away with benevolence, gradually influencing them over months and years; draw them close with generosity, showing compassion for what they cannot accomplish. Then correct and guide those nearby, so that they rest content with my instruction; comfort and encourage them, so that they delight in my virtue. Thus there is a proper way to deal with both distant and nearby peoples.

“In the way of government, no matter demands greater rigor than advancing the worthy and dismissing the unworthy; yet the unworthy are harder still to remove. Thus, for those possessed of virtue, one must exalt their rank and increase their emoluments, never daring to slight them. For the benevolent and generous, one must act upon their remonstrances and heed their words, never daring to keep them at a distance. As for crafty men, gradually block their access so that they cannot put their schemes into effect; sever ties with them in accordance with righteousness so that they cannot give free rein to their wickedness. Thus there is a proper way to treat gentlemen and petty men.

“All such measures serve only to bring peace to my people. How could there be any deliberate intent to secure the submission of distant peoples? I see that wherever my moral influence and instruction extend, the eight Man peoples of themselves…”

translation_en:
…thereupon become upright in heart; wherever the Way’s transforming influence reaches, the Nine Yi of themselves turn toward our virtue. Though they need not bow their heads to the ground and declare themselves vassals, their aspirations all incline toward the Central Kingdom. Submitting to our righteousness, the myriad states share the same customs. Though they need not discharge their duties and present tribute, their hearts are all devoted to the royal house. Submitting to our teaching, all within the Four Seas take it as their standard. When the work of governing the people is accomplished, distant peoples submit of themselves in this way. We can thus see that the Central Kingdom is the pole toward which the four quarters turn. Can the Twelve Pastors fail to give this their attention?
Moreover, if we examine the sages’ government, nothing received more careful attention than affairs within their own realm; and in the way of influencing others, nothing took precedence over the foundation. Thus, bringing the myriad states into harmony necessarily rested upon the transforming influence of concord among kin; bringing the barbarians of the four quarters to acknowledge the king necessarily began with vigilance and admonition. The Doctrine of the Mean extends this into its nine guiding principles; the Great Learning elaborates it into its eight articles. All express this same principle. Later generations failed to understand it: they neglected internal government, yet sought to exert their armies to subdue distant peoples. Alas, how different this is from the admonitions of Shun’s court!
“I, Yin, together with Tang, both possessed a single virtue; we were able to win Heaven’s favor and receive Heaven’s illustrious mandate, thereby coming to possess the multitudes of the Nine Regions.”

心昭假自不能舍有商之君臣矣天之眷求者
punctuated:
此數言寫出當時告君意思，其亦忠愛溢發者歟！宜錄爲業經者式。
考試官左諭德温批：老臣愛君之意，發揮明白；一結猶有佳思，非庸筆可到。
考試官侍講學士李批：能發明伊尹所以佐湯及厚望太甲之意。
惟君臣有格天之德，自能得天人之歸也。盖惟德足以格天也，天旣享君臣之一德，則天人之歸有不能自已者矣。昔伊尹將歸，陳戒於太甲，其意若曰：天人有感應之符，一德有格天之理。昔尹之相湯、湯之有尹也，適當啓迪有命之時、眷求一德之際。于其時而君臣之德有一之不協，則天命去矣。而尹也以一德而事乎上，湯也以一德而臨乎下。純一不雜，而實天下之至德，其在湯也猶其在尹也；至誠不息，而實古今之恒德，其在尹也固實得之於湯也。咸有一德如此，故天之啓迪者，保之、佑之，而引翼之有加，天心昭假，自不能舍有商之君臣矣。天之眷求者，
translation_en:
…these few words convey the intent with which he admonished his ruler at that time. Do they not overflow with loyalty and affection? This should be recorded as a model for those studying the Classics.
Examiner Wen, Left Exhorter, comments: The old minister’s affection for his ruler is developed clearly. The conclusion also contains an excellent insight, beyond the reach of an ordinary writer.
Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: This brings out the intent behind Yi Yin’s assistance to Tang and his great expectations of Tai Jia.
Only when ruler and minister possess virtue that reaches Heaven can they naturally win the allegiance of Heaven and humankind. For virtue alone suffices to reach Heaven. Once Heaven has accepted the single virtue shared by ruler and minister, Heaven and humankind cannot help turning toward them. Formerly, when Yi Yin was about to retire, he set forth admonitions to Tai Jia. His meaning was as follows: There is a correspondence of stimulus and response between Heaven and humankind, and a principle by which single virtue reaches Heaven. When Yin assisted Tang, and Tang had Yin at his side, it was precisely the time when Heaven enlightened the possessor of its Mandate and graciously sought single virtue. Had the virtue of ruler and minister then been discordant in even one respect, Heaven’s Mandate would have departed. But Yin served his superior with single virtue, and Tang presided over those below with single virtue. Pure, unified, and unmixed, it was truly the highest virtue under Heaven: in Tang it was just as it was in Yin. Utterly sincere and unceasing, it was truly the abiding virtue of past and present: as possessed by Yin, it had indeed been acquired from Tang. Since both possessed single virtue in this way, Heaven, in enlightening them, protected and aided them, increasingly guiding and supporting them. Heaven’s heart manifestly responded and naturally could not abandon the ruler and minister of Shang. Heaven, in its gracious seeking…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
申之重之而意嚮之不貳帝心簡在自不能舍
君臣之一德矣一德格天如此吾知天命雖靡
常也今則眷命用懋申命用休而赫赫然如有
臨天休滋至帝命不違而昭昭乎其如在有不
受天之命者乎九有雖嘗屬於夏也今則民罔
常懷懷于有仁合億兆而歸心誕受多方式于
九圍撫方夏而咸有有不得民之歸者乎夫天
佑民歸咸於一德如此嗣王可不自純其德以
答天人之望也哉伊尹以是為言其所以陳戒
===
之者至矣嗟乎伊尹之所以事太甲者即其所
以事成湯也日新又新湯之所以聖也時乃日
新尹之所以望太甲為成湯也而一德之訓主
善克一之說又實本於精一之傳尹既以堯舜
之道相湯故又以相湯之道相太甲盖前聖之
心法有商之家法人臣事主不貳之道咸具於
一德篇而惓惓不忍去之意具見於反覆陳戒
之辭於乎老臣愛君憂國之心豈獨於居位之
時為然哉

punctuated:
申之重之，而意嚮之不貳，帝心簡在，自不能舍君臣之一德矣。一德格天如此，吾知天命雖靡常也，今則眷命用懋，申命用休，而赫赫然如有臨；天休滋至，帝命不違，而昭昭乎其如在，有不受天之命者乎？九有雖嘗屬於夏也，今則民罔常懷，懷于有仁，合億兆而歸心；誕受多方，式于九圍，撫方夏而咸有，有不得民之歸者乎？夫天佑民歸，咸於一德如此，嗣王可不自純其德，以答天人之望也哉？伊尹以是為言，其所以陳戒之者至矣。
嗟乎！伊尹之所以事太甲者，即其所以事成湯也。「日新又新」，湯之所以聖也；「時乃日新」，尹之所以望太甲為成湯也。而一德之訓，「主善克一」之說，又實本於精一之傳。尹既以堯舜之道相湯，故又以相湯之道相太甲。盖前聖之心法、有商之家法、人臣事主不貳之道，咸具於一德篇，而惓惓不忍去之意，具見於反覆陳戒之辭。於乎！老臣愛君憂國之心，豈獨於居位之時為然哉？
translation_en:
…Heaven reaffirmed and renewed its favor, its inclination toward them remaining undivided. They were chosen in the heart of the Lord on High, who could not abandon the single virtue shared by ruler and minister. Such was the power of single virtue to move Heaven. I know that although Heaven’s mandate is not constant, now its favoring charge brought encouragement, and its renewed charge brought blessing: resplendent, it seemed to look down upon them. Heaven’s blessings arrived in ever greater abundance, and the Lord on High’s mandate did not turn away: luminous, it seemed present before them. Could they fail to receive Heaven’s mandate? Although the nine regions had once belonged to Xia, now the people held no constant allegiance, cleaving instead to those possessed of benevolence; the hearts of the teeming multitudes turned to them as one. They received the many regions on a vast scale, became a model for the nine domains, and held and pacified all the lands of Xia. Could they fail to win the people’s allegiance? Since Heaven’s aid and the people’s allegiance thus both arose from single virtue, could the succeeding king fail to purify his own virtue and thereby answer the hopes of Heaven and humanity? Yi Yin spoke in these terms, carrying his admonition to the utmost.
Alas! The way Yi Yin served Tai Jia was precisely the way he had served Cheng Tang. “Renewing himself daily, and renewing himself yet again” was how Tang became a sage; “thus daily renew yourself” expressed Yi Yin’s hope that Tai Jia would become another Cheng Tang. The instruction concerning single virtue, and the teaching to “take goodness as one’s guiding principle and achieve singleness,” were indeed rooted in the transmitted teaching of refinement and singleness of mind. Having assisted Tang through the Way of Yao and Shun, Yi Yin therefore assisted Tai Jia through the same Way by which he had assisted Tang. The teachings of the former sages concerning the mind, the ancestral precepts of the Shang house, and the Way of a minister’s undivided service to his ruler are all contained in the chapter “Both Possessed a Single Virtue.” His devoted attachment and reluctance to leave are fully evident in its repeated words of admonition. Ah! Could this veteran minister’s love for his ruler and concern for the state have existed only while he held office?

“Not merely taking him by the hand, but showing him the matter; not merely instructing him face to face, but taking him by the ear.”

Cui Tong

Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: The topic is straightforward and balanced, yet most writers merely gather stale expressions, which is tiresome. This essay alone is clear, concise, and apt, vividly conveying Duke Wu’s intention to admonish himself. Surely this is the kind of writing that offers a warning to both speaker and listener!

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: A topic from the Greater Odes is not difficult to write on; the difficulty lies in treating it aptly. This essay alone develops “showing him the matter” and “taking him by the ear” clearly, exploring their implications fully and in detail. Moreover, the sincerity of its admonition overflows the words themselves. Its selection is not solely on account of its literary merit.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Professor: Duke Wu’s intention to admonish himself is brought out almost exhaustively.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Mentor: The language is gentle, but the meaning stern. Reading it three times each day would also help one advance in virtue.

Comment by Examiner Li, Expositor-in-waiting: “Poetry can stir the feelings.” This composition surely comes close to doing so!

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
所以告乎爾小子者亦無餘蘊矣若復不知謂
之何哉吁武公自懲自艾之意深矣抑是道也
雖古聖賢之撿身亦不過是而衛武公乃能身
體而力行之至使人直呼為小子而無一毫自
恃自高之意於乎其亦有得於切磋琢磨之力
而然歟後之君天下者疾人之規已至使之無
所容廼已況能自警之若是也哉讀詩至此不
能不三嘆焉
明明魯侯克明其德旣作泮宮淮夷攸服
===
矯矯虎臣在泮獻馘淑問如皐陶在泮
獻囚濟濟多士克廣德心桓桓于征狄
彼東南烝烝皇皇不吳不揚不告于訩
在泮獻功角弓其觼束矢其搜戎車孔
博徒御無斁旣克淮夷孔淑不逆式固
爾猶淮夷卒獲翩彼飛鴞集于泮林食
我桑黮懷我好音憬彼淮夷來獻其琛
元龜象齒大賂南金
馬津

所以告乎爾小子者，亦無餘蘊矣。若復不知，謂之何哉？吁！武公自懲自艾之意深矣！抑是道也，雖古聖賢之撿身亦不過是，而衛武公乃能身體而力行之，至使人直呼為小子，而無一毫自恃自高之意。於乎！其亦有得於切磋琢磨之力而然歟？後之君天下者，疾人之規已，至使之無所容廼已，況能自警之若是也哉？讀詩至此，不能不三嘆焉。
明明魯侯，克明其德。旣作泮宮，淮夷攸服。矯矯虎臣，在泮獻馘。淑問如皐陶，在泮獻囚。濟濟多士，克廣德心。桓桓于征，狄彼東南。烝烝皇皇，不吳不揚。不告于訩，在泮獻功。角弓其觼，束矢其搜。戎車孔博，徒御無斁。旣克淮夷，孔淑不逆。式固爾猶，淮夷卒獲。翩彼飛鴞，集于泮林。食我桑黮，懷我好音。憬彼淮夷，來獻其琛。元龜象齒，大賂南金。
馬津
translation_en:
…Nothing has been left unexpressed in what has been told to you, young fellow. If you still fail to understand, what more can be said? Ah! How profound was Duke Wu’s resolve to chastise himself and amend his faults! Indeed, even the ancient sages and worthies went no further than this in examining their own conduct. Yet Duke Wu of Wei could embody this way and earnestly put it into practice, even allowing others to address him directly as “young fellow,” without the slightest conceit or self-exaltation. Ah! Was this not also the fruit of his efforts at self-cultivation through cutting, filing, chiseling, and polishing? Later rulers of the world resented others’ admonitions of their own faults [?] and would not rest until those who offered them had no place left to stand. How could they possibly admonish themselves as he did? Reading the Odes to this point, one cannot help sighing three times.
Illustrious is the Marquis of Lu, able to make his virtue shine. Having built the Pan Palace, the state school, he brought the Huai Yi into submission. His valiant, tiger-like warriors present severed enemy ears at the Pan Palace. Those skilled in judicial questioning, like Gao Yao, present captives there. His many worthy officers can extend their virtuous purpose. Martial and mighty on campaign, they bring order to the southeast. Advancing in great numbers and splendid array, they are neither clamorous nor boastful. They bring no reports of contentious wrangling, but present their achievements at the Pan Palace. Their horn bows have their buckles [?], and their bundles of arrows are gathered in order. Their war chariots are very numerous; their foot soldiers and charioteers never weary. Having overcome the Huai Yi, they find them thoroughly compliant and no longer rebellious. Make firm your plans, and the Huai Yi will ultimately be captured. Fluttering in flight, those owls alight in the woods of the Pan Palace. They eat our mulberries and requite us with pleasing calls. Those far-off Huai Yi come to present their treasures: great tortoises and elephant tusks, and lavish gifts of southern gold.
Ma Jin.

Associate Examiner Zheng, a School Instructor, comments: The topic’s purport is clear, upright, and broad, but writers find it difficult to treat skillfully. This essay alone has rigorous, orderly composition and profound, closely woven language and meaning. Moreover, it places the emphasis on luminous virtue, showing particular insight. Its author is skilled at interpreting the Book of Odes; it should be recorded as a model.
Associate Examiner Liu, a Professor, comments: To handle a long topic with such concentration and concision surely marks an accomplished writer.
Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher to the Heir Apparent, comments: Making the submission of distant peoples through luminous virtue the substance of praise and prayer, this essay successfully conveys the meaning. Among the Book of Odes papers, this is the only one of its kind.
Examiner Li, an Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: Though the topic is long, the structure is closely knit; though its threads are many, its conclusion is entirely fitting. This is the finest exposition of the ode’s meaning.
Because their worthy lord was at the school, the people of Lu repeatedly expressed the wish that he might find the means to bring distant peoples into submission. How grievously the Huaiyi had troubled Lu! How long the people had cherished this wish for their ruler, and the ruler had cherished it for himself! Without achieving this, how could they find relief? In former times, when the Marquis of Lu drank at the Pan school, the poet carried his praise and prayers to this point, as though saying: The strength or weakness of the Huaiyi depends upon the flourishing or decline of our Lu. We wish only that our illustrious Marquis of Lu may make manifest his lofty virtue, so that everything bestowed by Heaven is fully realized; and that, having built the Pan school, he may bring into submission all the Huaiyi who have caused trouble. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
無安得武勇之臣有如虓虎者在泮以獻馘乎
彼之服而歸罪也又安得淑問之臣有如皐陶
者在泮以獻囚乎自其兵士言之凡我濟濟多
士莫不克廣德心而無一毫固蔽之私桓桓于
征用以狄彼東南而雪累世寇攘之耻兵進而
合有烝烝皇皇之盛師出以律有不吳不揚之
肅戰勝而和不告于訟焉功成而還爭獻于泮
焉又自其武備言之角弓則觩然體之健也可
知束矢則搜然聲之疾也可知戎車孔博而有
===
如霆如雷之勢徒御無斁而有同心同德之良
是固旣克淮夷孔淑而不逆矣盖能審固謀猶
則蠢兹淮夷豈終不獲也哉於是即物以興之
曰翩彼飛鴞顧泮林而萃止食我桑黮猶好音
之是懷况憬彼淮夷有不來獻其琛者乎吾知
曰元龜曰象齒盡異物以來輸曰荆金曰揚金
望我邦而大賂則其土地之所出固無有不獻
焉者矣由是觀之凡臣士之所以獻其功與夫
淮夷之所以獻其琛者由我侯之能明其德耳

translation_en:
…[The opening 無 is unclear.] How could there be warriors as fierce as roaring tigers presenting severed enemy ears at the Pan school? When the enemy submits and acknowledges its guilt, how could there be ministers of good repute, like Gao Yao, presenting prisoners at the Pan school?

Speaking of the soldiers, all our numerous worthy men can enlarge their virtuous hearts, without the slightest selfish obstinacy or blindness. Mighty on campaign, they punish those in the southeast and wipe away the shame of raids and plunder suffered over successive generations. As the troops advance and assemble, they display abundant grandeur; as the army marches under discipline, it maintains a solemn order, without noise or commotion. Victorious in battle, they remain harmonious, bringing no disputes to litigation; returning with their task accomplished, they vie to present their trophies at the Pan school.

Speaking also of their military equipment, the horn bows are curved and taut, showing the strength of their construction; the bundled arrows whistle as they fly, their sound revealing their speed. The war chariots are very broad, with the force of thunder and thunderclaps. The foot soldiers and charioteers never weary, possessing the excellence of a common purpose and shared resolve. Thus the Huai Yi have indeed been overcome and are thoroughly compliant, no longer defiant. For if plans are carefully considered and firmly settled, how could these unruly Huai Yi ultimately escape capture?

The poet then evokes the theme through an image, saying: “Those owls flying lightly turn toward the woods of the Pan school and gather there. Eating our mulberries, even they cherish pleasing calls. How much more, then, will those faraway Huai Yi come to present their treasures! I know that they will bring great tortoise shells and elephant tusks, delivering all their rare objects; they will bring metal from Jing and metal from Yang, turning toward our state with lavish gifts. Of what their lands produce, there will surely be nothing they do not offer.”

Viewed in this light, the reason the ministers and soldiers present the fruits of their achievements, and the Huai Yi present their treasures, is simply that our lord can make his virtue shine.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:

寓於言辭之表而忠愛之情不忘乎飲讌之間

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
軍作而舊法遂廢矣春秋致意於魯事也宜哉
且古者舞佾之數天子八諸侯六大夫四吾聞
魯以諸侯而僭八佾舊矣是成王過賜伯禽過
受非所以康周公也及隱之身初獻六羽者何
蓋仲子有别宮之祀問之衆仲而降用之耳奏
大樂於新庭損舞列於常數尊卑之制定降殺
之等明非復前日之故轍矣故春秋書曰初初
者事之始若曰八佾之舊以臣僭君想夫用之
太廟以祀周公用之列廟以祀羣公其習爲非
===
禮可知也噫禮樂之在天下不容一日紊也諸
侯僭於上大夫僭於下故季氏舞八佾于庭三
家歌雍詩于堂上下之辨何有哉聖人書之所
以正天下之大典也如此若古者制軍之法大
國三次國二小國一吾聞魯封大國其有三軍
舊矣故公車千乘公徒三萬詩所以頌僖公也
迨襄之世復作三軍者何蓋季氏以私門之強
謀之叔孫而更置之耳毀私乘以盡征析公室
而專有地皆三家之土民皆三家之兵非復先

punctuated:
軍作，而舊法遂廢矣。《春秋》致意於魯事也，宜哉！且古者舞佾之數，天子八，諸侯六，大夫四。吾聞魯以諸侯而僭八佾舊矣，是成王過賜，伯禽過受，非所以康周公也。及隱之身，初獻六羽者何？蓋仲子有别宮之祀，問之衆仲而降用之耳。奏大樂於新庭，損舞列於常數，尊卑之制定，降殺之等明，非復前日之故轍矣。故《春秋》書曰「初」。初者，事之始。若曰八佾之舊，以臣僭君，想夫用之太廟以祀周公，用之列廟以祀羣公，其習爲非禮可知也。噫！禮樂之在天下，不容一日紊也。諸侯僭於上，大夫僭於下，故季氏舞八佾于庭，三家歌《雍》詩于堂，上下之辨何有哉？聖人書之，所以正天下之大典也如此。

若古者制軍之法，大國三，次國二，小國一。吾聞魯封大國，其有三軍舊矣。故「公車千乘，公徒三萬」，詩所以頌僖公也。迨襄之世，復作三軍者何？蓋季氏以私門之強，謀之叔孫而更置之耳。毀私乘以盡征，析公室而專有，地皆三家之土，民皆三家之兵，非復先
translation_en:
…armies were established, and the old regulations were consequently abolished. How fitting that the Spring and Autumn Annals should attend so closely to the affairs of Lu!

In antiquity, the prescribed number of rows of ritual dancers was eight for the Son of Heaven, six for the feudal lords, and four for the grand masters. I have heard that Lu, though a feudal state, had long usurped the privilege of eight rows. King Cheng had bestowed more than was proper, and Boqin had accepted more than was proper: this was no way to honor the Duke of Zhou. Why, then, in Duke Yin’s time, were six rows of feather dancers presented “for the first time”? Because Zhongzi received sacrifices in a separate shrine; after consulting Zhongzhong, the duke merely reduced the number used there. Grand music was performed in the new courtyard, while the ranks of dancers were reduced to the prescribed number. The regulations distinguishing higher and lower status were established, and the graduated reductions were made clear. They no longer followed their former course. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals records “for the first time.” “First” means the beginning of a practice. It is as though it were saying that the longstanding use of eight rows constituted a subject’s usurpation of his ruler’s prerogative. Consider their use in the Grand Ancestral Temple to sacrifice to the Duke of Zhou, and in the other ancestral temples to sacrifice to the successive dukes: plainly, this customary practice violated ritual propriety.

Alas! The rites and music of the realm cannot be allowed to fall into disorder for even a day. The feudal lords usurped privileges above, and the grand masters usurped them below. Thus the Ji lineage had eight rows of dancers perform in its courtyard, and the three lineages sang the ode “Yong” in their halls. What distinction between higher and lower remained? Such was the sage’s purpose in recording these matters: to rectify the great institutions of the realm.

As for the ancient regulations governing armies, a great state had three, a middle-ranking state two, and a small state one. I have heard that Lu was enfeoffed as a great state and had long possessed three armies. Hence the lines, “The duke’s chariots number a thousand; the duke’s foot soldiers, thirty thousand”: these are how the Odes praise Duke Xi. Why, then, were three armies established anew in Duke Xiang’s time? Because the Ji lineage, relying on the strength of its private house, consulted the Shusun lineage and reorganized them. They abolished the private chariot units to impose a full levy, divided up the ducal establishment, and took exclusive possession of it. All the land became the territory of the three lineages, and all the people became their soldiers. This was no longer the established system of the former…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
王之成法矣故春秋謂之作作者不宜作也若
曰三軍之舊名存實亡觀夫命救台而季孫有
入鄆之行享范鞅而公臣無三耦之具其民不
屬公可知也噫兵權之在公室不可一日去也
威福移于上黨與成于下故昭公次陽州以出
定公待壞隤而入廢置之事何如哉聖人書之
所以謹天下之大權也如此吁明君之僭也而
馭臣之道以存惡臣之專也而戒君之意有在
春秋于魯君臣之際其嚴矣乎嗟夫天下之事
===
未始不積于微而成于著盖寵斯僭僭斯專專
斯偪偪斯危矣故諸侯僭而後大夫強大夫僭
而後家臣強門觀大閱有重祭也三桓強盛緣
世卿也南蒯侯犯據強邑也以此坊民猶有輕
授節鉞如唐藩鎮之禍者其亦可嘅也夫

曰三軍之舊名存實亡觀夫命敎台而季孫有
入鄆之行享范鞅而公臣無三耦之具其民不
屬公可知也噫兵權之在公室不可一日去也
威福移于上黨與成于下故昭公次陽州以出
定公待壞隤而入廢置之事何如哉聖人書之
所以謹天下之大權也如此吁明君之僭也而
馭臣之道以存惡臣之專也而戒君之意有在
春秋于魯君臣之際其嚴矣乎嗟夫天下之事
未始不積于微而成于著盖寵斯僭僭斯專專
斯偪偪斯危矣故諸侯僭而後大夫強大夫僭
而後家臣強門觀大閱有重祭也三桓強盛緣
世卿也南蒯侯犯據強邑也以此坊民猶有輕
授節鉞如唐藩鎮之禍者其亦可嘅也夫
楚子伐鄭晉郤缺帥師救鄭宣公九年
仲選
同考試官教諭何　批〔認傳明白敘事詳整春〕
===
秋義當如是
punctuated:
王之成法矣。故《春秋》謂之作，作者，不宜作也。若曰：三軍之舊，名存實亡。觀夫命救台，而季孫有入鄆之行；享范鞅，而公臣無三耦之具，其民不屬公可知也。噫！兵權之在公室，不可一日去也。威福移于上，黨與成于下，故昭公次陽州以出，定公待壞隤而入，廢置之事何如哉？聖人書之，所以謹天下之大權也如此。吁！明君之僭也，而馭臣之道以存；惡臣之專也，而戒君之意有在。《春秋》于魯君臣之際，其嚴矣乎！嗟夫！天下之事，未始不積于微而成于著。盖寵斯僭，僭斯專，專斯偪，偪斯危矣。故諸侯僭而後大夫強，大夫僭而後家臣強。門觀大閱，有重祭也；三桓強盛，緣世卿也；南蒯侯犯，據強邑也。以此坊民，猶有輕授節鉞，如唐藩鎮之禍者，其亦可嘅也夫！

楚子伐鄭，晉郤缺帥師救鄭。宣公九年。
仲選。
同考試官教諭何批：認傳明白，叙事詳整，《春秋》義當如是。
translation_en:
…the established institutions of the former kings. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals calls it “creating”: to call it a creation means that it ought not to have been created. It is as though the text said: the old institution of the three armies survived in name but had ceased to exist in substance. Consider how, when ordered to relieve Tai, Jisun instead marched into Yun; and how, when Fan Yang was entertained, the duke’s retainers could not furnish three pairs of archers. Clearly, the people were no longer subject to the duke. Alas! Military authority must not depart from the ducal house for even a single day. The power to punish and reward slipped away from those above, while partisan followings formed below. Thus Duke Zhao encamped at Yangzhou upon going into exile, and Duke Ding waited at Huaitui before entering the capital. What had become of the power to depose and enthrone rulers? Such was the Sage’s purpose in recording these events: to safeguard the supreme authority of the realm. Ah! By exposing a ruler’s usurpation of prerogatives, he preserved the proper way to control ministers; by condemning ministers’ monopolization of power, he also intended to admonish rulers. How strict the Spring and Autumn Annals is concerning the relationship between the rulers and ministers of Lu!

Alas! Affairs in the world invariably accumulate from small beginnings and develop into manifest consequences. Favor leads to usurpation; usurpation to monopolization of power; monopolization to coercion; and coercion to peril. Thus only after the regional lords usurped prerogatives did their grandees become powerful; only after the grandees usurped prerogatives did their household retainers become powerful. Gates and watchtowers, grand military reviews, and repeated sacrifices [?]; the flourishing power of the Three Huan families arose from hereditary ministerial office; Nan Kuai and Hou Fan relied on fortified towns. Even with these examples to restrain people, there were still those who lightly bestowed the credentials and axes of military command, bringing disasters like those caused by the regional military commands of the Tang. How lamentable!

“The Viscount of Chu attacked Zheng. Xi Que of Jin led an army to relieve Zheng.” Ninth year of Duke Xuan.
Second selection.
Associate Examiner He, Instructor, comments: “The interpretation of the commentary is clear, and the narration is detailed and orderly. An exposition of the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals should indeed be like this.”

帥師書其重者也則陵暴中華重兵臨鄭之罪
不于是而可見乎夫楚既陸梁憑陵上國斯時
也晉主夏盟舊矣使不引手一援荊尸之暴誰
其遏之幸而遂遣郤缺之師往解鄭人之厄念
punctuated:
考試官左諭德温批：簡而嚴，得書爵、書救之意。
考試官侍講學士李批：春秋謹華夷之辨，其旨盖如此。
春秋直紀外夷重兵虐貳之非，故特紀霸國用兵恤貳之善。觀諸楚書爵而晉書救，可見矣。春秋善善惡惡，皆致謹于華夷之辨也歟！𫠦自鄭與楚平，逃歸于厲，斯時也，楚未得志久矣。使不肆力一逞忿怒之心，豈遂已歟？于是再率方城之旅，伐我懿親之邦。歸生告斃，曾無討罪之可名；戎馬戒嚴，亦惟服鄭之為事。國君自將，大眾悉行，桓武之宗社幾危矣。視昔頻年之役，豈不為尤甚哉？在常情觀之，恃強壓弱，春秋之弊轍耳。聖人以為用夷猾夏之師，世道之大變于此乎攸係。故不稱人，舉號而書爵者，盖君將不言帥師，書其重者也。則陵暴中華、重兵臨鄭之罪，不于是而可見乎？夫楚既陸梁，憑陵上國，斯時也，晉主夏盟舊矣。使不引手一援，荆尸之暴誰其遏之？幸而遂遣卻缺之師，往解鄭人之厄，念
translation_en:
Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher, comments: “Concise yet rigorous; it grasps the meaning of recording the rank and recording the rescue.”
Examiner Li, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “The Spring and Autumn Annals carefully maintains the distinction between the Chinese states and the non-Chinese peoples. Its purport is surely as expressed here.”
The Spring and Autumn Annals directly records the wrong committed by an outside, non-Chinese state in deploying a great army to mistreat a state of divided allegiance; it therefore expressly records the good done by a hegemonic state in employing troops to succor that same state. This is evident in its recording Chu’s ruler by his rank and Jin’s action as a rescue. In approving good and condemning evil, does not the Spring and Autumn Annals exercise the utmost care over the distinction between the Chinese states and the non-Chinese peoples?
Ever since Zheng made peace with Chu and the flight back to Li [?], Chu had long been frustrated in its ambitions. Unless it unleashed its strength and gave vent to its anger, would it simply desist? Thus it again led the troops of Fangcheng to attack our state of close royal kinship. Guisheng had been reported dead, so there was no longer any plausible claim to be punishing a crime. The warhorses stood ready; the sole object was to subjugate Zheng. The ruler commanded in person, and the entire host marched out. The ancestral temples and altars of state of Dukes Huan and Wu were nearly imperiled. Compared with the campaigns of successive past years, was this not especially grave?
Viewed in ordinary terms, this was merely reliance on strength to oppress the weak—the familiar pernicious pattern of the Spring and Autumn period. The Sage, however, regarded it as an army of non-Chinese peoples employed to throw the Chinese states into disorder: a momentous change in the course of the world hinged upon this. Thus, rather than calling the commander merely a “man,” he designated the ruler by his title and recorded his rank. For when a ruler commands, the text does not say “led an army”: it records what carries greater weight. Is not the offense of brutalizing the Chinese states and confronting Zheng with a great army thereby made evident?
Now Chu was running rampant and overawing the central states. By this time, Jin had long presided over the alliance of the Chinese states. If it did not extend a helping hand, who would check the violence of Chu’s army? Fortunately, it dispatched the army under Que Que to relieve the distress of the people of Zheng, mindful …

彼無辜横罹蛇豕之憂恤我同盟聿申簡書之
義拯焚救溺去危即安抑楚之聲勢遂張矣視
彼楚人之虐豈不大相遠哉自常情言之救患
分災霸者之常職耳聖人以為攘夷安夏之師
天下之大防賴此以不潰故不沒其實而書救
者蓋凡書救未有不善之也救者善則伐者之
罪不于是而亦著乎是則楚可惡也而其君之
暴必書爵而後見晉可善也而於楚之罪則書

punctuated:
彼無辜，横罹蛇豕之憂，恤我同盟，聿申簡書之義，拯焚救溺，去危即安，抑楚之聲勢遂張矣。視彼楚人之虐，豈不大相遠哉？自常情言之，救患分災，霸者之常職耳。聖人以為攘夷安夏之師，天下之大防賴此以不潰，故不沒其實而書救者，蓋凡書救，未有不善之也。救者善，則伐者之罪不于是而亦著乎？是則楚可惡也，而其君之暴必書爵而後見；晉可善也，而於楚之罪則書救而亦顯。春秋之微詞奧義，有如是夫！抑考詳內畧外，先自治而後治人，春秋之法也。故楚討鄭亂，則予楚以治亂賊之黨；鄭無罪見伐，則予晉救以謹華夷之辨。自是徵舒不道，辰陵受盟，責楚益輕，罪在晉矣。吁！觀春秋進退抑揚之㫖，則知安中國待四夷之道也歟！

禮記

是故治世之音安以樂，其政和。

劉霽

translation_en:
…those innocent people, who had undeservedly suffered the menace of snakes and boars. Showing concern for our allies, Jin duly upheld the obligations expressed in the written summons: rescuing those in flames and those drowning, it brought them from danger to safety. Its power and prestige in restraining Chu thus increased. Compared with the cruelty of the men of Chu, was this not vastly different? In ordinary judgment, relieving distress and sharing the burden of calamity are merely the regular duties of a hegemon. The Sage, however, regarded this as an army that repelled the barbarians and secured the Chinese states; upon it depended the preservation of the great defensive barrier of the realm. Thus he did not obscure the facts but recorded the action as a “rescue.” Whenever he records a rescue, he invariably approves it. If the rescuer is approved, does not the guilt of the attacker thereby also become manifest? Thus Chu deserves condemnation, yet its ruler’s violence becomes apparent only when his rank is recorded. Jin deserves approval, while Chu’s guilt is likewise revealed by recording Jin’s action as a rescue. Such are the subtle wording and profound meanings of the Spring and Autumn Annals!

Moreover, on examination, treating internal affairs in detail and external affairs briefly, and first putting oneself in order before governing others, are principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals. Thus, when Chu punished disorder in Zheng, it approved Chu for bringing to justice the partisans of rebels and traitors. When Zheng was attacked despite being innocent, it approved Jin’s rescue, thereby safeguarding the distinction between Chinese and barbarians. Thereafter, in the cases of Zhengshu’s wickedness and the acceptance of a covenant at Chenling, the blame laid upon Chu became still lighter, while the guilt rested with Jin. Ah! By observing the purport of the advances and retreats, censure and praise, in the Spring and Autumn Annals, may we understand the way to secure the central states and deal with the barbarians of the four quarters?

Book of Rites

“Thus the music of a well-governed age is tranquil and joyous: its government is harmonious.”

Liu Ji

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: “Writers generally devote their attention to the phrase ‘a well-governed age’ …”

氣象其亦得政和之涵養者歟宜取以冠本房

而政和處則又短於措辭。冲淡含蓄，宛然寫出太平氣象，其亦得政和之涵養者歟？宜取以冠本房。
考試官左諭德温批：和平可讀。
考試官侍講學士李批：有藻思，有關鎖。
論盛世有至和之音，由盛世有善感之政。蓋音生於人心之所感也。盛世之政旣和，則音之發於人心，豈有不和者哉？記樂者謂夫人心不能無所感，聲音不可以僞爲。彼其形於詩歌，而雜出於閭閻里巷之情；著於諷誦，而不失乎清濁高下之節者，音也。惟治世之音，發乎性情，止乎禮義。凡其抑揚咏嘆之詞，莫不各中乎聲律之度，而無所謂怗懘者焉。啴諧而慢易，繁文而簡節。凡其紆徐委曲之際，莫不各得乎和順之正，而無所謂乖戾者焉。有優柔平中之趣，而無哀怨之聲；有欣喜歡愛之情，而無哀思之態。治世之音如此，豈非政事之和有以感動之乎？是故有禮樂以道志、以和聲，而爲用不同；有政刑以一行、以防姦，而其極則一。皆先王感人之政也。
translation_en:
…yet where the harmony of government is concerned, the wording is somewhat scant. Mild and restrained, it vividly depicts the atmosphere of an age of peace. Might its author also have been nurtured by harmonious government? This should be selected as the foremost answer in this examining room.
Examiner Wen, Left Mentor, comments: “Serene and harmonious; well worth reading.”
Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “It displays literary imagination and a tightly connected structure.”
The argument is that a flourishing age has music of consummate harmony because it has government that moves people toward goodness. Music arises from what stirs the human heart. Since the government of a flourishing age is harmonious, how could the music issuing from human hearts fail to be harmonious? The author of the Record of Music holds that the human heart cannot remain unstirred, and that sounds cannot be fabricated. What takes form in poetry and song, emerging variously from the feelings of people in lanes and neighborhoods, and finds expression in chanting and recitation without departing from the proper measures of clear and full tones, high and low pitches—this is music.
The music of a well-governed age arises from human nature and feeling and remains within the bounds of ritual and righteousness. Its words, with their rising and falling cadences and their sustained expressions of feeling, all conform to the measures of musical pitch and rhythm; there is none of what is called discordance. It is ample and harmonious, relaxed and unhurried, elaborate in its patterns yet simple in its rhythms. Throughout its lingering, winding passages, it invariably attains the proper balance of harmony and concord, with nothing perverse or jarring. It has a gentle, balanced quality, without sounds of grief and resentment; it expresses joy, delight, affection, and love, without an air of sorrowful brooding. Such is the music of a well-governed age. Is this not because harmony in government has stirred it into being?
Thus ritual and music guide aspirations and harmonize sounds, differing in their functions; government and punishments unify conduct and prevent wrongdoing, yet their ultimate aim is one. All are means by which the former kings governed so as to move the hearts of the people.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
惟治世之政出於君臣之所講畫而有以即乎
人心之所安則所謂禮者序也樂者和也薰蒸
浸漬乎人心而不可易矣惟治世之政本於天
下之所願欲而不失乎慎感之意則所謂政以
行之刑以防之流動充滿於天下而無所咈矣
保合天下而天下咸囿於樂利之中安養斯民
而人心悉歸於和平之域治世之政如此則音
之發於人心者豈有不和者哉夫以政和則音
和有不可偽為如此先王慎其所以感之者有
===
由然矣抑因是而知先王作樂之本矣采詩觀
風先王實欲求知夫天下之心也心和則聲和
聲和則樂和所謂本之情性稽之度數制之禮
義其制雖出於先王而實本於天下人心之和
之所被也然非善政養之於平時其能驟得於
一旦哉說者謂禮樂積德百年而後興又曰六
律五聲八音在治忽信矣
張而不弛文武弗能也弛而不張文武弗
為也一張一弛文武之道也

punctuated:
惟治世之政出於君臣之所講畫，而有以即乎人心之所安，則所謂禮者序也，樂者和也，薰蒸浸漬乎人心而不可易矣。惟治世之政本於天下之所願欲，而不失乎慎感之意，則所謂政以行之，刑以防之，流動充滿於天下而無所咈矣。保合天下，而天下咸囿於樂利之中；安養斯民，而人心悉歸於和平之域。治世之政如此，則音之發於人心者，豈有不和者哉？夫以政和則音和，有不可偽為如此，先王慎其所以感之者，有由然矣。抑因是而知先王作樂之本矣。采詩觀風，先王實欲求知夫天下之心也。心和則聲和，聲和則樂和。所謂本之情性，稽之度數，制之禮義，其制雖出於先王，而實本於天下人心之和之所被也。然非善政養之於平時，其能驟得於一旦哉？說者謂禮樂積德百年而後興，又曰六律五聲八音在治忽，信矣。

張而不弛，文武弗能也；弛而不張，文武弗為也。一張一弛，文武之道也。
translation_en:
Only when the government of an orderly age proceeds from the deliberations and plans of ruler and ministers, and accords with what puts people’s hearts at ease, do ritual, which brings order, and music, which brings harmony, permeate and steep people’s hearts so that their influence cannot be altered. Only when the government of an orderly age is grounded in what all under Heaven desire, without losing sight of the need for care in influencing them, do government, which puts these principles into practice, and punishments, which guard against transgressions, flow throughout all under Heaven without meeting resistance. It preserves and unites all under Heaven, encompassing everyone in happiness and well-being; it settles and nurtures the people, bringing all their hearts into the realm of peace and harmony. When the government of an orderly age is like this, how could the sounds arising from people’s hearts fail to be harmonious? Harmony in government thus produces harmony in sound, in a way that cannot be feigned. The former kings therefore had good reason to exercise care over the means by which they influenced the people.

From this we may also understand the foundation upon which the former kings created music. In collecting poems and observing local customs, the former kings truly wished to discover the hearts of all under Heaven. When hearts are harmonious, voices are harmonious; when voices are harmonious, music is harmonious. This is what is meant by grounding music in feelings and human nature, examining it against measures and numbers, and regulating it through ritual and righteousness. Although its forms were established by the former kings, they were actually rooted in the pervasive harmony of people’s hearts throughout all under Heaven. Yet unless good government had nurtured this in ordinary times, could it suddenly have been achieved in a single day? Commentators say that ritual and music arise only after virtue has accumulated for a hundred years. They also say that the six pitch standards, five tones, and eight classes of musical instruments depend upon whether government is orderly or negligent. How true this is!

To keep the bow drawn without relaxing it was beyond even Kings Wen and Wu; to relax it without drawing it was something Kings Wen and Wu would not do. To draw it at one time and relax it at another was the Way of Kings Wen and Wu.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭趙批以弓喻民特借此以明
治道耳作者於弗張弗弛處語意繁複而於一張一
弛處却晦而不暢間有專說文武事業而不顧本文
者獨此作明白條暢而於治道處甚詳故錄
考試官左諭德温批自是說治道文字
考試官侍講學士李批講張弛處非他卷所及
論民之勞息當以其時唯聖人為能得其道也
盖民力易使而亦易憊也張弛之得其道非文
===
武聖王其孰能哉昔子貢觀蜡祭而不知其樂
夫子曉之若曰蜡祭有恤民之義民樂實君上
之澤賜也知之乎彼弓之為用乆張而不弛則
其力必絕民之勞其弓之張乎勞而不暫息焉
則筋力憊於勤苦精神憚於役作雖有文武之
君以倡率於上民將改易而弗從矣文武愛民
之君也豈能強之乎弓之為器乆弛而不張則
其體必變民之息其弓之弛乎弛而不知勞焉
則勤苦不習於素養心志或逸於怠惰雖有文
