論民之勞息，當以其時，唯聖人為能得其道也。盖民力易使而亦易憊也，張弛之得其道，非文武聖王，其孰能哉？昔子貢觀蜡祭而不知其樂，夫子曉之，若曰：「蜡祭有恤民之義，民樂實君上之澤。賜也，知之乎？彼弓之為用，乆張而不弛，則其力必絕。民之勞，其弓之張乎？勞而不暫息焉，則筋力憊於勤苦，精神憚於役作。雖有文武之君以倡率於上，民將改易而弗從矣。文武，愛民之君也，豈能強之乎？弓之為器，乆弛而不張，則其體必變。民之息，其弓之弛乎？弛而不知勞焉，則勤苦不習於素養，心志或逸於怠惰。雖有文
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, an Instructor: The bow is used as an analogy for the people simply to illuminate the way of governing. Other writers are verbose and repetitive when discussing the failure to draw or to relax the bow, yet obscure and unclear when discussing alternation between drawing and relaxing it. Some dwell exclusively on the achievements of Kings Wen and Wu, disregarding the passage itself. This composition alone is clear, well ordered, and fluent, and treats the way of governing in considerable detail. It has therefore been selected for inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher: This is indeed an essay on the way of governing.

Comment by Examiner Li, an Academician Expositor-in-waiting: Its explanation of drawing and relaxing the bow is beyond the reach of the other papers.

In considering the people's labor and rest, each should come at its proper time; only a sage can grasp the right way to arrange them. For the people's strength is easily put to use but also easily exhausted. Who but the sage kings Wen and Wu could have mastered the proper alternation of exertion and relaxation? Once, Zigong observed the year-end zha sacrifice but did not understand its joy. The Master enlightened him, as though saying: “The zha sacrifice embodies concern for the people; their enjoyment is truly a blessing bestowed by their ruler. Ci, do you understand this? When a bow is kept drawn for a long time without being relaxed, its strength will inevitably fail. Is not the people's labor like the drawing of a bow? If they labor without even a brief rest, their bodily strength becomes exhausted by toil, and their spirits shrink from service and work. Even with rulers like Wen and Wu leading them from above, the people will change their allegiance and cease to follow. Wen and Wu were rulers who loved the people: how could they compel them?

“As an implement, a bow left relaxed for a long time without being drawn will inevitably lose its shape. Is not the people's rest like the relaxation of a bow? If they relax without knowing labor, they will not have acquired the habit of hard work through their ordinary upbringing, and their minds and wills may become indolent through idleness. Even if there were a ruler like Wen …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
武之君以鼓舞於上民將散亂而弗收矣文武
教民之君也忍能為此乎是以於一歲之中而
必勞之於三時凡其率作興事以盡力於田畝
者吾弗得而奪也於三時之勞而必息之於終
歲若其蜡畢醉飽以盡歡於一日者吾弗得而
禁也所以勞之者非厲民也使之足食利用以
厚生耳然有時而息焉則所謂說以使民民忘
其勞者也文武之道不其在茲乎所以息之者
非縱民也使之節力養銳以俟用耳然有時而
===
勞焉則所謂佚道使民雖勞不怨者也文武之
道不其如是乎由是觀之則百日之蜡一日之
澤其義固有攸在賜也顧不達於此乎雖然是
道也亦民之所自有者文武付之無心焉耳觀
天地動靜闔闢之義則天地亦不能違也而況
於人乎況於聖人乎是故張弛之道聖人馭民
之術也闔闢之義天地養物之宜也動靜失宜
天地不能以生萬物張弛失道聖人不能以成
化功後之勞民動衆久而不息者亦可以鑒矣

punctuated: 武之君以鼓舞於上，民將散亂而弗收矣。文武，教民之君也，忍能為此乎？是以於一歲之中，而必勞之於三時，凡其率作興事以盡力於田畝者，吾弗得而奪也；於三時之勞，而必息之於終歲，若其蜡畢醉飽以盡歡於一日者，吾弗得而禁也。所以勞之者，非厲民也，使之足食利用以厚生耳。然有時而息焉，則所謂「說以使民，民忘其勞」者也。文武之道，不其在茲乎？所以息之者，非縱民也，使之節力養銳以俟用耳。然有時而勞焉，則所謂「佚道使民，雖勞不怨」者也。文武之道，不其如是乎？由是觀之，則百日之蜡，一日之澤，其義固有攸在。賜也，顧不達於此乎？雖然，是道也，亦民之所自有者，文武付之無心焉耳。觀天地動靜闔闢之義，則天地亦不能違也，而況於人乎？況於聖人乎？是故張弛之道，聖人馭民之術也；闔闢之義，天地養物之宜也。動靜失宜，天地不能以生萬物；張弛失道，聖人不能以成化功。後之勞民動衆久而不息者，亦可以鑒矣。
translation_en:
…[even if rulers like Kings Wen and] Wu encouraged them from above, the people would scatter in disorder and could not be gathered together. Wen and Wu were rulers who instructed the people: could they bear to bring this about? Thus, within each year, the people must be put to work during the three seasons. When they undertake their tasks and set about their labors, devoting their strength to the fields, I may not take that time away from them. Yet after the toil of those three seasons, they must be allowed to rest at the year’s end. When, after the zha sacrifice, they drink and eat their fill, enjoying themselves to the utmost for a single day, I may not forbid it. Putting them to work is not intended to afflict them, but merely to ensure sufficient food and useful resources, thereby enriching their livelihood. Yet when they are given rest at the proper times, this is what is meant by: “Employ the people through making them glad, and they forget their toil.” Is this not where the Way of Wen and Wu lies? Giving them rest is not intended to indulge them, but merely to conserve their strength and restore their vigor in readiness for service. Yet when they are put to work at the proper times, this is what is meant by: “Employ the people in a way that brings them ease, and though they toil, they do not resent it.” Is this not the Way of Wen and Wu?

Viewed in this light, the zha sacrifice following a hundred days [of toil], with its bounty of a single day, certainly has a purpose. Ci, do you still not understand this? Nevertheless, this Way is also something inherent in the people themselves; Wen and Wu simply entrusted it to them without imposing designs of their own. Consider the principles of movement and stillness, closing and opening, in Heaven and Earth: even Heaven and Earth cannot depart from them. How much less can human beings—or sages! Thus the Way of tension and relaxation is the sages’ art of governing the people; the principle of closing and opening is the fitting means by which Heaven and Earth nourish things. If movement and stillness lose their proper balance, Heaven and Earth cannot bring the myriad things to life; if tension and relaxation depart from their proper Way, sages cannot accomplish their work of transformation. Those in later ages who toil the people and mobilize the multitude for long periods without respite may also take warning from this.

translation_en:
Second Session

Discourse: The Sage’s Art of Inspiring the Myriad People

Cui Tong

Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: The topic itself is upright and substantial, and candidates generally can develop it. Few, however, give due weight to the sage’s circumspection. This composition draws on antiquity to substantiate its discussion of the present. Its language and ideas are apt [?], and it brings out Yuancheng’s meaning. For this reason it has been selected for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: It unfolds tirelessly over more than a thousand words, without a single expression that copies old formulations or ventures into the bizarre. In its opening and closing, its sweep in every direction, it invariably observes the proper standards. Unhurried and smoothly flowing, it offers a lingering depth of meaning: one singing could elicit three answering sighs of admiration.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Professor: In the discourse examination, those who labor over fine carving err on the side of superficiality; those who give their writing free rein err on the side of diffuseness. This composition is precise in its examination of evidence and sound and correct in its arguments. It has the flavor of the unseasoned sacrificial broth and the plain water offered as ritual wine, yet one naturally never tires of it. Moreover, your performances in both the preceding and following sessions are equally commendable. For a high recommendation in the autumn Provincial Examination, no one could take your place.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Mentor: Ornament and substance are well matched; expression and meaning are both fully realized. Examination writing of this kind is indeed accomplished.

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: When a discourse concerns the principles of government, it readily lapses into borrowed arguments. Only this essay, among those I have seen, casts off habitual conventions and stands conspicuously above the rest. Selecting it to rank first in the Southern Metropolitan Region surely accords with everyone’s expectations.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
論曰聖人有風天下之道而天下不倦此天下
所以養于善而不自知也天下之心渙而不一
也天下之情靡而未易以起也非得其道以風
之則渙者將至於無所收拾靡者或至於無所
振立驅天下之人心之風俗於無所依藉揚厲
之地而始罪天下曰何其無法守也是誤天下
也故善理天下者必有立頹起懦之道而民不
倦必有勝殘去殺之道而民不知以此而制馭
群動以此而整齊六合以此而始以此而終而
===
後天下之志定而後天下之化成於乎此豈可
以易言哉元城劉安世當宋哲宗時有言曰命
令者聖人所恃以鼓舞萬民之術其亦有所警
矣命令何為者也書曰猷告爾四國多方禮曰
王言如絲其出如綸王言如綸其出如綍皆是
也虞夏殷周有典則有訓誥有誓命漢唐宋有
約法有詔令盖一王有一王之法雖損益沿革
繁簡文質之不同而同於軌衆率物齊一天下
之心志以新天下之耳目也天下如彼其大也

punctuated: 論曰：聖人有風天下之道，而天下不倦，此天下所以養于善而不自知也。天下之心渙而不一也，天下之情靡而未易以起也。非得其道以風之，則渙者將至於無所收拾，靡者或至於無所振立，驅天下之人心之風俗於無所依藉揚厲之地，而始罪天下曰：「何其無法守也？」是誤天下也。故善理天下者，必有立頹起懦之道而民不倦，必有勝殘去殺之道而民不知。以此而制馭群動，以此而整齊六合，以此而始，以此而終，而後天下之志定，而後天下之化成。於乎！此豈可以易言哉？元城劉安世當宋哲宗時有言曰：「命令者，聖人所恃以鼓舞萬民之術。」其亦有所警矣。命令何為者也？《書》曰：「猷！告爾四國多方。」《禮》曰：「王言如絲，其出如綸；王言如綸，其出如綍。」皆是也。虞夏殷周有典則，有訓誥，有誓命；漢唐宋有約法，有詔令。盖一王有一王之法，雖損益沿革、繁簡文質之不同，而同於軌衆率物，齊一天下之心志，以新天下之耳目也。天下如彼其大也，
translation_en: The discourse says: The sage has a way of influencing all under Heaven without wearying them. Thus they are nurtured in goodness without themselves knowing it. The hearts of the people are scattered and lack unity; their dispositions are languid and not easily stirred. Unless the proper way is found to influence them, those who are scattered will become impossible to gather together, and those who are languid may become impossible to rouse. To drive the hearts and customs of the people into a condition in which they have nothing to rely on and no means of being uplifted, and only then to blame them, saying, “Why do they have no standards to uphold?”—this is to lead the world astray. Those who govern well must therefore have a way of restoring the dispirited and rousing the timid without wearying the people, and a way of overcoming cruelty and dispensing with executions without the people being aware of it. By this means they regulate and direct all activity; by this means they bring order to the six directions. They begin with it and end with it. Only then are the purposes of all under Heaven settled, and only then is their moral transformation accomplished. Ah! How could this be spoken of lightly? Liu Anshi of Yuancheng, in the reign of Emperor Zhezong of the Song, said: “Commands are the means upon which the sage relies to inspire and stir the myriad people.” His words surely conveyed a warning. What do commands accomplish? The Book of Documents says: “Ah! I announce to you, the many regions of the four quarters.” The Book of Rites says: “The king’s words are like silk thread, but when issued they become like cord; the king’s words are like cord, but when issued they become like thick rope.” These both concern this matter. Yu, Xia, Yin, and Zhou had canons and regulations, instructions and proclamations, oaths and mandates; Han, Tang, and Song had compacts of law and imperial edicts. Each king has his own laws. Though these differ in what they subtract or add, retain or change, and in their complexity or simplicity, refinement or plainness, they are alike in guiding the multitude and leading all beings, unifying the hearts and purposes of all under Heaven, and renewing what the people hear and see. All under Heaven is so vast…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
智者愚者勇者怯者貴者賤者遠者邇者親者
疎者其趨其習又如彼其不同也故必有大君
焉以主宰之而後天下始定於一大君者豈必
家喻戶曉而後天下乃一哉故必有命令焉布
告於立國之初而持循於經世之遠洋溢乎封
牧之域而咸曁乎蠻貊之地使天下咸知有君
咸知有朝廷而民始不犯其勢盖有不得不然
者易曰天下有風姤后以施命誥四方又曰隨
風巽君子以申命行事風之為物也流行四時
===
周旋八極吹號萬籟無物不遇無物不動者也
聖人觀風之象體巽之義有命令焉呼天下之
昧而以起天下之仆伸天下之氣而以厭天下
之心如風自天而下觸之者折被之者立雨露
滋息之所不能遂日月照臨之所不能及妖氛
欝抑之所不能破水火燥濕之所不能運者而
惟風得以蕩之闢之而有除穢布新之象也是
故風者天之命也命令者聖人之風也而實天
下後世之法也法苟立矣令苟行矣吾見勇者

故風者天之命也命令者聖人之風也而實天
下後世之法也法苟立矣令苟行矣吾見勇者
punctuated:
智者、愚者、勇者、怯者、貴者、賤者、遠者、邇者、親者、疎者，其趨其習又如彼其不同也。故必有大君焉以主宰之，而後天下始定於一。大君者，豈必家喻戶曉而後天下乃一哉？故必有命令焉，布告於立國之初，而持循於經世之遠，洋溢乎封牧之域，而咸曁乎蠻貊之地，使天下咸知有君，咸知有朝廷，而民始不犯。其勢盖有不得不然者。易曰：「天下有風，姤；后以施命誥四方。」又曰：「隨風，巽；君子以申命行事。」風之為物也，流行四時，周旋八極，吹號萬籟，無物不遇，無物不動者也。
聖人觀風之象，體巽之義，有命令焉，呼天下之昧，而以起天下之仆，伸天下之氣，而以厭天下之心。如風自天而下，觸之者折，被之者立。雨露滋息之所不能遂，日月照臨之所不能及，妖氛欝抑之所不能破，水火燥濕之所不能運者，而惟風得以蕩之、闢之，而有除穢布新之象也。是故風者，天之命也；命令者，聖人之風也，而實天下後世之法也。法苟立矣，令苟行矣，吾見勇者
translation_en:
…the wise and the foolish, the brave and the timid, the noble and the lowly, those far away and those nearby, those closely related and those distantly related—their inclinations and habits are likewise so very different. Thus there must be a great ruler to govern them; only then can all under Heaven be settled in unity. But must the great ruler explain matters to every household and make every person understand before all under Heaven can be united? There must therefore be commands, proclaimed at the founding of the state and upheld throughout the long course of governing the world. They must spread throughout the territories of the regional lords and governors and reach even the lands of the Man and Mo peoples, so that everyone under Heaven knows there is a ruler and an imperial court. Only then will the people cease to transgress. The circumstances make this unavoidable. The Book of Changes says: “Under Heaven there is wind: Encounter [Gou]. The sovereign accordingly issues commands and proclaims them to the four quarters.” It also says: “Wind following wind: The Gentle [Xun]. The noble man accordingly reiterates commands and carries out affairs.” Wind flows through the four seasons and circulates to the eight extremities, blowing and sounding through the myriad hollows. There is nothing it does not encounter, nothing it does not move.
The sage observes the image of wind and embodies the meaning of Xun. He issues commands to awaken the benighted throughout the world and raise up the fallen, to invigorate the spirit of all under Heaven and satisfy their hearts. Like wind descending from Heaven, they break what they strike and raise up what receives their influence. What the nourishing rain and dew cannot bring to fruition, what the illuminating sun and moon cannot reach, what malign vapors keep pent up and unbroken [?], and what the drying and moistening powers of fire and water cannot set in motion—wind alone can sweep through and open up, presenting the image of clearing away impurity and spreading renewal. Thus wind is Heaven’s command; commands are the sage’s wind, and indeed the law for all under Heaven and for later generations. Once the law is established and commands are put into effect, I see the brave…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
奪其氣智者奪其謀貴者奪其僭親者邇者奪
其貪而怯者愚者賤者疎者莫不有所憑而為
善有所制而不為惡如六軍之行而有耳目旗
鼓以為之令如舟車之用而有師工以為之導
如醫藥之用而有法案以為之方由此者安不
由此者危用此者生不用此者死所以奔走天
下之豪傑所以制伏天下之奸回所以感激天
下之忠義所以嘘拂天下之晦潜鼓之舞之其
機在我而彼自不識也有天下者亦豈好為是
===
改作以求勝於下哉盖無令是無法也無法是
無君也故法為上君位次之君與法固不可一
日而離者是法也其始也為天下立之其既也
君亦不得而踰焉故賞罰以法予奪以法廢置
以法禮自我議也而法之所在則等威由之而
立度自我制也而法之所在則界限由之而明
執法之吏日以法告我而吾自不敢過效法之
子孫日以法視我而吾自不敢違前疑後丞左
史右書日以法事我而吾自不敢亂懲忘之訓

史右書曰以法事我而吾自不敢亂愆忘之訓
punctuated: 奪其氣，智者奪其謀，貴者奪其僭，親者邇者奪其貪，而怯者愚者賤者疎者，莫不有所憑而為善，有所制而不為惡。如六軍之行，而有耳目旗鼓以為之令；如舟車之用，而有師工以為之導；如醫藥之用，而有法案以為之方。由此者安，不由此者危；用此者生，不用此者死。所以奔走天下之豪傑，所以制伏天下之奸回，所以感激天下之忠義，所以嘘拂天下之晦潜。鼓之舞之，其機在我，而彼自不識也。有天下者，亦豈好為是改作，以求勝於下哉？盖無令是無法也，無法是無君也。故法為上，君位次之。君與法，固不可一日而離者。是法也，其始也為天下立之，其既也君亦不得而踰焉。故賞罰以法，予奪以法，廢置以法。禮自我議也，而法之所在，則等威由之而立；度自我制也，而法之所在，則界限由之而明。執法之吏，日以法告我，而吾自不敢過；效法之子孫，日以法視我，而吾自不敢違；前疑後丞，左史右書，日以法事我，而吾自不敢亂。懲忘之訓
translation_en:
…are stripped of their spirit; the clever are stripped of their schemes; the high-ranking are stripped of their usurpations; relatives and intimates are stripped of their greed. Meanwhile, the timid, the foolish, the lowly, and the distant all have something to rely upon in doing good and something to restrain them from doing evil. It is like the march of the six armies, with flags and drums serving as their eyes and ears and conveying commands; like the use of boats and carriages, with masters and craftsmen to guide them; or like the use of medicines, with established procedures and case records to furnish prescriptions. Those who follow this are secure; those who do not are imperiled. Those who employ it live; those who do not die. By these means, the outstanding men of the realm are set in motion, its treacherous and perverse men are subdued, its loyal and righteous men are inspired, and its obscure and hidden men are nurtured and brought forward. I stir them and set them dancing: the moving impulse lies with me, yet they themselves do not perceive it. Does the possessor of all under Heaven delight in making such changes merely to gain the upper hand over those below him?

For to have no commands is to have no law, and to have no law is to have no ruler. Thus law stands highest, and the ruler’s position comes next. Ruler and law cannot be separated for even a single day. Such law is initially established for all under Heaven; once established, even the ruler may not transgress it. Thus rewards and punishments accord with law, granting and taking away accord with law, and dismissal and appointment accord with law. Ritual is deliberated upon by me, yet wherever law applies, distinctions of rank and dignity are established through it. Standards are instituted by me, yet wherever law applies, boundaries are clarified through it. The officials who enforce the law daily admonish me by the law, and I dare not overstep it. My descendants, who take the law as their model, daily judge me by the law, and I dare not violate it. The counselor before me and the assistant behind me, the historian to my left and the scribe to my right, daily serve me according to law, and I dare not throw it into disorder. The admonition against forgetfulness…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
得於詩渙汗之說得於易儆戒無虞得於書如
神物之不敢侮如天墜地設而不敢犯以之而
制馭群動以之而整齊六合以之而安人心以
之而定天下天下之人相安於法守之中而無
倍叛侵陵之禍如陰陽異位而不瀆如萬物長
養而不衂此之謂同天下之道而民不倦天下
養於善而不自知聖人之道大矣哉自古有天
下者不患無法而患法立而不能久不患法不
行而患法行而或變誠能訏謨遠猶而不為一
===
時之計詢謀用中而不出於一己之私是惟無
發發而必信是惟不行行之必堅不朝令而夕
改不既舉而復墜則何患其不能久然而復有
變焉者何哉變者變其所以害吾法者耳若法
善可久而妄者或欲有所改易是之謂亂法亂
法者不容於堯舜之世此秦皇漢武之所以自
斃而祖宗不足法之說安石以之而誤神宗也
當哲宗時宋家法度不知其幾變而安世為是
言於乎其亦有所警矣

變焉者何哉變者變其所以害吾法者耳若法
善可久而妄者或欲有所改易是之謂亂法亂
法者不容於堯舜之世此秦皇漢武之所以自
斃而祖宗不足法之說安石以之而誤神宗也
當哲宗時宋家法度不知其幾變而安世為是
言於乎其亦有所警矣
punctuated:
得於《詩》，渙汗之說得於《易》，儆戒無虞得於《書》。如神物之不敢侮，如天墜地設而不敢犯，以之而制馭群動，以之而整齊六合，以之而安人心，以之而定天下。天下之人相安於法守之中，而無倍叛侵陵之禍，如陰陽異位而不瀆，如萬物長養而不衂。此之謂同天下之道而民不倦，天下養於善而不自知。聖人之道大矣哉！
自古有天下者，不患無法，而患法立而不能久；不患法不行，而患法行而或變。誠能訏謨遠猶，而不為一時之計，詢謀用中，而不出於一己之私，是惟無發，發而必信；是惟不行，行之必堅。不朝令而夕改，不既舉而復墜，則何患其不能久？然而復有變焉者，何哉？變者，變其所以害吾法者耳。若法善可久，而妄者或欲有所改易，是之謂亂法。亂法者，不容於堯舜之世。此秦皇、漢武之所以自斃，而祖宗不足法之說，安石以之而誤神宗也。當哲宗時，宋家法度不知其幾變，而安世為是言。於乎，其亦有所警矣！
translation_en:
…is derived from the Book of Poetry; the teaching that proclamations, once issued, are like sweat that cannot be drawn back is derived from the Book of Changes; and the injunction to remain vigilant when there is no cause for anxiety is derived from the Book of Documents. One must no more dare to slight the laws than sacred objects, nor dare to violate them than what Heaven has brought down and Earth established [?]. Through them, one governs all activity, orders the six directions, sets people’s hearts at ease, and brings stability to all under Heaven. The people of the realm live peaceably together within the bounds of the laws they uphold, free from the calamities of rebellion, aggression, and oppression. They are like yin and yang, occupying distinct positions without encroaching upon each other, or the myriad things, growing and flourishing without injury. This is what is meant by unifying the Way throughout the realm without wearying the people: all under Heaven are nurtured in goodness without themselves knowing it. Great indeed is the Way of the sages!
Since antiquity, those who possess the realm have had reason to fear not the absence of laws, but that laws, once established, might not endure; not that laws would go unenforced, but that, once enforced, they might be altered. If they could truly devise broad plans with distant aims, rather than calculate merely for the moment, and consult others in their deliberations and adopt the proper mean, rather than act from personal self-interest, then they would issue nothing lightly, but whatever they issued would assuredly be trustworthy; they would undertake nothing lightly, but whatever they undertook would assuredly be pursued firmly. If they did not issue an order in the morning and change it that evening, or let something fall away after putting it into effect, why should they fear that their laws would not endure? Yet why should there still be changes? What is changed is only that which harms our laws. If laws are good and capable of enduring, yet reckless people wish to alter them, this is called subverting the laws. Those who subvert the laws would not have been tolerated in the age of Yao and Shun. This is how the Qin emperor and Emperor Wu of Han brought ruin upon themselves; and it was through the claim that the ancestral rulers need not be taken as models that Anshi 安石 led Shenzong astray. By the time of Zhezong, the laws and institutions of the Song ruling house had undergone who knows how many changes, and Anshi 安世 made this statement. Alas! Surely he too had something against which he wished to warn!

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
從其視聖人不啻如神明在上莫敢仰視駭而
弗安渙而弗一而聖人之所以建法設教以為
圖治之道者亦將沮格而莫之信矣於乎曾謂
聖人神天下之術而有出于言之外者乎元城
劉氏論聖人鼓舞萬民之術而歸于命令此愚
所謂神之說而非□之者也請申其意今夫聖
人之心之於天下之民道始欲其變也德始欲
其漸也禮始欲其飾倫節行也樂始欲其平欲
釋躁也刑始欲其不干也賞始欲其感受也然
===
天下若是其大也生民若是其衆也廣谷大川
通衢巨邑若是其異域也嗜欲言語習俗好尚
若是其不齊也不能一一盡如聖人之願徒使
聖人鬱紆其心而不平也不平非尤之也尤之
則將棄之矣聖人棄其民者乎聖人不棄其民
不得已而假命令以為鼓舞之術焉于以新天
下之耳目定天下之心志同天下之習尚自朝
廷遍於田野自天門敷於日出偃者起之退者
進之弱者強之畏者悅之洽比其懸絕之勢和

translation_en:
…whom to follow. They would regard the sage as nothing less than a divine being on high, whom none dared look up to: terrified and uneasy, scattered and disunited. The laws and teachings that the sage establishes as a means of achieving good government would consequently be obstructed, and no one would trust them. Alas! Could anyone suppose that the sage’s means of transforming the world with numinous efficacy lies outside words? Master Liu of Yuancheng discussed the sage’s means of inspiring and stirring the myriad people and traced it to commands and ordinances. This is what I mean by acting with numinous efficacy rather than [illegible] them [?]. Allow me to elaborate.

As for the sage’s intentions toward the people of the world: through the Way, his original wish is to transform them; through virtue, to imbue them gradually; through ritual, to refine their relationships and regulate their conduct; through music, to temper their desires and dispel their restlessness; through punishments, to keep them from transgression; and through rewards, to move them by what they receive. Yet the world is so vast, its people so numerous; broad valleys and great rivers, busy thoroughfares and mighty cities occupy such different regions; appetites and desires, speech, customs, and preferences are so varied. They cannot all, one by one, fully accord with the sage’s wishes. This merely leaves the sage’s heart troubled and unable to rest. His unrest does not mean that he blames them; to blame them would lead to abandoning them. Would the sage abandon his people? He does not abandon them, and thus has no choice but to employ commands and ordinances as the means of inspiring and stirring them.

Through these he renews the eyes and ears of all under Heaven, steadies their hearts and resolves, and brings their customs and preferences into accord. They extend from the court throughout the countryside, spreading from the Gate of Heaven to the place of sunrise. Those who lie prostrate he raises; those who withdraw he advances; the weak he strengthens; the fearful he gladdens. He brings together those whose positions are vastly separated, and harmonizes…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同其疎遠之情道大如天因令之發而變於道
也德輶如毛因令之發而漸於德也禮如履守
禮於發令之餘樂如豫陶樂於發令之後刑如
秋之肅殺惴惴聴罪而惟令之畏也賞如春之
煕和亹亹若德而惟令之悅也改更之均齊薰
染之神速趨向之果决不以高下如天地而息
流通之美也不以貴賤如冠屨而絶融貫之妙
也夫聖人之所以為術者亦神矣非申韓之刻
非黃老之深非儀秦之詐揆之於人情本之於
===
天道參之於群議决之於一心温良而有制簡
肅而有和厚重而有變渾涵而有方用無窮之
意無津涯推無滯礙出無疑謗公卿之所厲翼
郡縣之所欽承綴衣虎賁之所密觀吉士正人
之所樂遇懸之於並觀之地而無所訾議傳之
於無窮之世而無所改遷問之於所甚不屑之
人而無所誹間堅如金石信如寒暑著如日月
驚如雷霆沛如江河詩之所謂遐不作人書之
所謂四方風動孔子之所謂綏來動和者皆是

同其疎遠之情。道大如天，因令之發而變於道也；德輶如毛，因令之發而漸於德也。禮如履，守禮於發令之餘；樂如豫，陶樂於發令之後。刑如秋之肅殺，惴惴聴罪而惟令之畏也；賞如春之煕和，亹亹若德而惟令之悅也。改更之均齊，薰染之神速，趨向之果决，不以高下如天地而息流通之美也，不以貴賤如冠屨而絶融貫之妙也。
夫聖人之所以為術者亦神矣！非申韓之刻，非黃老之深，非儀秦之詐。揆之於人情，本之於天道，參之於群議，决之於一心。温良而有制，簡肅而有和，厚重而有變，渾涵而有方。用無窮之意，無津涯，推無滯礙，出無疑謗。公卿之所厲翼，郡縣之所欽承，綴衣虎賁之所密觀，吉士正人之所樂遇。懸之於並觀之地而無所訾議，傳之於無窮之世而無所改遷，問之於所甚不屑之人而無所誹間。堅如金石，信如寒暑，著如日月，驚如雷霆，沛如江河。《詩》之所謂「遐不作人」，《書》之所謂「四方風動」，孔子之所謂「綏來動和」者，皆是
translation_en:
…and bring their estranged feelings into harmony. The Way is as vast as Heaven: through the issuing of commands, people are transformed in accordance with the Way. Virtue is as light as a feather: through the issuing of commands, people become steeped in virtue. Ritual means treading the proper path: people observe ritual after commands are issued. Music means delight: people are nurtured by music after commands are issued. Punishment resembles autumn’s killing severity: trembling as they await judgment upon their offenses, people stand in awe of the commands. Rewards resemble spring’s warm harmony: diligently responding to beneficence [?], people rejoice in the commands. How uniform the reform, how wondrously swift the transforming influence, how resolute the direction of people’s efforts! Differences between high and low, as great as those between Heaven and earth, do not halt this admirable circulation; differences between noble and humble, like those between cap and shoe, do not sever this marvelous interpenetration.
Indeed, the methods employed by the sage are wondrous! They are neither the harshness of Shen Buhai and Han Fei, nor the profundity of Huangdi and Laozi, nor the deceit of Zhang Yi and Su Qin. He measures them against human feelings, roots them in the Way of Heaven, tests them through collective deliberation, and decides upon them in his own mind. They are gentle yet regulated, simple and solemn yet harmonious, weighty yet adaptable, capacious yet possessed of definite principles. Their application and intent are inexhaustible and boundless [?]; their extension encounters no obstruction, and their promulgation occasions neither suspicion nor slander. They inspire the high ministers to diligent assistance, command reverent obedience in prefectures and counties, receive close attention from wardrobe attendants and imperial guards, and are welcomed by worthy scholars and upright men. Displayed where all may view them, they invite no criticism; transmitted through endless generations, they require no alteration; submitted even to those most disdainful of them, they offer no grounds for slander or faultfinding. They are firm as metal and stone, dependable as cold and heat, manifest as sun and moon, awe-inspiring as thunder, and abundant as rivers. What the Book of Odes calls “Does he not raise up men?”, what the Book of Documents calls “The four quarters stirred as by the wind,” and what Confucius calls “Give them peace, and they come; set them in motion, and they respond in harmony”—all these are this…

translation_en:
…are instances of this art. Thus, when the sage possesses this art, his resplendent ceremonial robes and pendant crown tassels are not [?]; in bearing great responsibilities and undertaking difficult tasks, he is not alone; and his receipt of precious objects and gold is not without justification. For the sage’s relationship with the people is like that between members of a household, between father and son, yet he does not arouse in them the suspicion that his intentions are hidden and difficult to fathom. The people, in turn, become accustomed to his purposes and thoroughly familiar with his plans, so that those formerly alarmed become reassured, and those formerly scattered become united. Ah! Can the wondrous efficacy of the sage’s art reach such a height? How could this be a matter of making the people ignorant? We can see that the sage is master of all under Heaven, commands are master of the sage, and the sage’s heart is in turn master of commands.

Following this reasoning, I have also examined the emperors and kings of antiquity. Yao and Shun were like Heaven and like spirits; yet when they consulted the Four Peaks and sought counsel from the regional governors, and appointed the Yuan and Kai [?], they too issued commands that reached their ministers. With Tang and Wu, their commands offered repeated, earnest admonitions, explaining matters fully and in detail, returning to them again and again without ceasing. Compared with Yao and Shun, Tang and Wu differed in their deeds: punitive conquest as against yielding the throne with ceremonial deference. They also differed in their virtue: returning to virtue through cultivation as against possessing it by nature. Thus their times differed in obedience and resistance, and their commands in elaborateness and simplicity; but the essential art was the same. Ah! This too was brought about by circumstances. How could it have been what the sages themselves desired? Respectfully submitted as a discourse.

Memorial

A memorial composed in the persona of a Grand Secretary, expressing thanks for the bestowal of a silver seal inscribed “Correct faults and rectify errors.” The twenty-second year of Yongle (1424).

舜達聰而明目，禹懸鐘鼓，期以道而教寡人；說作舟霖，兾同心以匡乃辟。粤自三代以往，重于一德之成。願逐龍干，屈意師臣之辱；顧求匕櫕，甘心少主之疑。僅止輦以受言，勞牽裾而進諫。免冠宗廟，温言偶戒于乗危；置笏殿階，怒色遂形于顧命。盖望臣者固重，言或未必盡從；待下者雖周，中亦不能無愧。
兹盖伏遇皇帝陛下，運膺千載，德配兩間。誠孝因心，監國却千秋之賀；寬仁為度，閲奏原一字之差。夙侍高皇，曁承文考，便宜發廩，洞察民心嚮背之機。
translation_en:
…Shun opened his ears and sharpened his sight; Yu hung bells and drums, hoping that others would instruct him in the Way. Yue served as a boat and as timely rain, hoping to work with one heart to set his sovereign right. From the Three Dynasties onward, great weight was placed on achieving unity in virtue. Wishing to drive away Longgan [?], a ruler humbled himself before the rebuke of a minister whom he treated as his teacher; seeking 匕櫕 [text unclear; ?], he willingly bore the young sovereign’s suspicion. He merely halted his carriage to receive counsel, leaving a minister to tug at his robe to offer remonstrance. When a minister removed his cap in the ancestral temple, gentle words occasionally warned against courting danger; when a minister laid his audience tablet on the palace steps, an angry expression appeared over the charge entrusted at a ruler’s death. For although rulers’ expectations of their ministers were weighty, they did not necessarily heed all their words; although their treatment of subordinates was punctilious, inwardly they could not be without shame.
Now we have humbly encountered Your Majesty the Emperor, whose destiny answers an opportunity arising once in a thousand years, and whose virtue matches Heaven and Earth. Sincerity and filial devotion spring from your heart: while overseeing the realm as regent, you declined congratulations on your birthday. Generosity and benevolence govern your conduct: on reading a memorial, you pardoned an error of a single character. In earlier days you attended Emperor Gao, and then succeeded your illustrious deceased father. You exercised discretion in opening the granaries, discerning profoundly the circumstances that turn the people’s hearts toward or away from their ruler…

関免求賢，深知王業艱難之自；率由舊典，祓飾洪圖。頃因踐阼之餘，煥有圖書之賜。謂毫釐之謬，或遺患于歷年；而晷刻有愆，將致弊于環海。聖心不憚于改過，治道亦謹乎防微。顧取涓埃，奚裨海嶽？嘅銅尊之寵，徒耀觀瞻；彼金筯之褒，何關獻納？自有君臣以來所未見，雖或帝王之聖無以加。臣等叨遇先朝，置諸輔弼；逮事陛下，過於尊崇。荷造化之陶鎔，敢自忘於百鍊？冀鬼神之呵護，庶以永于斯傳。
伏願體周文未見之心，緝熈敬止；法商湯不吝之德，終始念兹。宮中府中之相符，
translation_en:
…granting exemptions [?] and seeking worthy men, you understood profoundly the origins of the hardships of royal rule; following established precedents in all things, you purified and embellished the grand imperial enterprise. Recently, following your accession to the throne, you bestowed a splendid gift of books. You declared that an error as slight as a hair’s breadth might leave trouble for years to come, and that a lapse lasting but a moment might bring harm throughout the realm. Your sagely heart does not shrink from correcting faults; in the way of governance, too, you take care to forestall trouble at its slightest beginnings. Yet what benefit can our mere drops of water and specks of dust bring to the seas and mountains? Alas, the favor of the bronze wine vessel merely dazzles the eye; what connection does the commendation conveyed by golden chopsticks have with our presentation of counsel? Such treatment has never been seen since rulers and ministers first existed; even the sageliest emperors and kings could not surpass it. We, your servants, undeservedly enjoyed the favor of the preceding reign and were placed among the throne’s chief advisers. Since coming to serve Your Majesty, we have received honor beyond our deserts. Having benefited from the molding and refining of your creative power, how dare we forget to subject ourselves to a hundred refinings? We hope for the protection of spirits, so that this legacy may endure.
We humbly wish that you embody King Wen of Zhou’s disposition to seek the Way as though he had not yet seen it, continuing in luminous virtue and abiding in reverence; and emulate King Tang of Shang’s virtue of being unstinting in correcting his faults, keeping this in mind from beginning to end. May the palace and the government offices be in accord…

…the sage instructions and has gained understanding from them. Moreover, the loyal devotion expressed in the submission at the essay’s close is deeply earnest. How worthy of respect!

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Professor: “The compilation of our dynasty’s Collected Statutes (Huidian) surpasses all antiquity and provides enduring standards for myriad generations. Candidates generally can extol it, but this response alone examines the great questions of continuity and change, diminution and augmentation, with precise and detailed supporting evidence and clear, lucid exposition. Moreover, comparison with his work in the preceding two sessions shows that those compositions, too, are powerful and distinguished. For first place in the autumn examination, whom could we choose but you?”

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher: “Establishing laws brings about the good government of a dynasty; observing laws extends its enterprise through myriad generations. Among those who have discussed government, ancient or modern, none has altered this principle. You have answered point by point with clarity, and your sincere loyal devotion is especially earnest in the hopes you express for preserving the achievements already established. How could examination compositions alone encompass your abilities?”

Comment by Examiner Li, Academician Expositor: “The Collected Statutes comprehensively records our dynasty’s ritual institutions. Those who recognize its principal features can certainly expound and extol them, but this policy essay alone fully comprehends the excellence of our sagely founder’s establishment of institutions and the appropriateness of the successive sage emperors’ continuation of his work. The few sentences at the end reveal your loyal devotion especially clearly. Ah! Having found you, we who preside over the examination have something worthy to present when appearing before His Majesty!”

Response: The institutions of a dynasty are first established by an earlier sage ruler and cannot be altered for myriad generations; they are brought to completion by a later sage ruler and must be preserved for myriad generations. For the fact that these institutions cannot be altered is precisely that the Way cannot…

…cannot be changed; what must be preserved in the institutions is precisely what must be preserved in the Way. Ah! This is why our dynasty’s Collected Statutes (Huidian) participates in the subtle workings of creation and accords with what is fitting in both present and ancient times. None but our sagely ancestor could have initiated it, and none but our Emperor Jing and the present emperor could have brought it to completion thereafter! How splendid and admirable! Permit me respectfully to explain.
When a dynasty rises, it must have its own body of statutes. These sustain the hearts of the people; these nurture the vitality of the state. Thus, in the age of Tang and Yu, the Canons and Counsels were composed; in the age of Yu of Xia, statutes and rules were bequeathed. Shang had its counsels, and Zhou its ritual institutions. All these were rooted in personal practice and understanding gained in the heart, and found outward expression in laws, standards, and actions. They were applied within households, the state, and the court, and their reach extended beyond the Four Seas and Nine Regions. Thus Yao and Shun held All under Heaven for nearly a hundred years; Xia held it for more than four hundred years, Shang for more than six hundred, and Zhou for more than eight hundred. It was probably through these institutions that they could enjoy Heaven’s favor and secure lasting blessings for their successors.
Coming down to Han, there was the compact of three articles. Though seemingly simple and easy to follow, it did not encompass the methods of moral transformation and good governance. Tang promulgated the Six Statutes (Liudian) and the Collected Essentials (Huiyao); although…

…though seemingly comprehensive, they were not the institutions of the perfected Zhou. The Song Compendium of Essential Documents (Huiyao) was compiled following the Tang precedent; yet already at the time there was criticism that it was grounded in contemporary preferences and confined to the “three gates” [?]. The Yuan Statecraft Compendium (Jingshi) drew on both the Tang and Song. Yet could those with the rank and rancid customs of the barbarians participate in the great Way of our former kings?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, endowed with sagely and divine qualities and civil and military accomplishments, encountered the moment when Heaven granted its favor and the people gave their allegiance. Thus he could win the realm from those not of our own kind and carry forward the states and ruling houses established by the ancient emperors and kings. This was an achievement unprecedented since the beginning of the world. He once commanded the compilation of the Duties of the Various Offices (Zhusi Zhizhang), which fully recorded the official institutions, regulations, and statutes of the time. Drawing on antiquity, he established offices and apportioned responsibilities among the Six Ministers. His sagacious plans and divine calculations far surpassed those of all preceding ages: this was truly a grand and enduring canon. Yet the book was compiled in the middle years of the Hongwu reign, and many changes were made in its final years. Under [?] our successive sage sovereigns, the work of carrying forward their predecessor’s achievements became ever more illustrious. Nevertheless, after successive eras of prosperity and harmonious government, differences in retaining or changing, reducing or augmenting institutions could hardly be avoided [?]: these arose from the times and from circumstances. Yet none departed from the intention with which our sagely founder established the institutions.
When Emperor Yingzong Rui was restored to the throne, he once wished to compile regulations and statutes to continue the Duties…

translation_en:
…as a continuation of the Duties of the Various Offices (Zhizhang), but the undertaking was not brought to completion. Heaven surely awaited its proper time; how could this have been mere chance? In the tenth year of his reign, Emperor Xiaozong Jing, deeply intent on carrying forward his predecessors’ work, commanded scholarly officials to collect the institutions and regulations of successive reigns and compile them into a single work, entitled the Collected Statutes of the Great Ming (Da Ming huidian). Its institutions took the Sagely Progenitor as their sole model, and its organizing principles took the Duties of the Various Offices as their foundation. The various officially promulgated works were arranged by category, and precedents from successive years were appended, so that each official had charge of his affairs and each affair belonged to its proper office. Thus the institutions of our Ming dynasty were fully set out, with nothing great omitted and no detail overlooked. Like the sun and stars shining down, like heaven and earth sheltering and sustaining all things, this work truly accords, across different ages, with the ancient canons and counsels, statutes and rules, words of counsel, and ritual institutions. Looking down upon the works produced under the Han, Tang, and Song, would it not put them to shame?
In the fourth year after ascending the throne, the present emperor again commanded scholarly officials to revise and correct the work, and to print and distribute it at court and throughout the realm, so that all might know and observe its provisions. Might this offer some small consolation to the spirits in heaven of our one progenitor and two ancestral sovereigns, who were so devoted to this book? You, honored sir, have further condescended to inquire of [?] about the major instances of continuity and change, reduction and addition…

… learning. Yet how could a humble commoner such as I presume to know the deliberations of the imperial court? Let me offer one or two examples.
At the dynasty’s founding, an imperial prince once headed the Court of the Imperial Clan. Now only a single high minister drawn from the meritorious nobility or imperial relatives is appointed, and the full complement of officials is not provided. At the dynasty’s founding, offices were established for the Three Dukes. Now these titles are merely conferred upon high ministers as additional or posthumous honors, and the offices themselves are no longer maintained. The seal of the secretaries in the Ministry of Personnel was abolished, and responsibility for affairs devolved largely upon the bureau directors. Posts for expectant officials at the palace gates were reduced, and their duties came under the concurrent supervision of the Hanlin Academy. The Supervisorate of Imperial Instruction had not originally existed; later, officials including a Supervisor of Imperial Instruction, a Junior Supervisor, and an administrative assistant were appointed to divide responsibility for its affairs, thereby emphasizing the importance of the heir apparent’s staff. Supervising secretaries and investigating censors had formerly been selected together by category [?]. Now their abilities and appearance must be examined before they receive office, thereby emphasizing the importance of censorial and remonstrance duties. Other examples include the transformation of the Office of Ceremonial into the Court of State Ceremonial, the incorporation of the Muslim Astronomical Office into the Directorate of Astronomy, the abolition of the judicial offices of the Five Chief Military Commissions, and the increase in the authorized number of secretaries in the Six Ministries. …the sagely founder; truly, the provision thereby made to aid and guide our sagely sons and divine grandsons was most complete. Huang Luzeng

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子之所負則大矣如有用我者請執此以往
對治天下必資于官建官惟其賢而不必
備其人威天下必資于兵治兵惟其要而
不必論其勢此成周建官之制所以名雖
存而實不具事雖瑣而規寔閎西京治兵
之灋所以内若輕而寔則重外若重而寔
則輕者有以也哉今夫無曠庶官天工人
代官之不可不建也其昉于庖犧之代乎
唐虞之疇咨夏商之用乂一皆祖述其道
===
云耳降及于周監觀二代文治蔚興建官
之制始為備矣今周禮一書固可以覽其
切焉天生五材誰能去兵兵之不可不設
也其肇于軒轅之世乎虞廷之命士成周
之詰兵一皆依緣其法云耳下至于漢甫
離戰國去古未遠治兵之灋猶有存者今
班固一史固可以攷其凡焉雖然周禮作
而冬官失其傳班史脩而兵制失其紀是
亦豈非宇宙間之一大缺典也哉且執事

唐虞之疇咨夏商之用乂一皆祖述其道

之誥兵一皆依緣其法云耳下至于漢甫
離戰國去古未遠治兵之濫猶有存者今
班固一史固可以考其凡焉雖然周禮作
而冬官失其傳班史脩而兵制失其紀是
亦豈非宇宙間之一大缺典也哉且執事
punctuated:
子之所負則大矣！如有用我者，請執此以往。
對：治天下必資于官，建官惟其賢，而不必備其人；威天下必資于兵，治兵惟其要，而不必論其勢。此成周建官之制，所以名雖存而實不具，事雖瑣而規寔閎；西京治兵之灋，所以内若輕而寔則重，外若重而寔則輕者，有以也哉！今夫無曠庶官，天工人代，官之不可不建也，其昉于庖犧之代乎？唐虞之疇咨，夏商之用乂，一皆祖述其道云耳。降及于周，監觀二代，文治蔚興，建官之制始為備矣。今《周禮》一書，固可以覽其切焉。天生五材，誰能去兵？兵之不可不設也，其肇于軒轅之世乎？虞廷之命士，成周之詰兵，一皆依緣其法云耳。下至于漢，甫離戰國，去古未遠，治兵之灋猶有存者。今班固一史，固可以攷其凡焉。雖然，《周禮》作而冬官失其傳，班史脩而兵制失其紀，是亦豈非宇宙間之一大缺典也哉？且執事
translation_en:
…Your capacities are indeed great! Should someone employ you, I ask that you take these ideas with you.

Answer: Governing All under Heaven necessarily depends upon officials. In establishing offices, what matters is the worthiness of their occupants, not filling every post. Commanding awe throughout All under Heaven necessarily depends upon armed forces. In organizing troops, what matters is grasping the essentials, not discussing their apparent strength. Thus there are reasons why, in the mature Zhou system of offices, the titles remained although not all the posts were actually filled, and why, though its duties were detailed, its design was broad; and why, in the Western Han system of military organization, the forces within appeared weak but were actually strong, while those outside appeared strong but were actually weak.

Now, “Let none of the various offices lie neglected”: human beings perform Heaven’s work in its stead. As for the indispensable establishment of offices, did this begin in the age of Paoxi? The consultations of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, and the employment of officials to govern under the Xia and Shang, all simply followed and transmitted his way. Coming down to the Zhou, which surveyed the two preceding dynasties, civil governance flourished, and the system of offices first became complete. In the book Rites of Zhou, we can indeed examine its particulars [?].

“Heaven produces the five materials; who can dispense with weapons?” As for the indispensable establishment of armed forces, did this originate in the age of Xuanyuan? The appointment of the Director of the ‘Shi’ at Shun’s court and the ordering of military preparations under the mature Zhou all simply followed his methods. Coming down to the Han, which had only just emerged from the Warring States and was not far removed from antiquity, some methods of military organization still survived. In Ban Gu’s history, we can indeed investigate their general outlines.

Nevertheless, although the Rites of Zhou was composed, its section on the Offices of Winter was lost to transmission; although Ban Gu’s history was compiled, the military system went unrecorded. Is this not also a great lacuna in the documentary heritage of the world? Furthermore, you, honored examiners …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之所以疑于周之制者謂其官多而民擾
也愚則以為六官之屬雖衆至五萬餘人
大氐多兼官也何以言之周公以三公而
兼冢宰召公以三公而兼宗伯蘇公以三
公而兼司寇畢公毛公以三公而兼司馬
司空夫其大者然且兼之而况于百官羣
有司乎故三公或兼鄉老如二鄉則公一
人是已六卿或兼鄉大夫如一鄉則卿一
人是已六卿或兼六軍之將如軍將皆命
===
卿是已甚者太公以太師而兼司盟之職
所謂載在盟府太師職之是已蘇公以三
公而兼太史之職所謂太史司寇蘇公是
已以至掌荼掌葛之屬無事則不置也行
司馬輿司馬之類臨事而後設也矧又以
成王之賢輔以周公之聖論定而官而官
不及私昵位定而祿而爵罔及惡德而焉
至如執事之所慮也哉愚所謂建官惟其
賢而不必備其人者良以是耳執事之所

punctuated: 之所以疑于周之制者，謂其官多而民擾也。愚則以為六官之屬雖衆至五萬餘人，大氐多兼官也。何以言之？周公以三公而兼冢宰，召公以三公而兼宗伯，蘇公以三公而兼司寇，畢公、毛公以三公而兼司馬、司空。夫其大者然且兼之，而况于百官羣有司乎？故三公或兼鄉老，如二鄉則公一人是已；六卿或兼鄉大夫，如一鄉則卿一人是已；六卿或兼六軍之將，如軍將皆命卿是已。甚者，太公以太師而兼司盟之職，所謂「載在盟府，太師職之」是已；蘇公以三公而兼太史之職，所謂「太史司寇蘇公」是已。以至掌荼、掌葛之屬，無事則不置也；行司馬、輿司馬之類，臨事而後設也。矧又以成王之賢，輔以周公之聖，論定而官，而官不及私昵；位定而祿，而爵罔及惡德。而焉至如執事之所慮也哉？愚所謂建官惟其賢而不必備其人者，良以是耳。執事之所
translation_en:
…your reason for doubting the Zhou system is that its numerous officials troubled the people. In my humble opinion, although the personnel of the Six Ministries numbered more than fifty thousand, most probably held concurrent offices. How can I substantiate this? The Duke of Zhou, as one of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Minister of State; the Duke of Shao, as one of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Minister of Rites; the Duke of Su, as one of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Minister of Justice; and the Dukes of Bi and Mao, as members of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Minister of War and Minister of Works. If even the highest offices were held concurrently, how much more must this have been true of the hundred officials and the various subordinate functionaries? Thus, members of the Three Dukes sometimes served concurrently as District Elders: the provision of one duke for every two districts is precisely an example. The Six Ministers sometimes served concurrently as District Grand Masters: the provision of one minister for each district is precisely an example. The Six Ministers sometimes served concurrently as commanders of the Six Armies: the stipulation that army commanders were all appointed ministers is precisely an example.
Indeed, the Grand Duke, while serving as Grand Preceptor, also performed the duties of Supervisor of Covenants. This is what is meant by the saying, “It is recorded in the covenant repository, and the Grand Preceptor is responsible for it.” The Duke of Su, as one of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Grand Scribe. This is what is meant by “the Grand Scribe and Minister of Justice, the Duke of Su.” As for such offices as those responsible for rushes and kudzu, no appointments were made when there was no work to do. Offices such as Campaign Commander and Chariot Commander were established only when circumstances required them. Moreover, with the worthy King Cheng assisted by the sagely Duke of Zhou, appointments followed a settled assessment of merit, and offices were not bestowed on personal favorites; stipends followed the determination of rank, and titles were not granted to those of bad character. How, then, could matters have reached the state you fear? This is precisely why I say that, in establishing offices, the essential thing is to appoint worthy men, without necessarily filling every post. As for your…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以疑於漢之灋者謂其將不專而兵不衆
也愚則以為兵制之善自三代以還莫漢
若也何以言之民年二十始傅二十三為
正卒五十六免為庶人是調民有限也每
歲戍邊不過三日至于治城郭築堤防轉
輸力役皆官予庸直是役民有限也其調
發也率皆近地而無遠征之勞其繇役也
率皆自悉而無供億之費有事則檄召而
官無困于贅食事已即罷歸而民亦得以
===
力作將帥奉朝請而無擁兵專制之虞都
試課殿最而無驕蹇難用之患兵農未分
内外相制故當時兵之隷于南北軍者雖
僅盈萬人而不聞有單弱之虞盖兵不常
役則佚而不怨在官之日少則有餘力而
不疲矧又上有仁明之主下有畫一之臣
公卿子弟咸備宿衛材官騎士徧滿郡國
而亦焉至如執事之所云也哉愚所謂治
兵惟其要而不必論其勢者職此之繇耳

punctuated: 以疑於漢之灋者，謂其將不專而兵不衆也。愚則以為兵制之善，自三代以還，莫漢若也。何以言之？民年二十始傅，二十三為正卒，五十六免為庶人，是調民有限也。每歲戍邊不過三日，至于治城郭、築堤防、轉輸力役，皆官予庸直，是役民有限也。其調發也，率皆近地，而無遠征之勞；其繇役也，率皆自悉，而無供億之費。有事則檄召，而官無困于贅食；事已即罷歸，而民亦得以力作。將帥奉朝請，而無擁兵專制之虞；都試課殿最，而無驕蹇難用之患。兵農未分，内外相制，故當時兵之隷于南北軍者，雖僅盈萬人，而不聞有單弱之虞。盖兵不常役，則佚而不怨；在官之日少，則有餘力而不疲。矧又上有仁明之主，下有畫一之臣，公卿子弟咸備宿衛，材官騎士徧滿郡國，而亦焉至如執事之所云也哉？愚所謂治兵惟其要而不必論其勢者，職此之繇耳。
translation_en: …the reason you doubt the Han system is that its generals lacked exclusive command and its troops were not numerous. I, however, believe that since the Three Dynasties no military system has equaled that of the Han. Why do I say this? Men were first enrolled at twenty, became regular soldiers at twenty-three, and at fifty-six were discharged to civilian status: thus there were limits to conscription. Annual frontier garrison duty did not exceed three days; as for repairing city walls, constructing dikes, transport duties, and other labor services, the government paid wages for them all: thus there were limits to the labor exacted from the people. Mobilizations generally took men only to nearby places, sparing them the toil of distant campaigns; their labor services were generally undertaken through their own provision [?], without the expense of supplying provisions. When trouble arose, they were summoned by written orders, so the government was not burdened with feeding supernumeraries; once the affair was over, they were immediately discharged and sent home, so the people could also return to productive labor. Commanders attended court audiences, so there was no fear of their monopolizing power through control of troops. General military reviews assessed the best and worst performances, so there was no danger of soldiers becoming arrogant, insubordinate, and difficult to employ. Soldiers and farmers had not yet become separate groups, and forces within and outside the capital checked one another. Thus, although the troops attached to the Southern and Northern Armies at that time numbered barely ten thousand, we hear of no concern that they were too few and weak. For when soldiers are not constantly on duty, they are rested and free of resentment; when their days in government service are few, they retain strength and do not become exhausted. Moreover, above there was a benevolent and enlightened ruler, and below, ministers who upheld uniform standards. The sons and younger kinsmen of dukes and high ministers all served as palace guards, while trained infantry and cavalry filled the commanderies and kingdoms. How, then, could matters have reached the condition you describe? This is precisely why I say that managing an army requires grasping its essentials, without necessarily judging its apparent strength.

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
於乎由西周之制觀之使其子孫能守而
勿失則天下至今猶存可也惜也穆王耄
荒而周之道缺焉陵遲至于幽厲極矣由
西京之灋觀之使其子孫能守之弗忘則
天下至今猶存可也惜也武帝紛更而漢
之業衰焉因循至於哀平蕩矣然則後之
君天下者必欲盡行周禮固不能也姑取
其遺訓而斟酌之師其意而不師其迹可
也必欲盡行漢灋亦不能也姑取其遺制
===
而參會之損其過而益其所不及可也不
然則亦奚足以為治也哉今
國家建官倣于周禮而適夫繁簡之宜治兵

Alas! Judging from the institutions of the Western Zhou, had its descendants been able to preserve them without loss, its rule over the realm might have endured even to this day. Regrettably, King Mu grew old and neglectful, and the Way of Zhou became impaired; its gradual decline reached its utmost under Kings You and Li. Judging from the laws of the Western Han, had its descendants been able to preserve them without forgetting them, its rule over the realm might have endured even to this day. Regrettably, Emperor Wu introduced a profusion of changes, and the imperial enterprise of Han declined; through continued neglect, it was brought to ruin under Emperors Ai and Ping. Thus, for later rulers of the realm, to insist on implementing the Rites of Zhou in their entirety is certainly impossible. It is enough to take their surviving teachings and weigh them carefully, following their intent rather than their outward forms. To insist on implementing Han laws in their entirety is likewise impossible. It is enough to take their surviving institutions and adapt them in combination, reducing their excesses and supplementing their deficiencies. Otherwise, how could they suffice to bring about good government?
Now our dynasty has modeled its establishment of offices on the Rites of Zhou, appropriately balancing complexity and simplicity; in managing its armies, it regards the Western Han arrangements as inferior and has grasped the essentials of relative weight and authority. These matters certainly leave no room for criticism. Yet over the past hundred years and more, some departure from the original arrangements has been unavoidable: circumstances themselves have brought this about. In planning for the present, since offices have fixed complements and posts have regular duties, there is nothing wrong with continuing established practices. 當宁獻
第三問
晉憲
同考試官教諭楊批人物一策非素有學識
者莫能品其高下場中作者互有異同殊無定見是
篇有藻鑑有斷制其亦尚友千古而當仁不讓者歟
同考試官學正蕭批礙人於疑似論事於彷
彿正欲觀士子窮理之學也此對事核而詳言博而
約使千百年上下人物心跡隱微低昂輕重錙銖不
爽他日所就當大有可觀者矣
考試官左諭德温批平易近人而語自不亂知子
之所蘊豈但論人於千載之上哉
考試官侍講學士李批古人事蹟散見諸史舉而論
之一一帖當如漢廷老吏坐斷疑獄片言之出是非
自不能逃也敬服敬服
嘗謂論事於已然當攷其時勢之難易論

Third Question
Jin Xian
Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: In a policy essay concerning historical figures, only someone with well-established learning and discernment can assess their relative merits. The candidates’ essays differed in their views, but notably lacked firm judgments. This essay displays discrimination and decisiveness. Is its author not one who takes the ancients as his friends across the ages and yields to none when duty calls?
Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: To obstruct judgments of people with ambiguities [?] and discuss events whose outlines are indistinct is precisely to test candidates’ learning in the investigation of principle. This response is accurate and detailed in its treatment of events, comprehensive yet concise in its language. In assessing figures across hundreds and thousands of years—the subtleties of their motives and actions, their relative standing and importance—it does not err by the smallest measure. His future accomplishments should be well worth seeing.
Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Admonisher: Plain and accessible, yet orderly in its expression. From this one can recognize what you have within you: surely your abilities extend beyond judging people of a thousand years ago!
Comment by Examiner Li, Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting: The deeds of the ancients are scattered throughout the histories. This essay brings them forward for discussion, handling each appropriately, like a seasoned official at the Han court sitting in judgment on doubtful cases: once a brief pronouncement is made, right and wrong cannot escape detection. Most admirable! Most admirable!
I have often maintained that, when discussing events already past, one must examine the difficulties and advantages of their circumstances; when judging people of former times, one must investigate whether their motives were corrupt or upright. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
未必宜於彼得其一而未得其二非善論
事者也人之處事無定苟不究其心術之
邪正則暴於顯者或得以掩其微形於外
者未必能保其内非善論人者也知此則
所謂折衷之道夫豈外是也哉請復執事
之問今夫霍去病之無以家為為將之道
得矣而王翦因伐荆之舉顧乃多請田宅
非翦之貪去病之潔也漢武之志狃于征
伐秦王之心過于疑忌故爾然翦之失亦
===
不能無焉蓋成敗利鈍非人所能為則亦
何可過為身後之慮也哉申屠嘉之召斬
鄧通為相之道得矣而孔光以丞相之尊
顧乃下拜董賢非嘉之過光之恭也文帝
之優禮相國故嘉得以行其志哀帝之昵
比匪人故光諂之而固其寵耳然嘉之賢
誠不可少焉蓋小臣矜寵汙衊王章則將
焉用彼相哉詩書禮樂唯卻縠可晉之彊
縠之力也然能作賦如陸機者乃有河橋

translation_en:
…may not necessarily be appropriate there. To grasp one aspect without grasping the other is not to judge affairs well. People have no fixed manner of handling affairs. Unless one investigates whether their underlying intentions are depraved or upright, what is openly displayed may conceal what is hidden, and outward appearances may offer no assurance of inward character. This is not to judge people well. Once this is understood, could the so-called method of balanced judgment lie anywhere beyond it? Allow me to answer your question.
Now Huo Qubing’s refusal to concern himself with a household accorded with the proper way of a general. Yet Wang Jian, on undertaking the campaign against Jing, repeatedly requested fields and residences. This was not because Wang Jian was greedy and Huo Qubing incorruptible. It was because Emperor Wu of Han was habituated to conquest, whereas the king of Qin was excessively suspicious. Nevertheless, Wang Jian cannot be entirely free of fault. Success and failure, favorable and adverse outcomes, are beyond human control; why, then, should one concern oneself excessively with what will happen after one’s death?
Shentu Jia’s summoning Deng Tong with the intention of executing him accorded with the proper way of a chief minister. Yet Kong Guang, despite his dignity as Counselor-in-Chief, bowed low before Dong Xian. This was not a matter of Shentu Jia being excessive and Kong Guang being respectful. Emperor Wen treated his chief minister with exceptional courtesy, so Shentu Jia could carry out his intentions. Emperor Ai was intimate with an unworthy man, so Kong Guang flattered that man to secure his own favor. Nevertheless, Shentu Jia’s worthiness was indeed indispensable. If a petty official presumed upon imperial favor and defiled the sovereign’s laws, what use would there be for such a chief minister?
For knowledge of the Odes and Documents, ritual and music, only Xi Hu [?] would do; Jin’s strength owed itself to his efforts. Yet even someone as capable of composing rhapsodies as Lu Ji had his experience at Heqiao …

text:
之敗晋史譏其志不逮言宜矣禮義廉耻
為國四維齊之覇仲之功也然能作論如
柳宗元者乃有伾文之附韓愈譏其僥倖
速進當矣蕭何卒而曹參相盖大臣薦舉
之公而何舊隙之有張耳王而陳餘戮盖
小人勢利之交而何舊德之云張安世之
事君以謹厚聞李泌之事君以謀畧著鈞
之為賢相也然薦人而却其謝履道而懼
于盈優于好談神仙詭怪為世所輕者多
===

經其優劣不待言矣然萬年廉平内行甚
脩咸亦言事抗直刺譏近臣盖亦或有足

translation_en:
…the defeat at Heqiao. The History of Jin criticized him for having aspirations that fell short of his words, and rightly so. Ritual propriety, righteousness, integrity, and a sense of shame are the four mainstays of a state; Qi’s hegemony was Guan Zhong’s achievement. Yet even Liu Zongyuan, so accomplished in writing discourses, attached himself to Wang Pi and Wang Shuwen. Han Yu was right to criticize him for seeking rapid advancement through a lucky break.

When Xiao He died, Cao Can became chief minister. This exemplified the impartiality of a great minister in recommending men: what weight did their old animosity carry? Zhang Er became a king, while Chen Yu was put to death. Theirs was the association of petty men seeking power and profit: what was there to say of past kindnesses? Zhang Anshi was known for caution and generosity in serving his ruler; Li Mi was renowned for strategic planning in his ruler’s service. Both were worthy chief ministers. Yet the man who recommended others but declined their thanks, followed the Way, and feared the fullness of success was far superior to the man who delighted in discussing immortals and strange marvels and was consequently held in low esteem by the world.

Chen Wannian taught his son flattery; Wei Changru bequeathed the Classics to his son. Which was superior needs no explanation. Yet Wannian was incorruptible and fair, and his private conduct was highly cultivated. His son Xian, too, spoke out firmly and frankly on affairs, criticizing the ruler’s intimate ministers. They thus had qualities worth valuing and were not devoted solely to flattery.

Gongsun Hong drew criticism for using a cloth quilt, whereas Ji Zun was praised for doing so. One was a chief minister who practiced deceit; the other was a general of cultivated scholarly bearing. How could Hong dare hope to equal Zun? Zhao Guanghan skillfully used probing interrogations to ascertain the facts; Pei Yanling employed such methods extensively to secure the ruler’s favor. One still kept the people in mind; the other thought only of himself. Could Yanling possibly be Guanghan’s equal?

Because his father’s personal name was Jinsu, Li He did not…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
舉進士桑維翰以主司惡其姓而卒不改
業二子之見審矣然賀以少年英銳之資
而所志若彼君子嘉之崔隱甫不欲見牛
仙客韓昌黎三上宰相書二子之心異矣
然愈以平生山斗之望而所為若茲君子
羞之蕭何從高祖而獨收圖籍房玄齡從
秦王而獨收人物盖非圖籍則無以知天
下阨塞戶口疆弱之處非人物則無以為
平定海內之資要之何知天下之勢玄齡
===
其知天下之本乎衛青威震朝廷汲黯獨
違衆而長揖司馬昭位極人臣荀顗獨違
衆而下拜盖揖之所以明折其驕踞之勢
拜之所以陰示其讇屈之心要之黯守人
臣之節顗其姦人之雄乎不從三國之言
而俾齊堅守者路中大夫也不聽楚子之
令而俾宋不下者解揚也其忠不亦同乎
然佯從之以餌敵國不若不從之為全也
卻金以杜故人之請者楊震也縣魚以章

而所志若彼君子嘉之崔隱甫不欲見牛
仙客韓昌黎三上宰相書二子之心異矣
然愈以平生山斗之望而所為若茲君子
羞之蕭何從高祖而獨收圖籍房玄齡從
秦王而獨收人物蓋非圖籍則無以知天
下阨塞戶口彊弱之處非人物則無以為
平定海內之資要之何知天下之勢玄齡
其知天下之本乎衛青威震朝廷汲黯獨
違衆而長揖司馬昭位極人臣嵇顗獨違
衆而下拜蓋揖之所以明折其驕倨之勢
拜之所以陰示其諷屈之心要之黯守人
臣之節顗其姦人之雄乎不從三國之言
而俾齊堅守者路中大夫也不聽楚子之
令而俾宋不下者解揚也其忠不亦同乎
然佯從之以餌敵國不若不從之為全也
卻金以杜故人之請者楊震也縣魚以章
punctuated: 舉進士。桑維翰以主司惡其姓，而卒不改業。二子之見審矣，然賀以少年英銳之資，而所志若彼，君子嘉之。崔隱甫不欲見牛仙客，韓昌黎三上宰相書。二子之心異矣，然愈以平生山斗之望，而所為若茲，君子羞之。蕭何從高祖而獨收圖籍，房玄齡從秦王而獨收人物。盖非圖籍，則無以知天下阨塞戶口疆弱之處；非人物，則無以為平定海內之資。要之，何知天下之勢，玄齡其知天下之本乎？衛青威震朝廷，汲黯獨違衆而長揖；司馬昭位極人臣，荀顗獨違衆而下拜。盖揖之，所以明折其驕踞之勢；拜之，所以陰示其讇屈之心。要之，黯守人臣之節，顗其姦人之雄乎？不從三國之言而俾齊堅守者，路中大夫也；不聽楚子之令而俾宋不下者，解揚也。其忠不亦同乎？然佯從之以餌敵國，不若不從之為全也。卻金以杜故人之請者，楊震也；縣魚以章
translation_en:
…sit for the jinshi examination. Sang Weihan, because the presiding examiner disliked his surname, nevertheless refused to abandon his chosen pursuit. Both men had considered their decisions carefully. Yet Li He, endowed with youthful brilliance and vigor, set his aspirations as he did, and the gentleman commends him.

Cui Yinfu was unwilling to meet Niu Xianke, whereas Han Changli—Han Yu—submitted letters to the chief councilor three times. The intentions of these two men differed. Yet Han Yu, whose lifelong reputation made him as revered as Mount Tai and the Northern Dipper, acted in this fashion, and the gentleman feels shame for him.

Xiao He followed Gaozu and alone collected maps and registers; Fang Xuanling followed the Prince of Qin and alone gathered talented men. Without maps and registers, there was no way to know the empire’s strategic passes, households and population, or areas of strength and weakness; without talented men, there were no resources with which to pacify all within the seas. In sum, Xiao He understood the strategic circumstances of the empire; did Xuanling not understand its foundations?

Wei Qing’s imposing authority shook the court, yet Ji An alone departed from the crowd and offered a standing bow. Sima Zhao had attained the highest position a subject could hold, yet Xun Yi alone departed from the crowd and bowed down before him. The standing bow openly checked the other man’s arrogant bearing; the prostration covertly revealed a heart bent on flattery and submission. In sum, Ji An upheld the integrity proper to a subject; was Xun Yi not a leader among treacherous men?

The man who refused to follow the words of the three states and urged Qi to hold firm was the grand master Luzhong [?]; the man who refused to obey the command of the ruler of Chu and urged Song not to surrender was Jie Yang. Was their loyalty not alike? Yet feigning compliance in order to bait an enemy state was less unimpeachable than refusing to comply at all.

The man who rejected gold to foreclose an old friend’s request was Yang Zhen; the man who hung up a fish to make manifest…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
府丞之餽者羊續也其廉不亦同乎然而
受之以愧寮友不若不受之為高也郭子
儀之見回紇薛仁貴之見突厥苟非吾之
恩信素有以結其心吾之兵威素有以奪
其氣則亦安得不如或者之所慮也哉史
臣之稱許是矣馮奉世之破莎車甘陳之
誅郅支大抵皆乘危徼幸之謀而非中國
之利啓釁招禍之漸而生夷狄之心則亦
安得不如議者之所云也哉劉向輩之論
===
建非矣張釋之為廷尉而天下無寃民戴
胄居大理而天下無寃獄史之所稱豈無
見乎夷攷其時如渭橋犯蹕之議如選人
詐冒之爭舉一以例其餘則亦何寃之有
子產治鄭國而民不能欺子賤治單父而
民不忍欺傳之所稱豈無謂乎夷攷其政
一則仁而且明一則清靜無欲執此以臨
其民則亦何欺之有恥其君不為堯舜伊
尹之所以任天下之重蓋如此而唐臣周

translation_en:
…the gift from the prefectural assistant was Yang Xu. Was their incorruptibility not alike? Yet accepting it in order to put a fellow official to shame was less noble than refusing it outright. When Guo Ziyi met the Huihe and Xue Rengui met the Tujue, had their kindness and trustworthiness not long since won those peoples’ allegiance, and had their military might not long since broken their spirit, how could matters have failed to turn out as some feared? The official historians were right to praise them. Feng Fengshi’s defeat of Shache and Gan Yanshou and Chen Tang’s killing of Zhizhi were, on the whole, schemes that courted danger and sought success through luck, rather than benefiting the Central States. They were the beginnings of provocations that invited disaster and stirred ambitions among the foreign peoples. How, then, could matters have failed to turn out as the critics said? The proposals of Liu Xiang and his fellows were mistaken.

When Zhang Shizhi served as Chamberlain for Law Enforcement, no one in the realm suffered injustice; when Dai Zhou served in the Court of Judicial Review, there were no unjust cases in the realm. Could the historians’ praise have lacked a basis? Examine their times dispassionately: consider the deliberation over the violation of the imperial procession’s road closure at Wei Bridge, or the dispute over fraudulent claims by candidates for office. Taking one instance as representative of the rest, what injustice could there have been? When Zichan governed the state of Zheng, the people could not deceive him; when Zijian governed Shanfu, the people could not bear to deceive him. Could the accounts’ praise have been without reason? Examine their government dispassionately: one was benevolent and discerning, the other tranquil and free of desires. With these qualities guiding their governance of the people, what deception could there have been?

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
墀乃以堯舜美文宗於乎文宗豈堯舜之
匹哉墀之諛甚矣人主不當觀史褚遂良
之所以對太宗之言盖如此而異時房玄
齡乃錄而上之於乎史豈人主之所宜觀
者哉玄齡之罪大矣此愚所謂論事當攷
其時勢之難易論人當究其心術之邪正
者盖以此也此亦執事之所謂折衷之道
者也雖然是二者又有本焉窮理是已盖
天下之理散于事天下之事原于理苟理
===
有未窮則凡事之來紛紜迷繆卒無一定
之歸而又奚足以知人也哉管見如此未
知是否惟執事進而教之
第四問
程然
同考試官教諭趙批守令親民固宜慎選然
任法既久得人為難不專倚之考課而兼行久任之
法區處有方不迂不畧此策亦庶幾有裨於
今日乎經生而能留意世務固當為得人慶矣

第四問
程然
同考試官教諭趙批：守令親民，固宜慎選。然任法既久，得人為難。不專倚之考課，而兼行久任之法，區處有方，不迂不畧。此策亦庶幾有裨於今日乎？經生而能留意世務，固當為得人慶矣！
translation_en:
…Zhou Chi nevertheless praised Emperor Wenzong by comparing him to Yao and Shun. Alas! Could Wenzong possibly match Yao and Shun? Chi’s flattery was excessive indeed! A ruler ought not to read the historical record: such was the substance of Chu Suiliang’s reply to Emperor Taizong. Yet on another occasion Fang Xuanling transcribed it and presented it to the emperor. Alas! Is the historical record something a ruler ought to read? Xuanling’s fault was grave indeed! This is why I humbly say that, in judging events, one should examine the difficulties or advantages of the circumstances of the time, and in judging people, one should investigate whether their intentions were upright or corrupt. This is also what you, sir, call the way of arriving at a balanced judgment. Yet these two approaches have a further foundation: the exhaustive investigation of principle. The principles of the world are dispersed throughout its affairs, and its affairs originate in principle. If any principle remains unexplored, then as affairs arise, they will seem bewilderingly confused, and ultimately no settled judgment can be reached. How, then, could one be capable of understanding people? Such is my limited view. I do not know whether it is correct; I ask you, sir, to offer me further instruction.
Fourth Question
Cheng Ran
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: Prefects and magistrates deal directly with the people, so they certainly ought to be chosen carefully. Yet the system of appointment has long been in use, and finding suitable men is difficult. Rather than relying exclusively on performance evaluations, this essay proposes also implementing a system of extended tenure. Its arrangements are well conceived, neither impractical nor perfunctory. Might this policy essay indeed be of some benefit in our own day? When a student of the Classics can attend to the affairs of the world, we surely ought to celebrate having found a worthy man!

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官左諭德温批考課當嚴而倚之不專久任
當行而行之不驟論時務而得通融之術主司固為
子拭目也
考試官侍講學士李批久任守令士子固有及之者
至于中今之難與夫考課之不足倚則此對言之詳
矣噫子豈不識天下事者邪
對設官以為民也課功以為官也而實以
為民也夫官為民而立又為民而課試焉
固宜其無不愛民之官無不可行之課試
===
其或不盡然者是必有所以然之故矣今
夫以一郡一邑之民而寄之於人牧猶以
牛羊之羣寄於受牧之人也求牧與芻而
不得將反諸其人歟抑亦立而視其死歟
天下之民望於羣牧如父母然飢寒困踣
賦役昏訟苟可以告之父母者即赴愬於
有司故非豈弟樂易敏銳通達者未可輕
授非真知子民之義者未必能稱守令之
任也我

Examiner Wen, Left Mentor, comments: Performance evaluations should be strict, but should not be relied upon exclusively; extended tenure should be instituted, but not abruptly. In discussing current affairs, you have found a method of flexible accommodation. The presiding examiner certainly looks upon you with renewed regard.

Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: There have certainly been candidates who have touched upon extended tenure for prefects and magistrates. But this answer discusses in detail the difficulty of making it suit present circumstances [?] and the inadequacy of relying on performance evaluations. Ah! Could you possibly be someone who does not understand the affairs of the realm?

Answer: Offices are established for the people. Merit is assessed for the sake of officials, but in truth this too is for the people. Since officials are appointed for the people, and are also evaluated and tested for the people, surely there ought to be no official who does not cherish the people, and no evaluation that cannot be put into practice. If matters do not always turn out thus, there must be reasons why.

To entrust the people of a prefecture or county to a shepherd of men is like entrusting a herd of cattle or sheep to someone charged with tending them. If pasture and fodder are sought but cannot be obtained, should one turn back to that person and hold him responsible, or simply stand by and watch the animals die? The people of the realm look to their shepherds as to their parents. Hunger and cold, distress and collapse, taxes and labor services, marriage disputes and litigation—whatever they might report to their parents, they bring directly before the responsible authorities. Thus these offices must not lightly be entrusted to anyone who is not kindly and genial, alert and perceptive, and broadly discerning. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
國家重守令之選率取諸科目之傑其才有
小大其歷世有淺深其資性有迂速其喜
好有內外輕重之不同者必擇焉其郡邑
有南北燥濕其風俗有剛柔強弱之異劑
者必擇焉因人而授因地而官使之一志
畢力以福斯民意至渥也故被兹選者既
欲副科目之名之榮人欲稱守令之責之
重其肯偷惰委靡自取課殿也哉
國家考課之法行於貴近者既嚴而於外守
===
令之遠者尤備郡守古諸侯也觀察者一
不滿意即劾去之矣縣令有不待言者故
考課之法主之銓衡主之內臺叅之觀察
而又博訪於士論疇咨於數歲之升達
覲廷之敷奏而其議始定其偷惰委靡法當
速去者不與焉則其法固得於黜陟幽明
之意為多而豈若京房劉邵之煩碎晉魏
唐宋之失實哉夫守令既責之重考之嚴
而其人又自欲勉副

唐宋之失實哉夫守令既責之重考之嚴
而其人又自欲勉副
punctuated:
國家重守令之選，率取諸科目之傑。其才有小大，其歷世有淺深，其資性有迂速，其喜好有內外輕重之不同者，必擇焉。其郡邑有南北燥濕，其風俗有剛柔強弱之異劑者，必擇焉。因人而授，因地而官，使之一志畢力以福斯民，意至渥也。故被兹選者，既欲副科目之名之榮，人欲稱守令之責之重，其肯偷惰委靡，自取課殿也哉？

國家考課之法，行於貴近者既嚴，而於外守令之遠者尤備。郡守，古諸侯也；觀察者一不滿意，即劾去之矣。縣令有不待言者。故考課之法，主之銓衡，主之內臺，叅之觀察，而又博訪於士論，疇咨於數歲之升達、覲廷之敷奏，而其議始定。其偷惰委靡，法當速去者，不與焉。則其法固得於黜陟幽明之意為多，而豈若京房、劉邵之煩碎，晉、魏、唐、宋之失實哉？夫守令既責之重，考之嚴，而其人又自欲勉副
translation_en:
…the state attaches great importance to selecting prefects and county magistrates, generally choosing outstanding men from the examination ranks. Their abilities vary in scope, their experience of the world in depth, and their natural dispositions in deliberateness or quickness; their preferences differ as to inner and outer concerns and the relative weight assigned to them. All these require careful selection. Prefectures and counties differ in their northern or southern location and in the dryness or dampness of their climate; their customs differ in their mixture [?] of firmness and gentleness, strength and weakness. These too require careful selection. Appointments are made according to the individual, and offices assigned according to the locality, so that those appointed may devote their whole purpose and strength to benefiting the people. The intention is most generous. Thus those selected wish both to live up to the honor of their examination distinction and to meet the weighty responsibilities of prefect or magistrate [?]. Would they willingly become negligent and dispirited, bringing upon themselves the lowest performance rating?

The state's system of performance evaluation is already strict when applied to the eminent officials close to the throne, and is still more comprehensive for prefects and magistrates serving far away. A prefect is the counterpart of an ancient regional lord; yet if an inspecting official is displeased with him, he is immediately impeached and removed. The situation of county magistrates goes without saying. Thus performance evaluation is directed by the Ministry of Personnel and the Censorate, with inspecting officials participating. Opinions are also sought widely among scholars, and careful consultation is made concerning advancement over several years [?] and reports presented at court audiences; only then is the assessment settled. Those whose negligence and lassitude warrant prompt removal under the rules are excluded from this procedure. This system therefore largely realizes the intention of demoting the obscure and promoting the illustrious—that is, distinguishing poor officials from good ones. How could it resemble the excessive intricacy of Jing Fang's and Liu Shao's methods, or the failure to reflect actual performance under the Jin, Wei, Tang, and Song? Now, prefects and magistrates bear weighty responsibilities and undergo strict evaluation, while they themselves also wish to strive to fulfill…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
上意不為偷惰委靡之習固宜其百姓富庶政
平訟理者而今之民日益窮訟日益繁轉
徙流亡者日益衆近自
畿輔重地已有然者他藩可知矣是獨無其
故哉愚不識天下事竊謂久任之法不行
也孔子曰善人為邦百年亦可以勝殘去
殺矣又曰苟有用我者朞月而已可也三
年有成子產為政累年而後化成伯禽治
魯三年而後報政今之人未必皆聖賢也
===
聰明得於簡冊之緒言志力奪於舉業之
舊習一旦寄以民牧之任上而監臨觀察
責其成下而府史胥徒伺其隙其奮翼策
步不安小成者必一二年治乃有緒焉彼
方有治緒可尋也而旁郡別邑已有遷陟
內拜者矣於是而速進之念生速進之念
生則為民之意短而求上之意急謀身之
術巧而取民之計多百姓固何利於是哉
下之人知其意欲速也吏胥得以肆其謾

punctuated: 上意，不為偷惰委靡之習，固宜其百姓富庶、政平訟理者，而今之民日益窮，訟日益繁，轉徙流亡者日益衆。近自畿輔重地，已有然者，他藩可知矣。是獨無其故哉？愚不識天下事，竊謂久任之法不行也。孔子曰：「善人為邦百年，亦可以勝殘去殺矣。」又曰：「苟有用我者，朞月而已可也，三年有成。」子產為政，累年而後化成；伯禽治魯，三年而後報政。今之人未必皆聖賢也，聰明得於簡冊之緒言，志力奪於舉業之舊習。一旦寄以民牧之任，上而監臨觀察責其成，下而府史胥徒伺其隙。其奮翼策步、不安小成者，必一二年，治乃有緒焉。彼方有治緒可尋也，而旁郡別邑已有遷陟內拜者矣。於是而速進之念生。速進之念生，則為民之意短，而求上之意急；謀身之術巧，而取民之計多。百姓固何利於是哉？下之人知其意欲速也，吏胥得以肆其謾
translation_en:
…the imperial wishes, and refrain from habits of indolence and listlessness, surely their people ought to be prosperous and numerous, their government equitable, and their lawsuits properly adjudicated. Yet today the people grow poorer by the day, lawsuits multiply, and ever more people wander or flee their homes. Such conditions already exist close at hand, even in the vital metropolitan region; one can readily imagine conditions in the other provinces. Can this alone have no cause? Ignorant as I am of the affairs of the realm, I venture to suggest that it is because the practice of keeping officials long in office is not observed.

Confucius said: “If good men governed a state for a hundred years, they could overcome cruelty and dispense with executions.” He also said: “If someone were to employ me, matters could be put in order in just a full year, and in three years there would be results.” Zichan governed for several years before his transforming influence was fully realized; Boqin governed Lu for three years before reporting on his administration. The men of today are not necessarily all sages or worthies. Their understanding comes from the inherited sayings in books, while their resolve and energy are sapped by ingrained habits of examination study. Once entrusted with the responsibility of shepherding the people, they find supervisory and inspecting officials above demanding results, and clerks and runners below watching for their vulnerabilities. Even those who spread their wings and urge their steps onward, unwilling to rest content with small achievements, must take a year or two before their administration begins to take shape.

Just as their administration begins to show discernible progress, men in neighboring prefectures and other counties have already been promoted or appointed to posts at the capital. Thus the desire for rapid advancement arises. Once it arises, their concern for the people diminishes, while their eagerness to court superiors intensifies; their arts of furthering their own interests grow more ingenious, and their schemes for extracting resources from the people multiply. What benefit can the common people possibly derive from this? Those below them know that they desire swift advancement, and the clerks are consequently able to give free rein to their deceit…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
豪猾得以窺其弊上下之間一切苟且而
已雖考課日嚴賞罰日加彼速進者固不
俟是而已有岐路可鄉矣其不畏刺舉者
又或中有所倚焉如是則信有如杜子恕
所謂歷代累聖而考績之法不著課試之
要未立也蘇軾曰有官必有課有課必有
賞罰有官無課是無官也有課無賞罰是
無課也天下之吏不可勝考必刺舉於其
所屬之長而賞罰得以加焉其意以為守
===
令之賢否考於職司而於御史臺別立一
司中丞舉其綱屬官之強明者治其事彼
蘇軾固為宋言也今始於觀察升於銓衡
內臺內臺銓衡又第其品而黜陟於其
上此亦軾之意而益加詳者也夫久任之意不
堅而專倚之考課則所課者時日之近効
而其所以為最者又或得於悅上偽增之
私當道者亦何所按哉其拙於逢迎篤意
撫字而上不之知者又非考課之所能得

所屬之長而賞罰得以加焉其意以為守
===

内臺内臺銓衡又第其品而黜陟於其
