而其所以為最者又或得於悦上偽增之
私當道者亦何所按哉其拙於逢迎篤意
撫字而上不之知者又非考課之所能得
punctuated: 豪猾得以窺其弊，上下之間，一切苟且而已。雖考課日嚴，賞罰日加，彼速進者固不俟是，而已有岐路可鄉矣。其不畏刺舉者，又或中有所倚焉。如是，則信有如杜子恕所謂「歷代累聖，而考績之法不著，課試之要未立」也。蘇軾曰：「有官必有課，有課必有賞罰。有官無課，是無官也；有課無賞罰，是無課也。」天下之吏不可勝考，必刺舉於其所屬之長，而賞罰得以加焉。其意以為守令之賢否，考於職司，而於御史臺別立一司，中丞舉其綱，屬官之強明者治其事。彼蘇軾固為宋言也。今始於觀察，升於銓衡、內臺，內臺、銓衡又第其品，而黜陟於其上。此亦軾之意而益加詳者也。夫久任之意不堅，而專倚之考課，則所課者時日之近効，而其所以為最者，又或得於悅上偽增之私，當道者亦何所按哉？其拙於逢迎、篤意撫字，而上不之知者，又非考課之所能得
translation_en:
…and powerful rogues can exploit their weaknesses. Between superiors and subordinates, everything becomes a matter of expediency. Though performance evaluations grow stricter by the day and rewards and punishments are increasingly applied, those seeking rapid advancement do not wait for these: they already have alternative paths to pursue. Those who do not fear investigation and impeachment may also have someone within the administration to rely upon. In such circumstances, it is indeed as Du Zishu said: “Through successive dynasties and many sage rulers, the methods of evaluating merit have remained undefined, and the essentials of assessment have not been established.”

Su Shi said: “Where there are offices, there must be assessments; where there are assessments, there must be rewards and punishments. To have offices without assessments is to have no offices; to have assessments without rewards and punishments is to have no assessments.” The officials of the empire are too numerous to assess exhaustively; investigation and impeachment must therefore be undertaken by their respective superiors, so that rewards and punishments can be applied. His intention was that the competence of prefects and magistrates should be assessed by the responsible supervisory officials, while a separate bureau should be established within the Censorate. The Censor-in-chief would direct its overall work, and capable, discerning subordinate officials would manage its affairs. Su Shi was, of course, speaking for the Song dynasty. Today, assessment begins with the inspecting authorities and proceeds upward to the Ministry of Personnel and the Censorate. The Censorate and Ministry of Personnel then further rank the officials and determine their demotion or promotion at the higher level. This, too, accords with Su Shi’s intention, but elaborates it still further.

Yet if the commitment to keeping officials long in their posts is not firm, and reliance is placed entirely on performance evaluations, what is assessed will be short-term results. Moreover, a rating of outstanding merit may sometimes be obtained through the self-serving practices of pleasing superiors and falsely inflating achievements. What, then, can those in authority actually examine? Those who are inept at currying favor but devoted to caring for the people, yet remain unknown to their superiors, are likewise beyond the ability of performance evaluations to identify…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也夫有志者拜一命之寄亦欲展布以為
久圖而速進者得以惑其意是使天下無
誠心為民者矣然轉移之機豈一言之所
能悉一日之所能變哉愚請試行之數人
可也盖人之材智器局大畧相同唯有志
者率其力之所不及以趨其志之所欲就
故其受若直也恒勉勉焉惟恐或負則其
所望寧小無大寧卑無崇而其所為也寧
拙無巧寧久無速誠得是人而任之則所
===
謂悃愊無華歲計有餘者於是而久任焉
秩當遷也不移其地祿當益也不奪其官
過可畧也不拘以文法之細人可諒也不
間以毀譽之言或璽書慰勉以新其意或
就加服命以旌其能若果有效也破格用
之異待之終身焉彼速進者曰吾所進者
在於格之内而彼乃獨超于格之外則彼
之所謂遲者速而吾之所謂速者遲矣故
速不必沮也自有權以遲之不必遍行於

punctuated: 也。夫有志者拜一命之寄，亦欲展布以為久圖，而速進者得以惑其意，是使天下無誠心為民者矣。然轉移之機，豈一言之所能悉、一日之所能變哉？愚請試行之數人可也。盖人之材智器局大畧相同，唯有志者率其力之所不及，以趨其志之所欲就。故其受若直也，恒勉勉焉，惟恐或負。則其所望，寧小無大，寧卑無崇；而其所為也，寧拙無巧，寧久無速。誠得是人而任之，則所謂悃愊無華、歲計有餘者，於是而久任焉。秩當遷也，不移其地；祿當益也，不奪其官；過可畧也，不拘以文法之細；人可諒也，不間以毀譽之言。或璽書慰勉，以新其意；或就加服命，以旌其能。若果有效也，破格用之，異待之終身焉。彼速進者曰：「吾所進者在於格之内，而彼乃獨超于格之外，則彼之所謂遲者速，而吾之所謂速者遲矣。」故速不必沮也，自有權以遲之。不必遍行於
translation_en: … either. When a man of resolve receives even his first official appointment, he too wishes to put his abilities into practice with a view to lasting achievements. Yet those who advance rapidly can unsettle his intentions; this leaves the realm without men who sincerely work for the people. But how could the means of bringing about a change be fully explained in a single statement, or the change accomplished in a single day? I humbly propose that it would suffice to try this with a few men. People are broadly alike in talent, intelligence, capacity, and breadth of outlook. Only those with resolve press beyond the limits of their strength to pursue what their ambitions seek to accomplish. Thus, when receiving their remuneration [?], they constantly exert themselves, fearing only that they may fail their charge. In what they hope for, they prefer the small to the great and the lowly to the exalted; in what they do, they prefer plain effort to cleverness and sustained work to quick results. If such men can indeed be found and entrusted with office—men of whom it is said that they are sincere and unadorned, and that, reckoned over a year, their achievements are more than sufficient—then let them remain long in their posts. When their rank merits advancement, do not move them elsewhere; when their stipend merits increase, do not remove them from their office. When their faults can be overlooked, do not bind them with the minutiae of legal formalities; when the men deserve understanding, do not let words of praise or blame come between them and those who trust them. Sometimes comfort and encourage them with an imperial letter under seal, renewing their purpose; sometimes confer higher insignia and rank upon them in their existing posts, recognizing their ability. If they truly produce results, employ them beyond the prescribed rules and accord them exceptional treatment for the rest of their lives. Those who advance rapidly will say: “My advancement lies within the prescribed rules, whereas he alone rises beyond them. Thus, what was called his slowness is speed, and what was called my speed is slowness.” There is therefore no need to obstruct rapid advancement: there are means of making it comparatively slow. Nor need this practice be extended everywhere throughout …

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
郡縣而獨行之數人而亦已化矣於乎於
上下相安之時而輒倡以久任之說故必
有駭視改聽不安其位者愚請得以意而
試行之可乎今天下仕者水陸舟車之用
不同遷轉調更其喜好不同彼方與民相
安於北而復任之於南其不願必矣故於
此亦必有調停之法不拂其情而俾彼得
以終其惠此亦久任之意也雖然久任之
事在上不在下在近不在遠唯執事擇焉
===
第五問
仲選
同考試官教諭何批財賦
國家大計也古人制賦有成法節財有定論子能舉以為
今日足
國裕民之助而辭意和厚區處的確必有用之士也敬服敬服
考試官左諭德温批用古人意思處
今日時務一一若出自其口而讀之不厭者此對是也昔有補綴疏草
而復以上者子其得之乎

punctuated:
郡縣，而獨行之數人，而亦已化矣。於乎！於上下相安之時，而輒倡以久任之說，故必有駭視改聽、不安其位者。愚請得以意而試行之，可乎？今天下仕者，水陸舟車之用不同，遷轉調更，其喜好不同。彼方與民相安於北，而復任之於南，其不願必矣。故於此亦必有調停之法，不拂其情，而俾彼得以終其惠，此亦久任之意也。雖然，久任之事，在上不在下，在近不在遠，唯執事擇焉。

第五問
仲選

同考試官教諭何批：「財賦，國家大計也。古人制賦有成法，節財有定論。子能舉以為今日足國裕民之助，而辭意和厚，區處的確，必有用之士也。敬服！敬服！」

考試官左諭德温批：「用古人意思，處今日時務，一一若出自其口，而讀之不厭者，此對是也。昔有補綴疏草而復以上者，子其得之乎？」
translation_en:
…prefectures and counties; applying it to just a few men would already bring about a transformation. Alas! When superiors and subordinates are at ease with one another, suddenly to advocate prolonged tenure will surely cause some to look on in alarm, listen with changed attention, and feel unsettled in their posts. May I venture to ask whether this proposal might be tried? Officials throughout the realm today differ in their use of boats and carriages for travel by water and land, and their preferences concerning promotion and reassignment also differ. If a man is just now living harmoniously with the people in the north, but is then appointed to a post in the south, he will certainly be unwilling to go. Here, too, there must therefore be some means of accommodation, so that his wishes are not thwarted and he can fully carry through his beneficent work. This, too, accords with the purpose of prolonged tenure. Nevertheless, prolonged tenure is a matter for those above, not those below; for those near the throne, not those far away. It rests with you, honored sir, to choose.

Fifth Policy Question
Second Selection

Comment by Associate Examiner He, Instructor: “Revenue and taxation are great affairs of state. The ancients had established methods for setting taxes and settled principles for regulating expenditure. You can draw upon these to help provide sufficient resources for the state and prosperity for the people today. Your language and meaning are measured and generous, and your proposed arrangements precise and sound. You must surely be a man capable of useful service. My admiration! My admiration!”

Comment by Examiner Wen, Left Mentor: “To use the ideas of the ancients to address the practical affairs of today, making each point seem to come from their own mouths, yet remain a pleasure to read—this response accomplishes that. In former times there were those who pieced together draft memorials and submitted them anew to the throne. Have you perhaps mastered their art?”

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官侍講學士李批理財之道人人知之人人能
言之有考據有斷制有歸宿若此對者盖亦鮮矣敬
錄以
獻
對天下之計一家之計也天下之財吾與
天下共理之也故上不必益而下不必損
君不必富而民不必貧如家人父子然父
有之將以遺其子也子有之將以致之父
也而後天下之情一而天下之用足百志
===
成而禮俗刑矣古之人所以大過人者理
天下之財而天下不疑其利擅天下之有
而天下不疑其貪家人父子之謂也唐楊
炎言於德宗曰財賦者邦國之大本生人
之喉命天下治亂輕重繫焉而不可忽也
盖自古有天下者未有不善理財而足國
裕民者獨怪夫儒者諱言利而聚斂之臣
廼竊善理財之名卒使民日益窮而用日
益蹙古今之禍可鑒也孔子罕言利而損

對：天下之計，一家之計也。天下之財，吾與天下共理之也。故上不必益，而下不必損；君不必富，而民不必貧。如家人父子然，父有之，將以遺其子也；子有之，將以致之父也。而後天下之情一，而天下之用足，百志成而禮俗刑矣。古之人所以大過人者，理天下之財，而天下不疑其利；擅天下之有，而天下不疑其貪，家人父子之謂也。唐楊炎言於德宗曰：「財賦者，邦國之大本，生人之喉命，天下治亂輕重繫焉，而不可忽也。」盖自古有天下者，未有不善理財而足國裕民者。獨怪夫儒者諱言利，而聚斂之臣廼竊善理財之名，卒使民日益窮，而用日益蹙。古今之禍，可鑒也。孔子罕言利，而損
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Li, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: Everyone knows the principles of managing wealth, and everyone can speak of them. Yet answers like this one—with evidence, decisive judgments, and a clear conclusion—are surely rare. I respectfully transcribe it for presentation to the throne.

Answer: Planning for the realm is like planning for a single household. The wealth of the realm is something I administer together with all the people of the realm. Thus those above need not gain, nor those below lose; the ruler need not grow rich, nor the people become poor. It is like the relationship between father and son within a household: what the father possesses, he intends to leave to his son; what the son possesses, he intends to offer to his father. Only then will the sentiments of the realm be united, its needs amply supplied, its many aspirations fulfilled, and its rites and customs properly formed.

The reason the men of antiquity so greatly surpassed others was that they administered the wealth of the realm without anyone suspecting them of seeking personal profit, and commanded all its possessions without anyone suspecting them of greed. This is what is meant by treating people as father and son within a household. Yang Yan of the Tang said to Emperor Dezong: “Revenue is the great foundation of the state and the very lifeline of the people. The order or disorder of the realm, and the gravity of its condition, depend upon it; it must not be neglected.” Since antiquity, no ruler of the realm has ever supplied the state adequately and enriched the people without managing wealth well. What is especially strange is that scholars shun speaking of profit, while ministers who exact wealth from the people usurp the reputation of being skilled financial administrators, ultimately making the people poorer by the day and resources ever more constrained. The calamities of past and present offer a warning. Confucius seldom spoke of profit, yet reducing…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
上益下自易發之孟子不言利曰無政事
則財用不足大學生財之道固即周官理
財之道也周官理財之道固即利用厚生
之說也聖賢何嘗不理財乎為民理之為
天下理之而不為巳也嘗考周官以九賦
斂財賄以九式均節財用以九貢致邦國
之用冢宰制其出司徒制其入其出也固
以稽其入也其入也固以稽其出也上無
侈心下無蔽奸法莫有善於此者彼安石
===
何人廼欲倣之而行新法其意不過為人
主斂財耳然卒以之而禍國家盖非周官
之過用之者之過也彼周官未作之前禹
貢任土作貢田賦什而稅一公田藉而不
稅制用必於歲杪夏殷之制可考也周官
既作之後一變而為春秋再變而為戰國
理財之法雖不可得而詳而有若對哀公
之數語孟子與齊梁君之問答而其時可
知矣秦孝公開阡陌盡地力至始皇而其

translation_en:
…taking from those above to benefit those below was expounded in the Book of Changes. Although Mengzi did not speak of profit, he said: “Without proper government, financial resources will be insufficient.” The way of producing wealth in the Great Learning is precisely the way of managing finances in the Offices of Zhou; the way of managing finances in the Offices of Zhou is precisely the teaching of making resources useful and enriching the people's livelihood. When did the sages and worthies ever fail to manage finances? They managed them for the people and for all under Heaven, not for themselves. Examining the Offices of Zhou, we find that the nine levies collected wealth and goods, the nine expenditure standards apportioned and regulated spending, and the nine tributes supplied resources from the regional states. The Minister of State controlled expenditure, and the Minister of Education controlled revenue. Expenditure was assessed against revenue, and revenue against expenditure. Above, there was no desire for extravagance; below, there was no concealment or fraud. No system could be better than this. Who was that Anshi, that he should presume to imitate it and implement his New Policies? His intention was merely to amass wealth for the ruler, yet in the end he thereby brought calamity upon the state. This was not the fault of the Offices of Zhou, but of the man who employed it.
Before the Offices of Zhou was composed, the Tribute of Yu prescribed tribute according to the land's capacities. The land levy took one part in ten; public fields were cultivated through obligatory labor rather than taxed, and expenditure was determined at year's end. The institutions of Xia and Yin can thus be examined. After the Offices of Zhou was composed, institutions changed first into those of the Spring and Autumn period and then into those of the Warring States. Although their methods of financial management cannot be known in detail, the circumstances of those times can be understood from You Ruo's few words in reply to Duke Ai and from Mengzi's exchanges with the rulers of Qi and Liang. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
賦益重盖二十倍於周矣漢懲秦弊田租
什五而稅一加以高惠之寬仁文景之恭
儉固宜有錢朽而不可校粟腐而不可食
矣柰之何武帝好大喜功有以盡耗之哉
隋文帝躬脩節儉益免田租至煬帝而賦
役繁重百姓始不勝怨矣唐承隋後口分
世業租庸調之法府衛兵之制無不善者
永淳以後賦役並起又繼以天寶之驕奢
如之何其不壞哉宋之理財也版部有左
===

使磨勘有司會計有錄祥符天禧之時可

於紹興以後之妄費而用不可支矣抑愚

賦益重，盖二十倍於周矣。漢懲秦弊，田租什五而稅一，加以高惠之寬仁、文景之恭儉，固宜有錢朽而不可校、粟腐而不可食矣。柰之何武帝好大喜功，有以盡耗之哉！隋文帝躬脩節儉，益免田租，至煬帝而賦役繁重，百姓始不勝怨矣。唐承隋後，口分、世業、租庸調之法，府衛兵之制，無不善者。永淳以後，賦役並起，又繼以天寶之驕奢，如之何其不壞哉！宋之理財也，版部有左計，有右計，有總計；其後三司有使，度支有使，磨勘有司，會計有錄。祥符、天禧之時，可謂盛矣。然一壞於熈寧君臣之變更，再壞於紹興以後之妄費，而用不可支矣。

抑愚嘗有考焉：三代授人以田，而未有戶賦；兩漢不授人以田，而輕其戶賦；魏至唐中葉，則因授田之名而重其戶賦；至宋熈寧以後，則日新月盛，賦日益增，而民日益困，國日益危矣。其間喜事之臣，如王銍有歲進
translation_en:
…taxation became still heavier, reaching some twenty times that of the Zhou. Taking warning from the abuses of the Qin, the Han levied a land tax of one part in fifteen. With the further benefits of the leniency and benevolence of Emperors Gao and Hui and the reverence and frugality of Emperors Wen and Jing, it was only natural that money accumulated until its strings rotted and it could no longer be counted, and grain until it spoiled and could no longer be eaten. How could Emperor Wu, with his fondness for grand undertakings and his craving for achievements, have exhausted it all! Emperor Wen of the Sui personally practiced frugality and further remitted the land tax. Under Emperor Yang, however, taxes and labor services became so burdensome that the common people could no longer contain their resentment. Succeeding the Sui, the Tang established regulations for individually allotted and hereditary fields and for the grain tax, labor-service commutation, and household levy, together with the system of militia and guard troops; all were sound. After the Yongchun era, taxes and labor services multiplied together, followed by the arrogance and extravagance of the Tianbao era. How could the system have failed to collapse! In the Song's management of finance, the revenue administration had Left Accounting, Right Accounting, and General Accounting offices. Later, the State Finance Commission had a commissioner, expenditure had a commissioner, auditing had responsible offices, and accounting had records. In the Xiangfu and Tianxi eras, this could be called a flourishing system. Yet it was first undermined by the changes made by ruler and ministers during the Xining era, and undermined again by reckless spending from the Shaoxing era onward, until expenditure could no longer be sustained.

I, in my humble judgment, have also examined this matter: under the Three Dynasties, people were allotted land, but there was no household tax. Under the two Han dynasties, people were not allotted land, but their household taxes were light. From the Wei through the middle of the Tang, the allocation of land became a pretext for imposing heavy household taxes. From the Song's Xining era onward, new exactions arose daily and multiplied monthly: taxes increased day by day, the people grew ever more distressed, and the state ever more imperiled. Among the ministers eager to undertake such projects were men such as Wang Zhi [?], who made annual contributions…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
韋皐有日進李兼有月進裴肅有刺史
進蕭綬有判官之進盖唐元宗德宗方屈
意於聚財故鉷皐兼肅之徒得以利而誘
之其後兵革繼起禍亂相仍朱泚之難竟
不能以內藏而助一鐼有瓊林大盈之積
何益哉宋亦有之封椿庫置於太祖景福
庫置於太宗其後神宗又更景福庫名自
製詩以揭之是亦內藏也然軍興賞賚則
用之水旱災傷則用之三司用乏則助之

百萬緡當問契丹贖幽薊又曰用絹二十
疋募一胡人首其意如此是非若唐人之
私用矣然以愚言之天子者有天下際天

translation_en:
…Wei Gao made daily contributions, Li Jian monthly contributions, Pei Su contributions as Prefect, and Xiao Shou contributions as Administrative Assistant. Because Emperors Yuanzong and Dezong of Tang were then willing to stoop to accumulating wealth, men such as Hong, Gao, Jian, and Su could entice them with profit. Thereafter, warfare broke out repeatedly and calamity followed upon disorder. During Zhu Ci’s rebellion, the inner treasury ultimately failed to contribute even a single coin [?]. What benefit, then, was there in the accumulated wealth of the Qionglin and Daying treasuries?

The Song also had such institutions. The Fengchun Treasury was established under Taizu, and the Jingfu Treasury under Taizong. Later, Shenzong renamed the Jingfu Treasury and personally composed a poem to display there. These, too, were inner treasuries. Yet their funds were used for rewards when armies were mobilized and for relief when floods or droughts caused devastation. They supplemented the funds of the State Finance Commission when these were insufficient, and likewise supplied the various circuits when their funds ran short. Emperor Taizu of Song once said: “When the money reaches five million strings of cash, I shall ask the Khitan to let us redeem You and Ji.” He also said: “Offer twenty bolts of silk as a bounty for the head of each Hu tribesman.” Such was his intention; this was unlike the private uses to which Tang rulers put their funds.

Yet in my humble opinion, the Son of Heaven possesses all under Heaven: to the limits of the sky and the shores of the seas, nothing is outside his possession. Why, then, must he maintain an inner treasury? Precisely because it is designated an inner treasury, the chief councilors cannot regulate its receipts and expenditures through the prescribed tribute assessments, and the revenue officials cannot audit its holdings and deficiencies through the account books. Established to provide for private enjoyment, it is depleted day by day and month by month, until it no longer suffices even for the ruler’s own needs. 取廉譬之小民之家方其平時所望不過
十金計其衣食妻子之費出入於十金之
中而亦已足矣及其稍富也意之所欲者
日以漸廣所入日益衆所欲日益不足不
知罪其用之不節而獨以為求之未至也
是以富而愈奢奢而愈貧嗚呼此愚所謂
天下之計一家之計也天下之財吾與天
下共理之而已善乎蘇軾之言曰為國有
三計三年耕必有一年之蓄以三十年之
===
通計可以九年而無飢歲之所入足用而
有餘是以九年之蓄常閒而無用此萬世
之計也其不能者一歲之入纔足以供一
歲之出天下之產僅足以供天下之用此
一時之計也其最下者量出以為入用之
不給取之益多天下晏然無大患難而盡
用衰世苟且之法不知有急何以加之此
不終月之計也以愚言之自古人君何嘗
不欲為萬世之計哉自井田之法壞寓兵

translation_en:
…and taking little. Consider the household of an ordinary person. In ordinary circumstances, his expectations amount to no more than ten units of gold. He reckons the expenses of clothing, food, wife, and children, keeping receipts and expenditures within those ten units, and finds this sufficient. Once he becomes somewhat wealthy, however, his desires gradually expand day by day. His income increases daily, yet falls ever further short of satisfying his desires. He does not blame his lack of restraint in spending, but thinks only that he has not sought enough. Thus, the richer he becomes, the more extravagant he grows; the more extravagant, the poorer. Alas! This is what I mean when I say that managing the realm’s finances is like managing a household’s. The wealth of the realm is simply something that I administer together with all under Heaven.
How well Su Shi put it: “There are three ways of planning a state’s finances. Three years of cultivation must yield reserves sufficient for one year. Reckoned over thirty years, these can sustain nine years without hunger. Annual receipts suffice for expenditure and leave a surplus, so the nine years’ reserves remain continually untouched and unused. This is a plan for ten thousand generations. Those unable to achieve this have annual receipts barely sufficient to meet annual expenditure, while the realm’s production barely suffices for its needs. This is a plan for the present alone. The worst approach is to determine revenue according to expenditure: when resources do not cover spending, ever more is extracted. Though the realm is peaceful and faces no great calamity, all the expedient measures of an age of decline are employed. No one knows how further demands could be met if an emergency arose. This is a plan that cannot last out a month.” In my humble view, when, since antiquity, have rulers ever not wished to plan for ten thousand generations? title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
於農之意失而養兵之費多矣自封建之
法壞郡縣天下之制立而供官之費多矣
况兵養於平時者不可得用而所費以給
之者又非可用之兵官建於制額者其祿
有常而所費以給之者率非有制之設故
蘇轍有曰方今之計莫如豐財非求財而
益之也去其害財者而已曰冗官也曰冗
兵也曰冗費也朱子有曰天下國家之大
務莫大於恤民恤民之實在省賦省賦之
===
實在治軍治軍省賦以為恤民之本則又
在人君正心術以立紀綱蓋心術正紀綱
立則大學之生財周官之理財大易損上
益下之說特有天下者治用之一事耳雖
有水旱盜賊邊防之擾又何足為意哉書
生與聞邦國之大計嫌於出位唯執事進
教之幸甚

punctuated: 於農之意失，而養兵之費多矣。自封建之法壞，郡縣天下之制立，而供官之費多矣。况兵養於平時者不可得用，而所費以給之者又非可用之兵；官建於制額者，其祿有常，而所費以給之者率非有制之設。故蘇轍有曰：「方今之計，莫如豐財，非求財而益之也，去其害財者而已：曰冗官也，曰冗兵也，曰冗費也。」朱子有曰：「天下國家之大務，莫大於恤民。恤民之實在省賦，省賦之實在治軍。治軍省賦，以為恤民之本，則又在人君正心術以立紀綱。」蓋心術正、紀綱立，則《大學》之生財、《周官》之理財、《大易》損上益下之說，特有天下者治用之一事耳。雖有水旱、盜賊、邊防之擾，又何足為意哉！書生與聞邦國之大計，嫌於出位，唯執事進教之，幸甚。
translation_en:
…the intention of embedding soldiers among the farmers was lost, and the expense of maintaining troops grew. Once the system of enfeoffment broke down and the system of governing all under Heaven through commanderies and counties was established, the expense of supporting officials likewise grew. Moreover, troops maintained in peacetime cannot be put to use: those whose support consumes these funds are not serviceable soldiers. Officials appointed within the authorized establishment have fixed stipends, yet those whose support consumes these funds are generally appointees outside that establishment. Thus Su Zhe said: “For present purposes, nothing is better than making resources abundant. This does not mean seeking wealth to increase them, but simply removing what depletes them: redundant officials, redundant troops, and redundant expenditure.” Master Zhu said: “Among the great tasks of governing the realm, none is greater than caring for the people. The substance of caring for the people lies in reducing taxation; the substance of reducing taxation lies in putting the army in order. To put the army in order and reduce taxation as the foundation of caring for the people depends, in turn, upon the ruler rectifying his heart and intentions so as to establish the governing principles and discipline of the state.”

Once the ruler’s heart and intentions are rectified and governing principles and discipline established, the teachings on producing wealth in the Great Learning, on managing wealth in the Offices of Zhou, and on diminishing those above to benefit those below in the Book of Changes become simply one aspect of the ruler’s management of expenditure. Even if there are disturbances from floods and droughts, bandits, or frontier defense, what cause would there be for concern? For a mere scholar to take part in deliberations on the great plans of the state may seem to overstep his station. I would count myself most fortunate if you, honored examiners, would offer me instruction.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Today, any scholar in the empire who seeks to distinguish himself through talent and accomplishments aspires to selection for office. The instruction given by fathers and teachers, and the talent that local communities seek and nurture, likewise frequently have this as their aim. Our dynasty treats scholars with great generosity and has made its method of selection uniform. It is therefore fitting that scholars should be settled in their aspirations and alike in their habits and customs.

Under the selection system of the Zhou at its height, responsibility rested with local communities, for these were the source of public judgment. Under the Han, responsibility sometimes rested with commanderies and kingdoms, ranked marquises, and officials of the two-thousand-bushel rank; sometimes it rested with the Three Dukes, the Chamberlain for Attendants, censors, the Metropolitan Commandant, and regional governors. Candidates were recommended under such categories as Flourishing Talent, Filial and Incorrupt, Understanding the Classics, and Worthy and Good, Capable of Forthright Remonstrance. title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
士進士制舉諸科宋亦有明
經詩賦進士制科其舉也或
間歲一行之或三歲一行之
或因災異而舉或遣使循行
而舉其在當時固已患乎多
岐而莫之鄉矣我
國家選舉之法獨仍成周之意
===
其在諸藩以諸藩舉在
兩畿以兩畿舉其期必以三歲
其取也必先經術他如賢良
方正經明行脩諸舉亦皆興
廢不常而亦不能有加乎常
舉之右夫法專則士有恒業
舉之者按業而考焉用之者

translation_en:
…outstanding scholars, metropolitan graduates (jinshi), and the various special examinations held by imperial decree. The Song likewise had examinations for elucidating the classics, metropolitan graduates in poetry and rhapsody, and special examinations by imperial decree. These selections were held sometimes every other year, sometimes once every three years; sometimes candidates were recommended in response to calamities and anomalies, and sometimes envoys were dispatched on inspection tours to recommend them. Even at the time, the multiplicity of paths was already considered a problem, leaving scholars unsure which way to turn.

Our dynasty’s method of selecting officials alone preserves the intent of the Zhou order at its maturity. Those in the provinces are selected through their respective provinces; those in the two metropolitan regions are selected through their respective metropolitan regions. The interval is invariably three years, and selection invariably gives priority to learning in the classics. Other forms of recommendation, such as those for the Worthy and Good, Upright and Correct, and for those Well Versed in the Classics and of Cultivated Conduct, have been instituted and discontinued irregularly; nor have they been able to surpass the regular examinations. When the method is uniform, scholars have a constant course of study. Those who select them examine them according to that learning; those who employ them…

punctuated: 一之者也。士苟不得於此，有自悔而終廢者，是曷敢弗慎且懼乎？不惟負今日之人才，抑恐有負他日之任用。凡臣等今日之責，固皆以人事君之事也。舉既得矣，錄既成矣，春官得而試焉，臨軒得而試焉，用人者得以次而舉焉。是今日之文字，固他日之課績；今日之名氏，固他日之勳階爵里也。其屢試弗舉，自悔而終廢者，國家固弗得而用之矣。是曷敢弗慎且懼乎？夫以羣材衆藝
translation_en: …unite them into one. If a scholar fails to gain selection here, some may reproach themselves and abandon their pursuits forever. How, then, could we dare to be anything but cautious and apprehensive? We would not only fail the talented men of today; we fear we would also fail to provide for appointments in years to come. All the responsibilities borne today by us, your servants, are indeed matters of serving the sovereign by furnishing him with men of talent. Those to be recommended have now been selected, and the record has been completed. The Ministry of Rites may now examine them; the emperor, presiding in person, may examine them; and those responsible for appointments may promote them in due order. Thus, today’s writings will become the basis for tomorrow’s assessments of achievement; today’s names will become tomorrow’s record of merit ranks, noble titles, and native places. As for those who repeatedly sit the examination without being selected, reproach themselves, and finally abandon their pursuits, the state will indeed be unable to employ them. How, then, could we dare to be anything but cautious and apprehensive? Now, with so many talents and so many accomplishments…

title: 正德十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
千百其多獨寄去取於數人
焉此
上以精擇責我也精擇之固欲得
人有效於世也是凡有我之
責固皆諸士子之責也仁和於
錄之成能勿以此意為諸士
子勗哉
===
奉訓大夫左春坊左諭德兼
翰林院侍讀温仁和謹序

punctuated:
千百其多，獨寄去取於數人焉，此上以精擇責我也。精擇之，固欲得人有效於世也。是凡有我之責，固皆諸士子之責也。仁和於錄之成，能勿以此意為諸士子勗哉？

奉訓大夫、左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍讀温仁和謹序。
translation_en:
…numbering in their hundreds and thousands, yet the decision to reject or select them is entrusted to just a few men. In this, His Majesty charges us with making a discerning selection. Such selection is surely intended to obtain men who will render effective service to the world. Thus, every responsibility incumbent upon us is also a responsibility incumbent upon all you candidates. As this record is completed, how could I, Renhe, fail to offer these thoughts as encouragement to you all?

Preface respectfully written by Wen Renhe, Grand Master for Instruction, Left Mentor of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy.
